scenarios.misconception: ketone bodies in a fast make the blood acidic
scenarios.setup: A hiker is lost in the mountains with water but no food. Compare her on day 3 with the morning after her last meal, when she had fasted only overnight.
scenarios.start: No food for three days

steps.gone: Liver glycogen is used up within about a day
steps.ins: Insulin falls further; glucagon and cortisol rise
steps.gng: All new glucose must come from gluconeogenesis
steps.fa: Fatty acids flood into the liver
steps.buf: A little insulin still limits fat release, and buffers take up the H+

variables.name: Liver glycogen
variables.why: Liver glycogen holds only about 100 g, which the brain and other tissues use up within about 24 hours without food.

variables.name: Blood insulin
variables.why: With no glucose coming from the gut or from glycogen, blood glucose drifts down and beta cells release less insulin, while glucagon and cortisol rise.

variables.name: Share of the liver’s glucose made by gluconeogenesis
variables.why: After an overnight fast, about half the glucose leaving the liver comes from glycogen. Once glycogen is gone, all of it must be made new, mostly from muscle amino acids.

variables.name: Lipolysis in adipose tissue
variables.why: Insulin is the brake on lipolysis. As it falls, and cortisol and growth hormone rise, stored fat is broken down faster.

variables.name: Blood ketone bodies
variables.why: Fatty acids reach the liver faster than its citric acid cycle can burn the acetyl CoA, so it makes ketone bodies, which rise over the first week.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: This is ketosis, not ketoacidosis. A little insulin is still present and limits fat release, so ketone bodies stay at a few mmol/L and the body’s buffers take up their H+.

scenarios.title: A long fast: day 3, then week 3
scenarios.misconception: the brain can use only glucose, so a fast always eats up muscle at the same rate
scenarios.setup: A man with normal fat stores takes part in a supervised fast with water only. Follow him from the first days to three weeks in.

stages.label: Day 3
stages.prompt: Day 3, compared with the morning after his last meal.
stages.start: Liver glycogen is gone

steps.gng: The liver makes all new glucose by gluconeogenesis
steps.aa: Amino acids come mainly from breaking down muscle protein
steps.need: The brain still needs about 120 g of glucose a day
steps.kb: The liver begins making ketone bodies

variables.name: Muscle protein broken down per day
variables.why: Glycerol and lactate cannot supply enough glucose, so most comes from amino acids. Cortisol drives the breakdown of about 75 g of muscle protein a day.

variables.name: Glucose made from amino acids
variables.why: With glycogen gone, gluconeogenesis must supply all the glucose, and amino acids are its largest source this early in the fast.

variables.name: Glucose used by the brain
variables.why: Ketone bodies are only starting to rise, and the brain burns little fatty acid, so it still depends on about 120 g of glucose a day.

variables.name: Blood ketone bodies
variables.why: Low insulin lets fatty acids flood into the liver, which makes ketone bodies from the extra acetyl CoA.

stages.label: Week 3
stages.prompt: Three weeks in, compared with day 3.
stages.start: Ketone bodies have risen to several mmol/L

steps.take: The brain takes up ketone bodies in proportion to their level
steps.share: Ketone bodies supply about two thirds of the brain’s energy
steps.less: The brain needs only about 40 g of glucose a day
steps.spare: Less amino acid is needed to make glucose
steps.prot: Muscle protein breakdown falls to about 20 g a day
steps.urea: Less nitrogen has to be turned into urea
steps.thy: Active thyroid hormone and sympathetic activity fall

variables.name: Ketone bodies burned by the brain
variables.why: Ketone bodies cross into the brain and are taken up in proportion to their blood level, so as they climb the brain burns more of them.

variables.name: Glucose used by the brain
variables.why: Every bit of energy the brain gets from ketone bodies is energy it no longer needs from glucose, so its need falls from about 120 g to about 40 g a day.

variables.name: Muscle protein broken down per day
variables.why: With less glucose to make, less amino acid is needed, so the breakdown of muscle protein falls. This protein sparing is what lets a fast last about two months.

variables.name: Urea made each day
variables.why: The nitrogen removed from amino acids leaves as urea. With fewer amino acids broken down, less urea is made.

variables.name: Energy used at rest
variables.why: Levels of active thyroid hormone and sympathetic activity fall during a long fast, so the body spends less energy at rest and its stores last longer.

scenarios.title: Training hard on a hot, humid day
scenarios.theme: exercising on a hot humid day
scenarios.misconception: more sweat always means more cooling
scenarios.setup: A soccer player trains hard for an hour at 34 °C in humid, still air and drinks nothing. Compare her late in the session with the first minutes.
scenarios.start: Working muscles release heat

steps.drip: Much of the sweat drips off instead of evaporating
steps.core: Heat gain outruns heat loss; core temperature rises
steps.sens: Temperature-sensitive neurons in the hypothalamus and warm thermoreceptors in the skin fire more
steps.poa: The preoptic area drives heat-loss responses
steps.chol: Sympathetic cholinergic nerves act on skin vessels and sweat glands
steps.loss: Water and salt are lost in sweat
steps.pool: Blood pools in the widened skin vessels
steps.vr: Less blood returns to the heart
steps.hr: Heart rate rises to hold cardiac output
steps.gut: Gut and kidney vessels narrow, shifting blood toward the skin

variables.name: Core temperature
variables.why: Near 34 °C the air is almost as warm as skin, so radiation and convection remove little heat and evaporation is the main route left. Humid air slows it, so heat made by the muscles builds up.

variables.name: Share of the sweat that evaporates
variables.why: Humid air can take up only a limited amount of vapor. As her sweat rate climbs past that limit, a growing share drips off instead of evaporating, and dripping sweat removes almost no heat.

variables.name: Blood flow through the skin
variables.why: In hairy skin, active dilation by sympathetic cholinergic nerves widens the vessels, bringing warm blood from the core to the surface.

variables.name: Sweat rate
variables.why: Acetylcholine from sympathetic cholinergic fibers drives the eccrine sweat glands harder as core temperature climbs, up to 1 to 2 L an hour.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Sweat is made from the extracellular fluid, and she drinks nothing to replace it, so plasma volume shrinks.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: A large share of the blood sits in the wide skin vessels, and plasma volume is falling, so less blood returns to fill the heart and each beat ejects less.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Baroreceptor reflexes and the demands of exercise raise heart rate as stroke volume falls, to keep cardiac output up for both the muscles and the skin.

variables.name: Blood flow to the gut and kidneys
variables.why: Heat stress and exercise narrow the vessels of the gut and kidneys, which frees blood for the skin and working muscles.

scenarios.title: Falling into a cold lake
scenarios.misconception: narrowing the skin vessels stops heat loss
scenarios.setup: A kayaker capsizes into a 10 °C lake and clings to the boat. Compare the first ten minutes in the water with the moment before he fell in.
scenarios.start: Cold water surrounds the skin

steps.therm: Cold thermoreceptors in the skin fire more
steps.poa: The preoptic area drives heat-gain responses before the core has cooled
steps.ne: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto skin arterioles
steps.flow: Less warm blood reaches the skin
steps.shiv: Muscles contract out of step; their energy becomes heat
steps.bat: Norepinephrine makes brown fat cells leak H+ in their mitochondria
steps.fast: Water carries heat away about 25 times faster than air
steps.loss: Heat loss rises despite the narrowed vessels
steps.sw: Sweating stays at its resting level

variables.name: Blood flow through the skin
variables.why: Norepinephrine narrows the skin arterioles, so less warm blood reaches the surface and the shell becomes insulation for the core.

variables.name: Heat made by skeletal muscle
variables.why: Shivering contractions do no outside work, so almost all their energy becomes heat, raising heat production several times over.

variables.name: Heat made by brown adipose tissue
variables.why: Brown fat mitochondria let H+ leak back through a channel protein, so the electron transport chain runs flat out and the energy leaves as heat instead of ATP.

variables.name: Heat lost from the body
variables.why: Water removes heat by conduction and convection far faster than air, so even with the skin vessels narrowed, he loses heat much faster than before.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: The control center is driving heat-gain responses, not heat-loss ones, so the sympathetic cholinergic drive to the sweat glands does not rise.

scenarios.title: A diet: the first week, then six months
scenarios.misconception: a steady 500 kcal daily deficit takes off weight at the same rate forever
scenarios.setup: A woman who spends about 2,200 kcal a day starts eating 1,700 kcal a day and keeps it up. Follow her body over the first week and then over months.

stages.label: The first week
stages.prompt: The end of the first week, compared with before the diet.
stages.start: Intake falls 500 kcal a day below spending

steps.draw: Stores are drawn on to cover the gap
steps.gly: Glycogen is used, and the water stored with it is lost
steps.wt: Weight falls faster than the fat loss alone

variables.name: Glycogen stores
variables.why: Part of each day’s gap is covered from glycogen in liver and muscle, which runs down in the first days of a deficit.

variables.name: Body fat
variables.why: Intake is below spending, so lipolysis releases stored fat to cover the rest of the gap.

variables.name: Body weight
variables.why: Glycogen is stored with several times its weight of water, so the first week’s loss is larger than 3,500 kcal per pound would predict.

stages.label: After six months
stages.prompt: After six months on the same diet, compared with the first weeks.
stages.start: She has lost fat and weight

steps.sp: A smaller body spends less energy to maintain and move
steps.gap: The gap between intake and spending narrows

variables.name: Blood leptin
variables.why: Fat cells release leptin in proportion to how much fat they hold, so leptin falls as fat is lost.

variables.name: Hunger
variables.why: Falling leptin signals the hypothalamus that stores are shrinking, and the neurons that drive hunger win out.

variables.name: Total energy spending per day
variables.why: A lighter body costs less to maintain and to move, so her total metabolic rate falls.

variables.name: Rate of weight loss
variables.why: She still eats 1,700 kcal, but now spends less, so the daily deficit shrinks and loss slows toward a new, lower stable weight. That is why 3,500 kcal per pound overestimates loss over months.

scenarios.title: A blocked bile duct and the fat-soluble vitamins
scenarios.misconception: all vitamins are absorbed the same way
scenarios.setup: A gallstone blocks a woman’s common bile duct, and she is not treated for several weeks. Compare her then with before the blockage.
scenarios.start: No bile reaches the duodenum

steps.fsv: Fat-soluble vitamins, dissolved in the fat, are poorly absorbed
steps.k: Vitamin K stores, which last only days to weeks, run down
steps.fac: The liver cannot finish clotting factors II, VII, IX and X
steps.wsv: Water-soluble vitamins cross by carriers without bile

variables.name: Fat absorbed from food
variables.why: Bile salts form the micelles that carry the products of fat digestion to the absorptive cells. Without them, much of the fat is not absorbed.

variables.name: Fat in the stool
variables.why: Fat that is not absorbed passes on to the colon and leaves in the stool, which becomes pale, greasy and bulky.

variables.name: Vitamin K absorbed
variables.why: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and are absorbed with it in micelles, so they are lost along with the fat.

variables.name: Time for blood to clot
variables.why: Vitamin K stores last only days to weeks. Without it, an enzyme in the liver cannot add the carboxyl groups that let factors II, VII, IX and X bind calcium, so clotting slows.

variables.name: Vitamin C absorbed
variables.why: Vitamin C is water-soluble. It crosses the intestinal lining by carriers straight into the blood and does not need bile.

scenarios.title: Three months without vitamin C
scenarios.misconception: vitamins are a source of energy
scenarios.setup: A man living alone on tea, toast and canned food has eaten no fruit or vegetables, and no vitamin C, for three months. Compare him now with before.
scenarios.start: The small vitamin C store runs out

steps.fe: The iron in the collagen-strengthening enzymes is no longer kept in its active form
steps.enz: The enzymes stop adding hydroxyl groups to new collagen
steps.weak: New collagen is weak and is broken down
steps.brui: Small vessels break: bruises and bleeding gums
steps.heal: Wounds heal poorly and old scars reopen
steps.iron: Plant iron is not kept in its easily absorbed form
steps.abs: Less iron is absorbed from plant foods

variables.name: Activity of the enzymes that strengthen new collagen
variables.why: These enzymes hold an iron atom that must stay in its reduced form, and vitamin C keeps it that way. Without it, the enzymes stop working.

variables.name: Strength of newly made collagen
variables.why: Without its added hydroxyl groups, new collagen cannot form stable triple helices or cross-link, so it is weak and is broken down.

variables.name: Bruising and bleeding gums
variables.why: Collagen is always being replaced, so the walls of small vessels weaken as old collagen is replaced by weak collagen, and they break easily.

variables.name: Rate of wound healing
variables.why: Healing lays down new collagen, which is now too weak to hold, so new wounds do not heal and old scars can reopen.

variables.name: Iron absorbed from plant foods
variables.why: Vitamin C eaten with a meal keeps plant iron in the form the intestine takes up best, so without it less plant iron is absorbed.

variables.name: Energy he gets from his food
variables.why: Vitamins are not fuel: vitamin C adds no kilocalories, so losing it does not change the energy his food supplies.

scenarios.title: The afferent arterioles constrict
scenarios.misconception: narrowing any kidney arteriole lowers filtration in the same way
scenarios.setup: A drug makes the smooth muscle of the afferent arterioles in both kidneys contract hard. Blood pressure in the aorta does not change. Predict the kidneys a few minutes later, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: The afferent arterioles narrow

steps.res: Resistance upstream of the glomerulus rises
steps.rbf: Less blood flows through the kidney
steps.gbhp: More pressure is lost before the glomerulus: GBHP falls
steps.ff: Plasma flow and GFR fall by about the same share
steps.ptc: Less pressure is left for the peritubular capillaries
steps.md: Less NaCl reaches the macula densa
steps.urine: Less filtrate means less urine

variables.name: Renal blood flow
variables.why: Flow = pressure gradient ÷ resistance. The aortic pressure is unchanged, but the narrowed arterioles add resistance, so less blood gets through the kidney.

variables.name: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (GBHP)
variables.why: The narrowing sits upstream of the glomerulus, so more of the pressure is used up in the afferent arteriole and less of it reaches the glomerular capillaries.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: GBHP is the only pressure pushing fluid out. With CHP and BCOP unchanged, a lower GBHP shrinks the net filtration pressure, and GFR = Kf × NFP falls with it.

variables.name: Filtration fraction
variables.why: Afferent constriction lowers both the plasma reaching the glomerulus and the fluid filtered from it, by roughly the same share, so the fraction filtered stays about the same. Efferent constriction is the one that raises it.

variables.name: Hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries
variables.why: The peritubular capillaries lie downstream of both arterioles. More pressure lost in the afferent arteriole leaves less for them.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: With less filtrate flowing through the tubule, less NaCl reaches the macula densa, which signals the juxtaglomerular cells to release more renin. Lower pressure at those cells adds to the same signal.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Every drop of urine starts as filtrate. With GFR lower, less fluid enters the tubules, and less comes out the end.

scenarios.title: The efferent arterioles constrict
scenarios.misconception: constricting a kidney arteriole always lowers GFR
scenarios.setup: A drug moderately narrows the efferent arterioles of both kidneys and has no other effect. Aortic pressure does not change. Predict the kidneys a few minutes later, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: The efferent arterioles narrow moderately

steps.res: Resistance downstream of the glomerulus rises
steps.rbf: Less blood flows through the kidney
steps.back: Pressure backs up behind the narrowing
steps.gfr: Net filtration pressure and GFR rise
steps.ff: A larger share of the plasma reaching the glomerulus is filtered
steps.prot: Proteins left behind become more concentrated
steps.ptc: Less pressure is left for the peritubular capillaries
steps.cop: Protein-rich blood enters the peritubular capillaries

variables.name: Renal blood flow
variables.why: Any added resistance in series with the kidney’s vessels lowers flow through them, wherever the narrowing sits.

variables.name: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (GBHP)
variables.why: The narrowing is downstream of the glomerulus, like pinching a garden hose past the nozzle: pressure builds up in the capillaries before it.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: Higher GBHP raises the net filtration pressure. With moderate constriction this outweighs the fall in blood flow, so GFR rises. Severe constriction slows flow so much that BCOP climbs along the capillary and GFR falls instead.

variables.name: Filtration fraction
variables.why: GFR rises while renal plasma flow falls, so GFR ÷ plasma flow rises.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure at the efferent end of the glomerulus
variables.why: More protein-free fluid leaves each milliliter of plasma, so the proteins left in the capillary are more concentrated by the time blood leaves it.

variables.name: Hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries
variables.why: Blood has passed an even higher resistance before reaching the peritubular capillaries, so less pressure is left there.

variables.name: Colloid osmotic pressure in the peritubular capillaries
variables.why: The protein-rich blood leaving the glomerulus flows straight into the peritubular capillaries, and its stronger oncotic pull draws reabsorbed fluid into them.

scenarios.title: A stone blocks one ureter
scenarios.misconception: a blockage below the kidney cannot change how much the kidney filters
scenarios.setup: A small stone lodges where the left ureter enters the bladder and blocks it completely. The right ureter is open. Predict the left kidney an hour later, compared with before.
scenarios.start: Urine cannot leave the left ureter

steps.back: Urine backs up into the left renal pelvis and tubules
steps.chp: Capsular hydrostatic pressure (CHP) rises in the left kidney
steps.nfp: Net filtration pressure falls in the left kidney
steps.gfr: GFR of the left kidney falls
steps.right: The right kidney’s pressures are unchanged

variables.name: Capsular hydrostatic pressure in the left kidney
variables.why: Fluid still enters the capsules but cannot drain, so it builds pressure all the way back from the ureter to the capsular space.

variables.name: Net filtration pressure in the left kidney
variables.why: NFP = GBHP − (CHP + BCOP). CHP pushes back against filtration, so when it rises NFP falls: from 15 to 22 mm Hg drops NFP from about 10 to 3.

variables.name: GFR of the left kidney
variables.why: GFR = Kf × NFP, so a lower net filtration pressure means less filtrate. Less NaCl then reaches the macula densa, so tubuloglomerular feedback widens the afferent arteriole a little and GBHP rises slightly, but that only partly offsets the rise in CHP.

variables.name: GFR of the right kidney
variables.why: The right ureter drains normally, so its capsular pressure and filtration are unchanged.

scenarios.title: An ACE inhibitor with narrowed renal arteries
scenarios.misconception: a drug that lowers blood pressure always protects the kidney
scenarios.setup: Both of a man’s renal arteries are narrowed by plaque, so less pressure reaches his kidneys, and his GFR is being held up by angiotensin II. He starts taking an ACE inhibitor. Predict his kidneys a few days later, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: Less angiotensin II is made

steps.ang: Angiotensin II in the blood falls
steps.gbhp: Pressure no longer backs up in the glomerulus: GBHP falls
steps.urine: Less filtrate enters the tubules
steps.md: Less NaCl reaches the macula densa

variables.name: Angiotensin II
variables.why: An ACE inhibitor blocks the enzyme that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II.

variables.name: Diameter of the efferent arterioles
variables.why: At moderate levels angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent. Take it away and the efferent arteriole widens.

variables.name: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (GBHP)
variables.why: With low inflow pressure from the narrowed renal arteries, the tight efferent arterioles were what kept pressure up in the glomerulus. Once they relax, it drains away.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: Lower GBHP means lower net filtration pressure, so GFR falls, sometimes sharply. This is why the drug is used with care in narrowed renal arteries.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: The drug acts after renin. With less filtrate, less NaCl reaches the macula densa, and the juxtaglomerular cells release more renin, though little of it can become angiotensin II.

variables.name: Urine output
variables.why: Every drop of urine starts as filtrate, so a sharp fall in GFR means less fluid enters the tubules and less urine is made.

scenarios.title: Damaged podocytes leak albumin
scenarios.misconception: losing protein in urine only affects the kidney
scenarios.setup: Disease damages a woman’s podocytes, and for several weeks large amounts of albumin pass her filtration membrane. Predict her state compared with before the disease.
scenarios.start: The slit diaphragms and podocytes are damaged

steps.urine: Albumin passes into the urine: proteinuria
steps.filt: Fluid filters out of systemic capillaries faster
steps.edema: Fluid collects in the tissues: edema

variables.name: Protein in the urine
variables.why: The damaged slit diaphragms no longer hold albumin back, and more reaches the tubule than the proximal tubule can take up, so it spills into the urine.

variables.name: Plasma albumin
variables.why: The liver cannot make albumin as fast as it is lost in the urine, so plasma albumin falls.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
variables.why: Albumin supplies most of the oncotic pull of plasma, so less albumin means a weaker pull.

variables.name: Swelling around the eyes and ankles
variables.why: With less oncotic pull holding fluid in, the Starling balance in every systemic capillary tips toward filtration. When filtration outpaces drainage, fluid collects as edema.

variables.name: Foaminess of the urine
variables.why: Protein in a liquid stabilizes bubbles, so heavily protein-laden urine looks foamy.

scenarios.title: Blood glucose at 400 mg/dL
scenarios.misconception: glucose appears in urine because the tubule stops reabsorbing it
scenarios.setup: A man with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus has a plasma glucose of 400 mg/dL instead of his usual 100. His GFR is normal. Predict his kidneys’ glucose handling, compared with a normal glucose.
scenarios.start: Plasma glucose rises to 400 mg/dL

steps.load: Filtered load = GFR × plasma glucose rises
steps.sat: Every glucose carrier in the proximal tubule is busy
steps.tm: Reabsorption reaches its ceiling, the transport maximum
steps.same: The number of carriers has not changed
steps.spill: Glucose beyond the carriers’ reach stays in the tubule
steps.water: Glucose left in the tubule holds water by osmosis
steps.urine: More urine is passed

variables.name: Filtered load of glucose
variables.why: Glucose is filtered freely, so four times the plasma concentration puts four times as much glucose into the tubules each minute: about 500 mg/min instead of 125.

variables.name: Glucose reabsorbed per minute
variables.why: Reabsorption does not stop; it rises from 125 mg/min to its ceiling of about 375 mg/min, because more carriers are now in use. It simply cannot rise any further.

variables.name: Transport maximum for glucose
variables.why: Tm is set by how many carriers the proximal tubule has. High glucose fills them but does not add any.

variables.name: Glucose excreted in the urine
variables.why: Excreted = filtered − reabsorbed = about 500 − 375 = 125 mg/min. At a normal glucose none is excreted.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Unreabsorbed glucose keeps water in the tubule by osmosis, so he passes more urine (polyuria) and grows thirsty.

scenarios.title: A drug blocks SGLT2
scenarios.misconception: blocking a proximal tubule carrier cannot change how much the glomerulus filters
scenarios.setup: A woman with type 2 diabetes starts a drug that blocks SGLT2, the main sodium–glucose symporter of the proximal tubule. Predict her state a week later, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: SGLT2 in the proximal tubule is blocked

steps.glu: Less glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
steps.excr: Glucose spills into the urine at normal blood levels
steps.na: Less sodium is reabsorbed with the glucose
steps.md: More NaCl reaches the macula densa
steps.aff: The macula densa signals the afferent arteriole to constrict
steps.water: Extra glucose and sodium hold water in the tubule

variables.name: Glucose in the urine
variables.why: Without SGLT2, the tubule reaches its limit at a far lower glucose, so glucose appears in urine even at normal plasma levels.

variables.name: Plasma glucose
variables.why: Glucose leaving in the urine is glucose removed from the blood: that is how the drug treats diabetes.

variables.name: NaCl reaching the macula densa
variables.why: SGLT2 carries sodium with every glucose. Block it and that sodium stays in the tubular fluid and flows on toward the macula densa.

variables.name: Diameter of the afferent arterioles
variables.why: More NaCl at the macula densa triggers tubuloglomerular feedback: its cells release ATP, which becomes adenosine and constricts the neighboring afferent arteriole.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: A narrower afferent arteriole lets less pressure reach the glomerulus, so GFR falls a little. Lowering the pressure in overworked glomeruli is thought to be part of how these drugs protect the kidneys.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Glucose and sodium that stay in the tubule hold water with them by osmosis, so a little more urine is passed.

scenarios.title: ADH is blocked
scenarios.misconception: without ADH the whole nephron stops reabsorbing water
scenarios.setup: A drug blocks the ADH receptor proteins on the principal cells of the collecting duct. The man taking it has normal ADH release and drinks when thirsty. Predict the changes over the next day, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: ADH can no longer act on principal cells

steps.camp: No rise in cAMP inside principal cells
steps.aqp: Aquaporins are pulled back out of the apical membrane
steps.perm: The collecting duct becomes nearly waterproof
steps.urine: Dilute fluid passes through the collecting duct and out
steps.loss: The body loses water faster than salt
steps.adh: More ADH is released, but it has no effect
steps.early: Segments before the collecting duct work without ADH

variables.name: Aquaporins in the apical membrane of principal cells
variables.why: ADH normally raises cAMP, which makes vesicles carrying aquaporins fuse with the apical membrane. Without that signal the cell pulls them back in by endocytosis.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Facultative water reabsorption largely stops, so much of the 15 to 20 percent of filtered water that reaches the collecting duct stays in it and leaves as urine, though some is still reabsorbed even without ADH.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: Fluid enters the collecting duct at about 100 mOsm/L. With no water leaving it, salt reabsorption there makes it more dilute still, down to about 50 mOsm/L.

variables.name: Osmolarity of fluid leaving the thick ascending limb
variables.why: ADH acts on the collecting duct. The proximal tubule and nephron loop do their work without it, so fluid still leaves the loop at about 100 mOsm/L.

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: Large volumes of dilute urine carry away more water than solute, so the solutes left in the plasma become more concentrated.

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: The osmoreceptors and posterior pituitary are unaffected. Rising plasma osmolarity makes them release more ADH, but the blocked receptor proteins cannot respond to it.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: The same rise in osmolarity drives thirst, and drinking is what keeps his plasma from climbing further.

scenarios.title: A loop diuretic
scenarios.misconception: a diuretic only makes you lose water
scenarios.setup: A patient with fluid overload from heart failure is given furosemide, which blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Predict the changes over the next few hours, compared with before the dose.
scenarios.start: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb is blocked

steps.nacl: NaCl stays in the tubular fluid
steps.grad: Less salt is added to the medulla; the gradient fades
steps.conc: The collecting duct has no salty medulla to lose water to
steps.water: The extra sodium holds water in the tubule
steps.urine: Urine volume rises
steps.kflow: More sodium and faster flow reach the principal cells
steps.pos: The lumen of the thick ascending limb loses its positive charge
steps.ca: Less calcium is reabsorbed between the cells

variables.name: Sodium reabsorbed by the thick ascending limb
variables.why: NKCC2 is the entry step for sodium in this segment. Blocked, it lets about a quarter of the filtered sodium flow on.

variables.name: Osmolarity of the inner medulla
variables.why: The countercurrent multiplier runs on NKCC2. Without its pumping, the vasa recta slowly carry away the salt already there, and the gradient runs down.

variables.name: Highest urine osmolarity the kidney can reach
variables.why: Water leaves the collecting duct only by osmosis into the medulla, so urine can never be more concentrated than the medulla around it.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Sodium left in the tubule holds water with it, and so much sodium is left that no later segment can catch it all. Loop diuretics are the most powerful kind.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Sodium and water leaving in the urine come from the extracellular fluid, which is how the drug relieves fluid overload.

variables.name: Potassium in the urine
variables.why: More sodium enters the principal cells, and faster flow sweeps secreted potassium away, so potassium secretion rises. Some patients develop low plasma potassium.

variables.name: Calcium in the urine
variables.why: Potassium recycling through NKCC2 normally makes the lumen positive, which pushes calcium and magnesium out between the cells. With that charge gone, more calcium stays in the urine.

scenarios.title: A thiazide diuretic
scenarios.misconception: all diuretics make you lose calcium
scenarios.setup: A woman with high blood pressure takes her first dose of hydrochlorothiazide, which blocks the sodium–chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Predict the changes over the first day, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: The DCT’s sodium–chloride symporter is blocked

steps.na: About 5% of filtered sodium is no longer reabsorbed
steps.water: The extra sodium holds water in the tubule
steps.urine: Urine volume rises a little
steps.kflow: More sodium and fluid reach the principal cells
steps.loop: The thick ascending limb still pumps salt into the medulla

variables.name: Sodium in the urine
variables.why: The symporter normally reabsorbs about 5% of filtered sodium. Blocked, most of that sodium is lost in the urine.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Sodium holds water with it, but the effect is moderate because only a small share of filtered sodium is involved, which suits long-term treatment. Over the next few days, aldosterone and the other segments catch up, and sodium excretion falls back to match intake, with a slightly smaller blood volume.

variables.name: Potassium in the urine
variables.why: More sodium and faster flow reaching the principal cells drive more potassium secretion, just as with a loop diuretic.

variables.name: Calcium in the urine
variables.why: Unlike a loop diuretic, a thiazide makes the distal tubule reabsorb more calcium, so less is lost. That is why thiazides are used to prevent calcium stones.

variables.name: Ability to make concentrated urine
variables.why: The thick ascending limb is untouched, so the medullary gradient remains and ADH can still concentrate the urine.

scenarios.title: A day without water: inside the kidney
scenarios.misconception: the kidneys can make up for any water loss by making less urine
scenarios.setup: A roofer works 10 hours in the heat, sweats about 3 liters, and drinks almost nothing. Sweat has less salt than plasma. Predict his state at the end of the shift, compared with the morning.
scenarios.start: He loses more water than salt

steps.adh: The posterior pituitary releases more ADH
steps.urea: More urea carriers open in the inner medullary collecting duct
steps.out: Water leaves the collecting duct into the salty medulla
steps.urine: A small volume of urine near 1,200 mOsm/L
steps.ald: Angiotensin II makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone
steps.pct: The proximal tubule still returns fluid at plasma osmolarity
steps.floor: Waste solute still needs at least about 0.5 L of urine

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: A rise in plasma osmolarity of just 1 to 2 percent is enough to make hypothalamic neurons release more ADH, and the fall in volume adds to it later.

variables.name: Aquaporins in principal cells’ apical membranes
variables.why: ADH raises cAMP in principal cells, and vesicles carrying aquaporins fuse with the apical membrane.

variables.name: Urea moving from the collecting duct into the inner medulla
variables.why: ADH also adds urea carriers in the inner medullary collecting duct. Urea concentrated by water loss upstream diffuses out and keeps the inner medulla highly concentrated.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: With aquaporins in place, the collecting duct loses water until its fluid nearly matches the medulla, up to about 1,200 mOsm/L.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: More water is reabsorbed, so less leaves. But it cannot fall below about 0.5 L a day: the day’s 600 mOsm of waste needs that much water even at 1,200 mOsm/L.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: The fall in blood volume raises renin release, and the angiotensin II that follows makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone, so he keeps sodium as well as water.

variables.name: Osmolarity of fluid leaving the proximal tubule
variables.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs solute and water together whatever ADH does, so its fluid leaves at plasma osmolarity. That is obligatory reabsorption.

scenarios.title: A liter of water, then the kidneys catch up
scenarios.misconception: drinking extra water dilutes the blood for hours
scenarios.setup: A student drinks a liter of water in five minutes on an empty stomach. First predict the state half an hour later; then predict three hours later, once most of the extra water has been passed.

stages.label: Half an hour after drinking
stages.prompt: Thirty minutes after the liter, compared with before drinking.
stages.start: Water is absorbed from the gut into the blood

steps.aqp: Principal cells pull aquaporins back into vesicles
steps.urine: The collecting duct lets dilute fluid through
steps.early: The loop still delivers fluid at about 100 mOsm/L

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: Absorbed water dilutes the plasma. A fall of 1 to 2 percent in osmolarity is enough for the osmoreceptors to cut ADH release.

variables.name: Urine flow
variables.why: Without ADH, the collecting duct becomes nearly waterproof, so the water reaching it flows out as urine instead of being reabsorbed.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: Fluid leaves the thick ascending limb at about 100 mOsm/L and loses no water on the way out, so urine can fall toward 50 mOsm/L: pale and dilute.

variables.name: Osmolarity of fluid leaving the thick ascending limb
variables.why: The loop pumps salt out without ADH’s help, so it keeps diluting the fluid to about 100 mOsm/L either way.

stages.label: Three hours later
stages.prompt: Three hours after the liter, once most of it has been passed, compared with the half-hour point.
stages.start: The extra water has been excreted

steps.osmo: Osmoreceptors fire at their usual rate again
steps.adh: ADH release returns to its usual level
steps.aqp: Aquaporins return to the apical membrane
steps.urine: Water is reabsorbed again in the collecting duct

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: Passing more water than solute undid the dilution, so osmolarity has risen back to its set point. The negative feedback removed its own stimulus.

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: Back at normal osmolarity, the osmoreceptors restore the usual level of ADH release.

variables.name: Urine flow
variables.why: ADH puts aquaporins back into principal cells, facultative water reabsorption resumes, and urine flow drops back to normal.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: Water leaving the collecting duct into the salty medulla concentrates the urine again.

scenarios.title: Hemorrhage and the kidney
scenarios.misconception: autoregulation protects GFR whatever happens to blood pressure
scenarios.setup: After a car crash, a man loses about 1.5 liters of blood, and his mean arterial pressure falls to about 65 mm Hg, below the range where the kidney can hold GFR steady. Predict his kidneys over the next hour, compared with before the crash.
scenarios.start: Blood volume and arterial pressure fall

steps.aff: Sympathetic fibers constrict the afferent arterioles strongly
steps.low: Pressure is below the autoregulatory range
steps.renin: Juxtaglomerular cells release more renin (beta-1 and low pressure)
steps.urine: Very little urine is made

variables.name: Renal blood flow
variables.why: Strong sympathetic constriction of the kidney’s arterioles cuts flow to the kidney and shifts blood toward the brain and heart.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: Below a MAP of about 80 mm Hg autoregulation can no longer hold GBHP up, and sympathetic constriction of the afferent arterioles lowers it further, so GFR falls.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: All three triggers act together: low pressure in the afferent arteriole, sympathetic stimulation through beta-1 receptor proteins, and less NaCl reaching the macula densa.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Renin leads to angiotensin II, which makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone.

variables.name: ADH
variables.why: A fall in blood volume of roughly 5 to 10 percent or more makes the posterior pituitary release ADH even when osmolarity is normal.

variables.name: Sodium in the urine
variables.why: Angiotensin II raises sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule and aldosterone adds sodium channels in principal cells, so almost no sodium escapes.

variables.name: Urine output
variables.why: Less filtrate enters the tubules and more of it is reabsorbed, so output can fall below 0.5 mL per kg per hour: the kidney is saving volume.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: ADH lets water leave the collecting duct into the salty medulla, so the little urine that is made is concentrated.

scenarios.title: Raising the pressure to one kidney
scenarios.misconception: because autoregulation holds GFR steady, the kidney ignores blood pressure
scenarios.setup: In an experiment, the arterial pressure reaching an animal’s kidney is raised from 100 to 140 mm Hg, while its hormones and kidney nerves are held constant. Predict the kidney’s output an hour later, compared with before.
scenarios.start: Arterial pressure to the kidney rises

steps.ptc: More pressure still reaches the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta
steps.int: Pressure in the kidney’s interstitial fluid rises
steps.nhe: Proximal tubule cells pull sodium–hydrogen exchangers out of their apical membrane
steps.back: Some reabsorbed fluid leaks back through leaky tight junctions
steps.na: Less sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
steps.out: More sodium and water flow on and leave in the urine

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: 140 mm Hg is inside the autoregulatory range of about 80 to 180 mm Hg, so the myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback hold GFR nearly steady.

variables.name: Pressure in the kidney’s interstitial fluid
variables.why: Autoregulation acts on the afferent arteriole and protects the glomerulus, but the higher pressure still reaches the capillaries around the tubules.

variables.name: Sodium reabsorbed by the proximal tubule
variables.why: Fewer exchangers bring sodium into the cells, and some fluid that was reabsorbed leaks back into the tubule between the cells.

variables.name: Sodium excreted in the urine
variables.why: This is pressure natriuresis: even with every hormone held constant, a higher pressure makes the kidney excrete more sodium, steeply.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Water leaves with the extra sodium (pressure diuresis). In a whole person, the lost volume lowers pressure back toward normal.

scenarios.title: GFR falls by half and stays there
scenarios.misconception: a plasma creatinine that is still a small number means the kidneys are fine
scenarios.setup: Kidney disease lowers a man’s GFR from 120 to 60 mL/min, and it stays there. His muscle mass does not change. Predict his state two weeks later, once things have settled, compared with before the disease.
scenarios.start: GFR halves

steps.make: Muscle keeps making creatinine at the same rate
steps.first: At first, less creatinine is filtered than is made
steps.load: Each milliliter filtered now carries more creatinine
steps.steady: Excretion climbs back until it equals production
steps.egfr: The lab’s estimate of GFR falls

variables.name: Plasma creatinine
variables.why: Creatinine is removed mainly by filtration. With half the filtering, creatinine accumulates until the plasma level has doubled, from about 1.0 to about 2.0 mg/dL.

variables.name: Creatinine made by muscle each day
variables.why: Production is set by muscle mass, not by the kidneys, so it stays the same.

variables.name: Creatinine excreted each day, once steady
variables.why: At steady state, excretion equals production. Half the GFR times twice the plasma level gives the same amount excreted as before.

variables.name: Estimated GFR (eGFR)
variables.why: eGFR is calculated from plasma creatinine, age and sex. A higher plasma creatinine gives a lower estimate, which is how the loss is caught.

scenarios.title: A drug for an overactive bladder
scenarios.misconception: relaxing the bladder muscle makes it empty more easily
scenarios.setup: An older woman with a sudden, frequent urge to urinate starts a drug that blocks muscarinic receptor proteins. Predict her bladder a week later, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: Muscarinic receptor proteins on the detrusor are blocked

steps.ach: Parasympathetic acetylcholine has less effect on the detrusor
steps.urge: Fewer unwanted contractions while the bladder fills
steps.pud: The pudendal nerve uses nicotinic signaling at skeletal muscle

variables.name: Strength of detrusor contractions
variables.why: Parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 make the detrusor contract by releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptor proteins. Blocking them weakens the contraction.

variables.name: Episodes of sudden urge
variables.why: The urge in an overactive bladder comes from the detrusor contracting while it should be relaxed. Weaker contractions mean fewer episodes, which is why the drug is used.

variables.name: Urine left in the bladder after voiding
variables.why: Emptying needs a strong, sustained detrusor contraction. Weakened, it can leave urine behind, and some people have trouble emptying fully.

variables.name: Strength of the external urethral sphincter
variables.why: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle driven by the pudendal nerve, whose acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptor proteins, not muscarinic ones.

scenarios.title: An older mother’s oocytes
scenarios.misconception: the risk of an extra chromosome is the same at every maternal age
scenarios.setup: Compare an oocyte released by a woman’s ovary at 42 with one released by the same woman at 25. Both oocytes began meiosis I before she was born and paused until shortly before release.
scenarios.start: The oocyte has paused partway through meiosis I for about 42 years instead of 25

steps.glue: The proteins laid down before birth to hold the paired chromosomes together have weakened and were never replaced
steps.early: Paired homologs come apart early or line up wrongly
steps.nd: Nondisjunction in meiosis I becomes more likely
steps.body: Her own body cells were made by mitosis long ago and keep their 46 chromosomes

variables.name: Strength of the links holding her oocytes’ paired chromosomes together
variables.why: The protein links that hold chromosomes together in the oocyte are made before birth and are not renewed, so after four decades many have worn away.

variables.name: Chance of nondisjunction in meiosis I
variables.why: With weak links, a pair of homologs can fall apart before anaphase I or both go to the same end, which is nondisjunction. That is why it happens mostly in meiosis I in oocytes.

variables.name: Share of her oocytes with an extra or missing chromosome
variables.why: Each nondisjunction gives one cell with an extra chromosome (24) and one with one missing (22). The risk rises steeply after about 35, which is why chromosome disorders in a pregnancy rise with the mother’s age.

variables.name: Chromosome number in her own skin cells
variables.why: Her body cells divide by mitosis and have nothing to do with the long pause in meiosis I, so they still hold 46 chromosomes.

scenarios.title: Stepping into cold water
scenarios.misconception: the testes are kept at body temperature like other organs
scenarios.setup: A man wades into a cold lake. Predict the changes in his scrotum over the next minute.
scenarios.start: Cold reaches the skin of the scrotum

steps.dartos: The dartos muscle under the skin contracts
steps.wrinkle: The scrotal skin wrinkles and its surface shrinks
steps.lift: Each testis is pulled up toward the warm body

variables.name: Contraction of the dartos muscle
variables.why: The dartos is smooth muscle just under the scrotal skin. Cold makes it contract, the first step in keeping the testes from getting too cold.

variables.name: Surface area of scrotal skin losing heat
variables.why: As the dartos contracts, the skin wrinkles and tightens, so less skin is exposed to the cold and less heat is lost.

variables.name: Distance between the testes and the body wall
variables.why: The cremaster, skeletal muscle around each testis and cord, contracts in cold and pulls the testes up toward the warmer body.

scenarios.title: After a vasectomy
scenarios.misconception: a vasectomy lowers testosterone and makes semen disappear
scenarios.setup: A man has a vasectomy: the ductus deferens is cut and sealed on each side. Predict his semen and hormones three months later, compared with before.
scenarios.start: Both ductus deferens are cut and sealed

steps.block: Sperm from the epididymis can no longer travel up to the ejaculatory ducts
steps.glands: The seminal vesicles and prostate, downstream of the cut, still add their fluid
steps.leydig: The interstitial cells in the testes and their blood supply are untouched

variables.name: Sperm in his ejaculate
variables.why: The ductus deferens is the only route from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct. Once the sperm already stored beyond the cut are cleared, the ejaculate holds essentially none.

variables.name: Volume of his ejaculate
variables.why: Sperm are only a few percent of semen. The seminal vesicles and prostate supply most of the volume, and their ducts join the route below the cut, so the volume barely changes.

variables.name: Testosterone in his blood
variables.why: Testosterone is a hormone released straight into the blood by the interstitial (Leydig) cells, with no duct. Cutting the sperm duct does not touch them.

scenarios.title: A PDE5 blocker for erectile dysfunction
scenarios.misconception: sildenafil causes an erection on its own
scenarios.setup: A man with erectile dysfunction takes sildenafil, which blocks the enzyme PDE5, an hour before sexual activity. Predict the changes during sexual stimulation, compared with stimulation without the drug.
scenarios.start: PDE5 in the smooth muscle of the erectile tissue is blocked

steps.breakdown: cGMP made in response to nitric oxide is broken down more slowly
steps.cgmp: cGMP builds up higher and lasts longer in the smooth muscle
steps.relax: The smooth muscle of the cavernosal arteries and blood spaces relaxes more
steps.inflow: More blood flows into the corpora cavernosa
steps.veins: The swelling tissue squeezes the draining veins flat against the tunica albuginea
steps.noNO: Without stimulation, parasympathetic nerves release no nitric oxide, so no cGMP is made to protect

variables.name: Rate at which cGMP is broken down
variables.why: PDE5 is the enzyme that breaks down cGMP. With it blocked, cGMP is removed more slowly.

variables.name: cGMP in the smooth muscle during stimulation
variables.why: Stimulation still makes nitric oxide, which raises cGMP. With its breakdown slowed, cGMP climbs higher and stays up longer.

variables.name: Blood flow into the corpora cavernosa
variables.why: cGMP relaxes the smooth muscle, so the cavernosal arteries widen and the blood spaces expand; more blood rushes in.

variables.name: Firmness of the erection
variables.why: More inflow swells the tissue, which presses the draining veins shut, so blood enters faster than it leaves and pressure in the corpora cavernosa rises.

variables.name: Erection with the drug but no sexual stimulation
variables.why: The drug only slows the breakdown of cGMP. Without stimulation, no nitric oxide is released and no cGMP is made, so there is nothing to protect and no erection.

scenarios.title: An alpha-1 blocker for an enlarged prostate
scenarios.misconception: alpha-1 blockers affect ejaculation by blocking erection
scenarios.setup: A 64-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia starts tamsulosin, which blocks alpha-1 receptor proteins on smooth muscle. Predict the changes over the next weeks.
scenarios.start: Norepinephrine can no longer act on alpha-1 receptor proteins in the smooth muscle of the prostate and the sperm ducts

steps.prost: Smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck relaxes
steps.urine: The prostatic urethra is squeezed less
steps.ducts: The ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate contract weakly during emission
steps.semen: Little semen is moved into the urethra
steps.para: Erection runs on parasympathetic nitric oxide, not on alpha-1 receptor proteins

variables.name: Strength of his urine stream
variables.why: Part of the squeeze on the urethra in BPH comes from contracted prostate smooth muscle. Relaxing it widens the prostatic urethra, which is why the drug is given.

variables.name: Contraction of the ducts and glands during emission
variables.why: Emission is sympathetic: norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins makes the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate contract. Blocked receptor proteins mean weak contractions.

variables.name: Volume of semen ejaculated
variables.why: With emission weakened, little semen reaches the urethra to be expelled, so little or none comes out. The main effect is on emission, not on flow back into the bladder.

variables.name: Ability to get an erection
variables.why: Erection depends on parasympathetic nerves releasing nitric oxide, which relaxes the erectile smooth muscle. Blocking alpha-1 receptor proteins does not interfere with that.

scenarios.title: Anabolic steroids and sperm production
scenarios.misconception: more androgen in the blood means more sperm
scenarios.setup: A 28-year-old man has injected high doses of testosterone for six months to build muscle. He and his partner have been trying for a baby. Predict his reproductive hormones and sperm, compared with before he started.
scenarios.start: A high level of injected androgen circulates in his blood

steps.brake: The androgen brakes GnRH release by the hypothalamus and LH release by the pituitary
steps.fsh: FSH falls too, as GnRH drive is lost
steps.leydig: Without LH, his Leydig cells make little testosterone
steps.local: Testosterone inside the seminiferous tubules falls far below its usual high level
steps.sperm: Sertoli cells lose the high local testosterone and FSH that spermatogenesis needs
steps.shrink: The tubules, which make up most of each testis, shrink

variables.name: LH in his blood
variables.why: Androgens exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. The injected dose keeps that brake on hard, so LH falls.

variables.name: FSH in his blood
variables.why: LH and FSH are both released in response to GnRH pulses. Braking GnRH lowers both.

variables.name: Testosterone inside his seminiferous tubules
variables.why: The tubules normally hold testosterone at 50 to 100 times the blood level, supplied by the Leydig cells next door under LH. With LH gone, that local supply collapses; the injected dose in the blood cannot recreate it.

variables.name: His sperm count
variables.why: Spermatogenesis needs the high local testosterone and FSH acting on the Sertoli cells. With both lost, sperm output falls, often to zero, even though his blood androgen is high.

variables.name: Size of his testes
variables.why: The seminiferous tubules make up most of the testis. As spermatogenesis winds down, the tubules shrink and so do the testes.

scenarios.title: Chemotherapy destroys the germ cells
scenarios.misconception: if sperm production fails, every reproductive hormone must be abnormal
scenarios.setup: After chemotherapy, a young man’s testes have lost their spermatogonia, but his Leydig cells still work. Predict his hormone levels and sperm a year later, compared with before treatment.
scenarios.start: The germ cells in his seminiferous tubules are gone; Sertoli and Leydig cells survive

steps.inhibin: Sertoli cells with no germ cells to support release less inhibin
steps.fsh: The inhibin brake on FSH weakens, so FSH rises
steps.leydig: Leydig cells keep responding to LH
steps.t: Testosterone stays in its normal range
steps.lh: Testosterone keeps its normal brake on LH

variables.name: Sperm count
variables.why: Every sperm comes from a spermatogonium. With the stem cells destroyed, spermatogenesis cannot restart.

variables.name: Inhibin in his blood
variables.why: Inhibin comes from the Sertoli cells, and how much they release depends on the germ cells they are supporting. With no germ cells, inhibin falls.

variables.name: FSH in his blood
variables.why: Inhibin is the brake that acts selectively on FSH. Less inhibin lets the pituitary release more FSH.

variables.name: Testosterone in his blood
variables.why: Testosterone comes from the Leydig cells between the tubules, not from the germ cells. They survived, so testosterone stays normal.

variables.name: LH in his blood
variables.why: Testosterone is the main brake on LH. With testosterone normal, the brake is unchanged and LH stays normal: a raised FSH alone points to lost germ cells.

scenarios.title: Testes that fail: Klinefelter syndrome
scenarios.misconception: low testosterone always comes with low LH
scenarios.setup: A 17-year-old with XXY sex chromosomes (Klinefelter syndrome) has small testes whose Leydig and Sertoli cells work poorly. Predict his hormone levels compared with a typical XY 17-year-old.
scenarios.start: His testes make little testosterone and little inhibin

steps.lowT: Testosterone in his blood is low
steps.lowInh: Inhibin in his blood is low
steps.offT: The testosterone brake on the hypothalamus and pituitary weakens
steps.offInh: The inhibin brake on FSH weakens
steps.sperm: Few or no sperm are made

variables.name: Testosterone
variables.why: His Leydig cells respond poorly to LH, so they release little testosterone.

variables.name: LH
variables.why: Testosterone normally brakes GnRH and LH. With little testosterone, the healthy pituitary works harder and LH rises: low testosterone with high LH means the testes themselves have failed.

variables.name: FSH
variables.why: Inhibin from the Sertoli cells brakes FSH. Little inhibin means little brake, so FSH rises.

variables.name: Sperm count
variables.why: Spermatogenesis needs a high local testosterone level and healthy tubules; in Klinefelter syndrome the tubules are scarred and few or no sperm are made, so most affected men are infertile.

scenarios.title: Continuous GnRH-like drug for prostate cancer
scenarios.misconception: a drug that mimics GnRH must always raise testosterone
scenarios.setup: A man with prostate cancer, whose cells grow faster in response to androgens, starts a long-acting drug that mimics GnRH. It keeps the pituitary exposed to steady GnRH activity instead of pulses. Follow his hormones.

stages.label: The first few days
stages.prompt: In the first days of treatment, compared with before.
stages.start: Pituitary cells meet a strong GnRH-like signal

steps.stim: The strong signal stimulates the LH- and FSH-releasing cells
steps.leydig: LH drives the Leydig cells harder

variables.name: LH
variables.why: At first the drug acts just like a big dose of GnRH, so the pituitary releases a burst of LH.

variables.name: Testosterone
variables.why: More LH reaching the Leydig cells means more testosterone, so for a week or two the cancer can briefly be stimulated.

stages.label: After several weeks
stages.prompt: After several weeks of steady treatment, compared with before treatment.
stages.start: The pituitary has been exposed to unchanging GnRH activity for weeks

steps.down: Pituitary cells stop responding to the unchanging signal
steps.t: Leydig cells get little LH, so testosterone falls to a very low level
steps.cancer: Prostate cancer cells lose the androgen that drives them

variables.name: LH
variables.why: The pituitary responds to rising and falling GnRH. Under steady, unchanging GnRH activity it stops responding, so LH falls.

variables.name: Testosterone
variables.why: Without LH, the Leydig cells make little testosterone, lowering it to the level after removal of the testes.

variables.name: Growth of the prostate cancer
variables.why: These cancer cells grow faster in response to androgens. With testosterone very low, their growth slows: the point of the treatment.

scenarios.title: Testosterone therapy in an older man
scenarios.misconception: testosterone therapy is a fertility treatment
scenarios.setup: A 58-year-old man with a low testosterone level starts daily testosterone gel, bringing his blood level into the normal range. Predict the changes after six months.
scenarios.start: Testosterone from the gel raises his blood testosterone

steps.epo: Testosterone raises erythropoietin release and marrow activity
steps.brake: Testosterone brakes GnRH and LH release
steps.local: His Leydig cells make less testosterone of their own, so the level inside the tubules falls
steps.muscle: Protein synthesis in skeletal muscle speeds up

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: Testosterone raises erythropoietin release and stimulates the marrow, which is why men’s hematocrit runs higher than women’s. Doctors check it on therapy, because too high a hematocrit thickens the blood.

variables.name: LH
variables.why: Testosterone from any source feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so LH falls.

variables.name: Sperm count
variables.why: Without LH, the Leydig cells stop supplying the high local testosterone the tubules need, so sperm production falls even though blood testosterone is normal.

variables.name: Muscle mass
variables.why: Testosterone binds androgen receptor proteins in muscle fibers and speeds protein synthesis, so muscle mass rises modestly.

scenarios.title: FSH injections in fertility treatment
scenarios.misconception: only one follicle can ever mature in a month
scenarios.setup: In a fertility clinic, a woman receives daily FSH injections that keep her FSH high for about ten days, starting just after her period. Predict her ovaries compared with an untreated month.
scenarios.start: FSH in her blood stays high instead of falling

steps.rescue: Every tertiary follicle that is ready keeps its FSH support
steps.many: Several follicles grow to the mature stage instead of one
steps.arom: FSH switches on aromatase in the granulosa cells of each growing follicle
steps.e2: Many follicles together release much more estradiol

variables.name: Number of follicles lost to atresia this month
variables.why: Normally FSH falls and every follicle except the most sensitive one loses its support and dies. Keeping FSH high keeps the others alive.

variables.name: Number of follicles reaching the mature vesicular stage
variables.why: Selection of one follicle depends on FSH falling. With FSH held high, several follicles keep growing, which is how clinics collect several oocytes.

variables.name: Estradiol in her blood
variables.why: Each growing follicle turns theca androgens into estradiol with aromatase, which FSH switches on. More follicles, and more granulosa cells, mean much more estradiol.

scenarios.title: High-dose prostaglandin blocker at mid-cycle
scenarios.misconception: if LH rises normally, the follicle must release its oocyte
scenarios.setup: A woman takes high doses of a drug that blocks prostaglandin synthesis for several days around the middle of her cycle. The sudden rise in LH happens normally. Predict what happens in her dominant follicle.
scenarios.start: Prostaglandins cannot be made in the follicle when LH rises

steps.lh: The rise in LH itself is not affected
steps.meiosis: LH still restarts meiosis I in the oocyte
steps.enzymes: The enzymes that digest the follicle wall at its thin spot are not activated enough
steps.rupture: The follicle wall does not give way on time
steps.release: The oocyte stays trapped in the follicle

variables.name: Peak LH level
variables.why: The drug acts on prostaglandin synthesis in the tissues, not on the pituitary, so the sudden rise in LH is unchanged.

variables.name: Completion of meiosis I in the oocyte
variables.why: LH restarts meiosis I without needing prostaglandins, so the oocyte still becomes a secondary oocyte with a first polar body.

variables.name: Breakdown of the follicle wall at its thin spot
variables.why: Prostaglandins are needed for the protein-digesting enzymes that weaken the follicle wall. Without them the wall stays strong.

variables.name: Release of the oocyte on time
variables.why: If the wall does not give way, the oocyte cannot ooze out, so its release is delayed or prevented even though LH rose normally.

scenarios.title: Taking the combined pill
scenarios.misconception: the pill works mainly by ending a pregnancy that has already begun
scenarios.setup: A 22-year-old starts the combined oral contraceptive, a daily synthetic estrogen and progestin. Predict the changes in the middle of her third pill pack, compared with the same days of a natural cycle.
scenarios.start: Steady synthetic estrogen and progestin circulate all month

steps.fb: Negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary stays switched on all month
steps.nodom: No follicle is selected to dominate
steps.e2: The ovary’s own estradiol never climbs high for two days
steps.nosurge: Positive feedback never starts: no LH surge
steps.mucus: The progestin keeps the cervical mucus thick
steps.lining: The progestin keeps the endometrium thin

variables.name: FSH
variables.why: The steady hormones hold the hypothalamus and pituitary under negative feedback, so GnRH pulses stay slow and FSH stays low.

variables.name: Estradiol made by her own ovaries
variables.why: Without the usual rise in FSH, no follicle grows to dominate, and a dominant follicle is what makes the steep rise in estradiol.

variables.name: Mid-cycle LH peak
variables.why: The LH surge needs high estradiol from a dominant follicle for about two days. That never happens, so positive feedback never switches on.

variables.name: Ovulation
variables.why: With no LH surge there is no trigger to release an oocyte. This is the pill’s main action; it prevents ovulation rather than ending a pregnancy.

variables.name: Thickness of cervical mucus
variables.why: Progestin acts like progesterone, which makes cervical mucus thick and sticky, a backup barrier to sperm.

variables.name: Thickness of the endometrium
variables.why: The progestin opposes the growth that estrogen alone would drive, keeping the lining thin. The bleed in the hormone-free days is a withdrawal bleed, not a true period.

scenarios.title: Both ovaries are removed
scenarios.misconception: removing the ovaries lowers every reproductive hormone
scenarios.setup: A 38-year-old has both ovaries removed because of a high inherited risk of ovarian cancer; her uterus is left in place and she takes no hormones. Predict her hormones and body three months later, compared with before surgery.
scenarios.start: All her follicles and any corpus luteum are removed

steps.e2: Estradiol falls to a very low level
steps.brake: Negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost
steps.lining: The endometrium is no longer built up and shed each month
steps.bone: Osteoclasts are no longer held back by estrogen

variables.name: Estradiol
variables.why: Before menopause, the granulosa cells of growing follicles make most of a woman’s estradiol. With the ovaries gone, it falls very low.

variables.name: FSH
variables.why: FSH is held down by both estradiol and inhibin. With both gone, FSH rises sharply, as it does after menopause.

variables.name: LH
variables.why: Estradiol and progesterone hold LH down. With no ovarian hormones, the healthy pituitary releases more LH.

variables.name: Monthly bleeding
variables.why: The uterus is still there, but without rising estradiol to build the functional layer and falling progesterone to shed it, periods stop.

variables.name: Rate of bone loss
variables.why: Estrogen keeps bone mass by limiting osteoclasts. Losing it suddenly speeds bone loss, which is why hormone therapy is often advised after this surgery in younger women.

scenarios.title: The corpus luteum dies: one cycle ends, the next begins
scenarios.misconception: the next cycle starts because the brain decides it is time
scenarios.setup: No pregnancy began this month. On about day 26 of a 28-day cycle, the corpus luteum starts to die. Follow the hormones and the uterus.

stages.label: Days 26 to 2
stages.prompt: Over the last days of the cycle and the first days of bleeding, compared with the middle of the luteal phase.
stages.start: The corpus luteum stops making hormones

steps.e2: Estradiol and inhibin from the corpus luteum fall
steps.lining: The functional layer loses its progesterone support, breaks down and is shed
steps.lift: Negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary lifts

variables.name: Progesterone
variables.why: The corpus luteum is the main source of progesterone. When it dies after 12 to 14 days, progesterone falls.

variables.name: Thickness of the functional layer
variables.why: Falling progesterone sets off inflammation and enzyme breakdown in the functional layer, which is shed as menstruation. The basal layer stays.

variables.name: FSH
variables.why: Progesterone, estradiol and inhibin had been holding FSH down. As they fall, the brake lifts and FSH rises: the small FSH bump at the start of a cycle.

stages.label: Days 5 to 10
stages.prompt: A week later, compared with the first days of bleeding.
stages.start: The raised FSH has rescued a group of tertiary follicles

steps.grow: The rescued follicles grow and add granulosa cells
steps.fb: Estradiol and inhibin exert negative feedback on the pituitary
steps.rebuild: Estradiol makes the basal layer’s cells divide and rebuild the functional layer

variables.name: Estradiol
variables.why: Growing follicles convert theca androgens into estradiol, and more granulosa cells make more of it.

variables.name: FSH
variables.why: The rising estradiol and inhibin feed back negatively, so FSH falls. That fall is what selects one dominant follicle: the rest lose their support.

variables.name: Thickness of the functional layer
variables.why: The proliferative phase: rising estradiol drives the basal layer to rebuild the functional layer, with its glands and coiled arteries.

scenarios.title: An endurance athlete who eats too little
scenarios.misconception: losing periods from heavy training is harmless
scenarios.setup: A 20-year-old distance runner trains hard while eating too little for her training load, and her periods stop. Predict the changes compared with a year earlier, when her cycles were regular.
scenarios.start: Energy intake falls short of the energy her exercise uses

steps.gnrh: Signals about low energy stores slow the GnRH pulse generator
steps.fol: Follicles do not grow to dominance
steps.noovul: No LH surge and no ovulation
steps.lining: The functional layer is not built up and shed
steps.bone: Low estrogen no longer holds back osteoclasts

variables.name: LH
variables.why: Too little energy for the amount of exercise slows GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus, so the pituitary releases less LH and FSH. The problem starts in the brain, not the ovary.

variables.name: Estradiol
variables.why: With little FSH and LH, no follicle grows to dominate, and without a dominant follicle estradiol stays low.

variables.name: Monthly bleeding
variables.why: Without estradiol to build the lining and a corpus luteum to withdraw progesterone from it, there is no cycle to shed: hypothalamic amenorrhea.

variables.name: Bone density
variables.why: Estrogen keeps bone mass by limiting osteoclasts. Low estrogen for months speeds bone loss, the combination seen in some endurance athletes.

scenarios.title: Four liters of water in an hour
scenarios.theme: drinking a large volume of water fast
scenarios.misconception: the kidneys can get rid of water as fast as you can drink it
scenarios.setup: Maya, 22, drinks 4 L of plain water in an hour during a contest. Her kidneys can excrete a little under 1 L an hour. Predict her state at the end of the hour, compared with before she started.
scenarios.start: Water is absorbed faster than the kidneys can excrete it

steps.dilute: Plasma osmolality falls, because water adds no solute
steps.cells: Water moves into cells by osmosis until the osmolality inside matches the ECF
steps.ecf: About one third of the absorbed water stays in the ECF
steps.osmo: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors swell and fire less
steps.adh: ADH release falls to almost nothing
steps.aqp: Principal cells pull their aquaporins back into vesicles
steps.urine: Large volumes of dilute urine are made
steps.brain: Brain cells swell inside the rigid skull

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Four liters of water with no added solute enter her body water. If none were excreted, her 12,180 mOsm of solute would be dissolved in 46 L instead of 42, and osmolality would fall from about 290 to 265 mOsm/kg. She does pass some urine in that hour, so the real value is a little higher, near 270, still far below normal.

variables.name: Volume of her intracellular fluid (cell size)
variables.why: The ECF is now more dilute than the inside of her cells, so water enters them by osmosis. Because the ICF is about two thirds of body water, about two thirds of the water ends up inside cells.

variables.name: ECF volume
variables.why: Pure water spreads through total body water in proportion to each compartment’s size, so about one third of it stays in the ECF, and a quarter of that share in the plasma.

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: A fall in osmolality of 1 to 2% is enough for the osmoreceptors to swell and cut ADH release. Her fall of 7 to 9% switches ADH almost fully off.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: The same osmoreceptors drive the thirst center. With the plasma dilute, thirst switches off; she is drinking for the contest, not because she is thirsty.

variables.name: Urine osmolality
variables.why: Without ADH, the collecting ducts become nearly waterproof, so dilute tubular fluid passes straight through. Urine falls toward about 50 mOsm/L.

variables.name: Urine flow
variables.why: Water that is no longer reabsorbed in the collecting ducts leaves as urine. Flow rises toward the kidneys’ top rate, a little under 1 L an hour.

variables.name: Pressure inside her skull
variables.why: She drank 4 L but can pass less than 1 L in that hour, so the extra water stays in her cells. Brain cells swell inside the rigid skull, raising the pressure there: headache, nausea and confusion. Her loop worked; the rate of drinking beat the kidneys’ top speed.

scenarios.title: A liter of 0.9% saline by vein
scenarios.misconception: fluid given into a vein stays in the blood
scenarios.setup: A patient with normal fluid balance is given 1 L of 0.9% saline, which has the same osmolality as plasma, into a vein. Predict her body fluids an hour later, before her kidneys have excreted much of it, compared with before the infusion.
scenarios.start: Isotonic fluid enters the plasma

steps.na: The added sodium stays outside cells, held there by the sodium–potassium pump
steps.share: Capillary walls let water and salt through, so the liter is shared between plasma and interstitial fluid
steps.isf: About three quarters of it moves into the interstitial fluid
steps.plasma: About one quarter, 250 mL, stays in the plasma

variables.name: ECF volume
variables.why: The sodium in the saline stays outside cells, and the water stays with it, so the whole liter is added to the ECF.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Plasma is about one quarter of the ECF, so about 250 mL of the liter stays in the plasma at steady state.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid volume
variables.why: Water and small solutes cross capillary walls freely, so about three quarters of the saline, 750 mL, moves out into the interstitial fluid.

variables.name: Intracellular fluid volume
variables.why: The saline has the same osmolality as plasma, so the ECF is neither more concentrated nor more dilute. With no osmotic gradient across plasma membranes, no water enters or leaves cells.

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Fluid with the same osmolality as plasma adds solute and water in the same proportion, so the concentration does not change. Only the volume of the ECF does.

scenarios.title: A liter of 5% glucose (D5W) by vein
scenarios.misconception: a fluid that is isosmotic in the bag acts like saline in the body
scenarios.setup: A patient is given 1 L of 5% glucose in water (D5W). It has about the same osmolality as plasma in the bag, but cells take up the glucose and use it. Predict his body fluids once the glucose has been used, compared with before the infusion.
scenarios.start: Cells take up and use the infused glucose

steps.free: What remains is 1 L of water with no lasting solute
steps.osmosis: Water moves into cells until osmolality is equal everywhere
steps.split: The water spreads through total body water: two thirds into cells, one third in the ECF
steps.plasma: Only a quarter of the ECF share, about 83 mL, stays in the plasma

variables.name: Intracellular fluid volume
variables.why: Once the glucose is gone, the liter behaves like pure water. It spreads through total body water, so about 667 mL ends up inside cells.

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: The water stays but its solute is used up, so the same body solute is now dissolved in a liter more water. Osmolality falls a little.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Plasma volume does rise, but only by about 83 mL: one third of the liter stays in the ECF, and one quarter of that in the plasma. That is why D5W replaces water but is a poor way to restore blood volume.

scenarios.title: Two days in the desert without water
scenarios.misconception: only the blood loses water when you are dehydrated
scenarios.setup: A hiker is lost for two days in hot, dry country with nothing to drink. He sweats and breathes out water, losing far more water than salt. Predict his state now, compared with before the hike.
scenarios.start: Water is lost faster than solute, and none is replaced

steps.out: Water leaves cells by osmosis until osmolality is equal again
steps.both: Both the ICF and the ECF shrink
steps.osmo: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors shrink and fire faster
steps.aqp: Principal cells insert aquaporins; water returns to the blood
steps.thirst: The thirst center drives intense thirst

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Sweat and exhaled water vapor carry far more water than solute, so the solute left behind is more concentrated. This is dehydration in the strict sense.

variables.name: Intracellular fluid volume
variables.why: The concentrated ECF draws water out of cells by osmosis, so cells shrink. Because the ICF is the largest compartment, it gives up most of the water lost.

variables.name: ECF volume
variables.why: The water lost comes from total body water, so the ECF shrinks too, although less than it would if cells did not share the loss.

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: Shrinking osmoreceptors fire faster, and the hypothalamus releases more ADH from the posterior pituitary.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH puts aquaporins into principal cells, so water leaves the collecting ducts into the salty medulla. A small volume of concentrated urine is made, though never less than about 0.5 L a day.

variables.name: Thirst
