variables.why: The rise in osmolality is far above the thirst threshold. Thirst is the only response that can replace lost water; the kidneys can only slow further loss.

variables.name: Size of his brain cells
variables.why: Brain cells lose water like all cells, which explains the confusion and irritability of severe dehydration.

scenarios.title: Leaky capillaries after a large burn
scenarios.misconception: a swollen patient cannot be short of blood volume
scenarios.setup: A man has a large burn. Over the next hours, damaged capillaries leak plasma fluid and protein into his tissues. Leave aside the water that evaporates from the burned skin and follow only the leak. Predict his state six hours later, compared with before the burn.
scenarios.start: Capillary walls let plasma fluid and protein through

steps.leak: Plasma fluid and protein pour into the interstitial fluid
steps.total: The fluid is still in the body: a fluid shift, not a loss
steps.bp: Venous return and blood pressure fall

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Fluid and protein leave the blood through the leaky capillary walls, so less fluid is left in the plasma.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid volume
variables.why: The leaked fluid collects in the tissues faster than the lymphatics can return it, so the tissues swell.

variables.name: Total body water, counting only the leak
variables.why: The fluid has moved from one compartment to another without leaving the body. That is a fluid shift, sometimes called third spacing.

variables.name: Arterial blood pressure
variables.why: Less plasma means less blood returning to the heart, so stroke volume and blood pressure fall: he can be hypovolemic and swollen at the same time.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Baroreceptors sense the fall in pressure, and the baroreflex raises sympathetic drive to the heart.

scenarios.title: A lung tumor that releases ADH
scenarios.misconception: a low plasma sodium means the body has lost sodium
scenarios.setup: A man’s lung tumor releases ADH all the time, whatever his plasma osmolality (SIADH). He keeps drinking his usual amount. Predict his state after a week, compared with before the tumor made ADH.
scenarios.start: ADH stays high although the plasma is dilute

steps.aqp: Principal cells keep aquaporins in their apical membranes
steps.keep: The kidneys keep water they would normally excrete
steps.dilute: Water is gained in excess of sodium, diluting the plasma
steps.swell: Water moves into brain cells, which swell

variables.name: Urine osmolality, compared with what his dilute plasma should produce
variables.why: Plasma this dilute should switch ADH off, and the urine would fall toward 50 to 100 mOsm/kg. With ADH present, water leaves the collecting ducts into the salty medulla, so his urine stays concentrated, often above 300 mOsm/kg, even though his plasma is dilute. The loop would normally switch ADH off; the tumor ignores it.

variables.name: Plasma sodium concentration
variables.why: His total body sodium has barely changed. The extra water he keeps dilutes it, so the concentration falls: hyponatremia is usually too much water, not too little sodium.

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Sodium and its anions make up almost all the solute of the ECF, so as plasma sodium falls, osmolality falls with it.

variables.name: Size of his brain cells
variables.why: The ECF is now more dilute than the inside of his cells, so water enters them. Swelling brain cells inside the rigid skull cause headache, nausea and confusion.

scenarios.title: Insulin and glucose for a high potassium
scenarios.misconception: lowering plasma potassium means potassium has left the body
scenarios.setup: A patient’s plasma potassium is 6.8 mmol/L. She is given insulin by vein, with glucose so her blood glucose does not fall too far. Predict her state 30 minutes later, compared with just before the injection.
scenarios.start: Insulin reaches her cells

steps.into: Potassium moves from the ECF into cells
steps.store: No potassium has left the body yet
steps.gap: The resting potential moves back from threshold

variables.name: Activity of her sodium–potassium pumps
variables.why: Insulin speeds the sodium–potassium pumps of muscle and liver cells, the same effect that stops a potassium-rich meal from raising plasma potassium sharply.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: The ECF holds under 2% of body potassium, so moving a small share of it into cells lowers the plasma value within minutes.

variables.name: Total potassium in her body
variables.why: Insulin only moves potassium between compartments. The potassium still has to be removed by the kidneys, binders or dialysis, and it can leak back out of cells as the insulin wears off.

variables.name: Gap between the resting potential of heart cells and threshold
variables.why: With less potassium outside, the resting potential becomes more negative again, further from threshold, so heart cells are less likely to be held partly depolarized.

scenarios.title: A crush injury releases cell contents
scenarios.misconception: a small release from cells cannot change plasma potassium much
scenarios.setup: A man’s legs are trapped under rubble for hours. When he is freed, crushed muscle releases its contents into the blood. Predict his plasma within an hour of release, before his kidneys can excrete much.
scenarios.start: Damaged muscle cells release their contents into the ECF

steps.k: Potassium, stored mainly inside cells, pours into the small ECF
steps.rmp: The resting potential of heart cells moves toward threshold
steps.p: Phosphate from inside cells is released

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: About 98% of body potassium is inside cells and the ECF holds only about 60 mmol. Releasing just 1% of cell potassium, 35 mmol, into 14 L raises plasma potassium by about 2.5 mmol/L.

variables.name: How close heart cells rest to threshold
variables.why: More potassium outside cells makes the resting potential less negative, closer to threshold. A large, lasting rise keeps cells partly depolarized, which is how hyperkalemia causes cardiac arrest.

variables.name: Plasma phosphate
variables.why: Most phosphate outside bone is inside cells, in ATP, nucleic acids and membrane phospholipids, so crushed muscle releases it too.

variables.name: Ionized calcium in the plasma
variables.why: Calcium and phosphate are linked in the blood: when phosphate rises, calcium phosphate forms and free calcium falls.

scenarios.title: Low albumin and the calcium result
scenarios.misconception: a low total calcium always means too little active calcium
scenarios.setup: A malnourished man’s plasma albumin falls from 4.0 to 2.0 g/dL. His parathyroid glands work normally. Compare his plasma calcium now with before.
scenarios.start: Less albumin is available to bind calcium

steps.bound: Less calcium is bound to albumin
steps.total: The lab’s total calcium, which counts bound calcium, reads low
steps.free: Ionized calcium is still held in range by the parathyroid glands

variables.name: Protein-bound calcium
variables.why: About 40% of plasma calcium normally rides on proteins, mainly albumin. Half the albumin binds less calcium.

variables.name: Total calcium on his lab report
variables.why: Total calcium adds together the ionized, protein-bound and anion-bound forms. With less bound, the total reads low: about 7.6 mg/dL instead of 9.2.

variables.name: Ionized (free) calcium
variables.why: The parathyroid glands sense ionized calcium and adjust PTH to hold it steady. Only the bound fraction has fallen, so the calcium that acts on nerves and muscles may be normal. Measuring ionized calcium settles it.

scenarios.title: A loop diuretic for swollen ankles
scenarios.misconception: a diuretic only removes water
scenarios.setup: A woman with heart failure starts a loop diuretic, which blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Predict her state after two weeks of daily doses, compared with before.
scenarios.start: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb is blocked

steps.na: Less sodium and chloride are reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb
steps.natri: More sodium, chloride and water leave in the urine
steps.raas: Renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone rise
steps.distal: More sodium and fluid reach the principal cells
steps.lumen: The positive lumen that drives magnesium between cells is lost

variables.name: Sodium in her urine in the hours after a dose
variables.why: The thick ascending limb normally reabsorbs about a quarter of filtered sodium on NKCC2. Blocked, it lets far more through than later segments can catch. Over days, aldosterone and the distal segments catch more between doses, so her total daily sodium output comes back to match her intake, at a smaller ECF volume.

variables.name: ECF volume
variables.why: Water follows the extra sodium into the urine. Because sodium sets ECF volume, losing it shrinks the ECF, which is what reduces her edema.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: The fall in volume and pressure switches on the RAAS, so aldosterone rises.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: More sodium entering principal cells makes the lumen more negative, faster flow carries secreted potassium away, and aldosterone adds more potassium channels and pumps. Potassium is lost in the urine.

variables.name: Plasma magnesium
variables.why: Most filtered magnesium is reabsorbed between the cells of the thick ascending limb, pushed by the positive lumen that NKCC2 creates. Without it, magnesium is lost too.

scenarios.title: Kidney failure: two missed dialysis sessions
scenarios.misconception: kidney failure affects only water and waste
scenarios.setup: Mr. Reyes, 66, has kidney failure and misses two dialysis sessions. Predict his blood panel now, compared with just after his last session.
scenarios.start: His kidneys cannot excrete what he takes in

steps.ksec: Principal cells cannot secrete the potassium he eats
steps.pex: Phosphate, normally excreted by the kidneys, builds up
steps.pth: The parathyroid glands sense the low calcium
steps.water: He keeps salt and water, and more water than salt

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: The kidneys remove about 90% of the potassium you eat. With none leaving, even normal meals raise plasma potassium, the most urgent danger because of its effect on the heart.

variables.name: Plasma phosphate
variables.why: The kidneys are the main exit for phosphate, so it builds up between dialysis sessions.

variables.name: Plasma calcium
variables.why: Phosphate that he cannot excrete binds calcium, so ionized calcium falls between sessions. His failing kidneys also make little calcitriol, which keeps his calcium absorption low all the time; that background does not change over two missed sessions.

variables.name: PTH
variables.why: The parathyroid glands respond to the fall in ionized calcium by releasing more PTH, which cannot fix the problem while phosphate stays high.

variables.name: Plasma sodium concentration
variables.why: He has too much salt and water in total, which causes edema, but more extra water than salt, so the concentration falls.

scenarios.title: Chronic low sodium, then a fast correction
scenarios.misconception: the faster a low sodium is corrected, the better
scenarios.setup: A woman taking a thiazide diuretic drifts to a plasma sodium of 118 mmol/L over a week. First predict what her brain cells have done after two days at that level. Then predict what happens if her sodium is raised by 20 mmol/L in the next 24 hours.

stages.label: Two days at a low sodium
stages.prompt: After two days at 118 mmol/L, compared with the first hours at that level.
stages.start: Brain cells sit in a dilute ECF

steps.release: Brain cells release potassium and small organic solutes
steps.less: With less solute inside, less water is drawn in
steps.size: Brain cells return toward their normal size

variables.name: Solute inside her brain cells
variables.why: Over about two days, brain cells adapt to the dilute ECF by losing potassium and small organic solutes, lowering their own osmolality to match it.

variables.name: Size of her brain cells
variables.why: In the first hours water entered her brain cells and they swelled. With their solute reduced, they draw in less water and shrink back toward normal, which eases the symptoms.

variables.name: Plasma sodium
variables.why: The adaptation happens inside brain cells. Her plasma sodium stays at 118 mmol/L until she is treated.

stages.label: Sodium raised too fast
stages.prompt: After her sodium is raised by 20 mmol/L in 24 hours, compared with the adapted state.
stages.start: Plasma sodium and osmolality rise quickly

steps.out: Water leaves the adapted brain cells, which have lost solute
steps.shrink: Brain cells shrink below their normal size
steps.myelin: The myelin of the pons is damaged

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Raising plasma sodium raises ECF osmolality almost twice as much, because each sodium ion is matched by an anion.

variables.name: Size of her brain cells
variables.why: The adapted cells have given up solute and cannot regain it in hours. The ECF is now more concentrated than they are, so water rushes out and they shrink.

variables.name: Risk of osmotic demyelination
variables.why: Shrinking cells damage the myelin of the pons, causing paralysis and trouble speaking and swallowing days later. That is why chronic hyponatremia is corrected by no more than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours.

scenarios.title: Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase
scenarios.misconception: bicarbonate reabsorption moves the filtered bicarbonate ion itself
scenarios.setup: A climber takes acetazolamide, which blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Predict her state a day later, compared with before the first dose.
scenarios.start: Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule is blocked

steps.noh: Tubule cells make less H+ to secrete
steps.nolumen: Filtered bicarbonate is not turned into carbon dioxide in the lumen
steps.urine: Bicarbonate stays in the tubular fluid and leaves in the urine
steps.cb: The carotid bodies sense the lower pH

variables.name: Bicarbonate in the urine
variables.why: Reclaiming bicarbonate needs carbonic anhydrase twice: inside the cell to make the H+ that is secreted, and on the brush border to turn carbonic acid into carbon dioxide. Blocked, filtered bicarbonate passes on and is excreted.

variables.name: Urine pH
variables.why: Bicarbonate is a base, so urine carrying more of it is more alkaline.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Every bicarbonate lost in the urine is one fewer in the plasma, so the top of the ratio falls.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: With less bicarbonate and the same PCO2, the ratio falls below 20 and pH falls.

variables.name: Breathing
variables.why: The carotid bodies sense the lower arterial pH and drive more breathing. At altitude that is the point: extra breathing raises oxygen uptake.

scenarios.title: A large steak dinner
scenarios.misconception: the lungs can get rid of any acid
scenarios.setup: A man eats a large steak dinner. Breaking down its sulfur-containing amino acids adds about 40 mmol of hydrogen ions, as sulfuric acid, to his blood over the evening. Predict the changes during the evening, compared with before the meal.
scenarios.start: Sulfuric acid adds hydrogen ions to the blood

steps.buffer: Bicarbonate takes up the H+, forming carbonic acid and then carbon dioxide
steps.cb: The carotid bodies sense the lower pH and breathing increases a little
steps.pco2: Arterial PCO2 falls just enough to keep the ratio near 20
steps.kid: The kidneys secrete more H+ onto phosphate and ammonia
steps.urine: Urine becomes more acidic
steps.new: Each H+ excreted adds one new bicarbonate to the blood

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate, early in the evening
variables.why: Bicarbonate is the first buffer to meet the acid. Each H+ it takes up uses one bicarbonate, so it falls a little until the kidneys replace it.

variables.name: Breathing
variables.why: The carotid bodies respond within seconds to a fall in arterial pH, whatever the acid, and the respiratory centers raise ventilation slightly.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: A little extra breathing blows off carbon dioxide, lowering the bottom of the ratio to match the lower top. The lungs restore the ratio but cannot remove sulfuric acid.

variables.name: Acid excreted in his urine (titratable acid and ammonium)
variables.why: Sulfuric acid cannot be breathed out, so the kidneys must excrete it. Type A intercalated cells secrete more H+, which leaves bound to phosphate and ammonia.

variables.name: Urine pH
variables.why: More secreted H+ in the urine lowers its pH, toward the limit of about 4.5.

variables.name: New bicarbonate added to his blood by the kidneys
variables.why: Every H+ excreted leaves a bicarbonate behind in the tubule cell, which enters the blood. Over hours to a day this replaces the bicarbonate the acid used up.

scenarios.title: Three days of vomiting: the acid–base picture
scenarios.misconception: healthy kidneys would simply excrete the extra bicarbonate
scenarios.setup: A man with a blocked stomach outlet vomits stomach contents many times a day for three days. His kidneys are healthy. Predict his blood now, compared with before he fell ill.
scenarios.start: Hydrochloric acid secreted by the stomach is vomited

steps.tide: Each H+ the parietal cells secreted left one bicarbonate in the blood (the alkaline tide)
steps.noneut: The acid never reaches the duodenum, so the pancreas does not secrete bicarbonate to neutralize it
steps.hco3: Extra bicarbonate stays in the blood
steps.cl: Chloride is lost in the vomit
steps.keep: Low volume and low chloride make the kidneys keep bicarbonate instead of excreting it
steps.vent: The carotid bodies sense the high pH and breathing slows
steps.k: Potassium is lost in vomit and, under aldosterone, in urine
steps.alb: Albumin binds more calcium in alkalemia

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: The alkaline tide adds bicarbonate that is never used up, because the acid is vomited instead of neutralized in the duodenum. Healthy kidneys could excrete it fast, but low volume (through angiotensin II and aldosterone) and low chloride make them keep it.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: The top of the ratio has risen, so pH rises above 7.45. The primary change is in bicarbonate, so this is a metabolic alkalosis.

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: Compensation moves in the same direction as the primary number: the higher pH slows breathing, so carbon dioxide builds up. It is limited, because slower breathing also lowers PaO2.

variables.name: Plasma chloride
variables.why: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, so vomiting removes chloride with the H+. With little chloride in the tubular fluid, type B intercalated cells, which trade bicarbonate for chloride, cannot excrete much bicarbonate.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Lost fluid lowers blood volume and pressure, switching on the RAAS. Angiotensin II speeds the proximal tubule’s sodium–hydrogen exchanger, so more bicarbonate is reclaimed.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Some potassium is lost in the vomit, but more in the urine: aldosterone and the extra sodium reaching the principal cells drive potassium secretion. Low potassium in turn speeds H+ secretion, sustaining the alkalosis.

variables.name: Ionized calcium
variables.why: In alkalemia albumin gives up hydrogen ions and binds more calcium, so ionized calcium falls: tingling and cramps, although total calcium is normal.

scenarios.title: Three days of severe diarrhea
scenarios.misconception: every metabolic acidosis comes from an added acid
scenarios.setup: A traveler has severe watery diarrhea for three days and cannot drink enough to keep up. Predict her blood now, compared with before she fell ill.
scenarios.start: Intestinal fluid rich in bicarbonate is lost in stool

steps.cl: Chloride is kept in bicarbonate’s place
steps.gap: No unmeasured anion is added, so the anion gap stays normal
steps.cb: The carotid bodies drive deeper, faster breathing
steps.kid: Tubule cells secrete more H+ and make more ammonium
steps.vol: Salt and water loss shrinks the ECF

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Intestinal secretions are rich in bicarbonate. Losing liters of them removes base from the body, so the top of the ratio falls.

variables.name: Plasma chloride
variables.why: Plasma must carry equal positive and negative charge. As bicarbonate is lost, the kidneys and gut keep chloride in its place: hyperchloremia.

variables.name: Anion gap
variables.why: Chloride, a measured anion, replaces the lost bicarbonate, so the gap stays normal: about 137 − (112 + 15) = 10. A normal anion gap points to bicarbonate lost, not acid gained.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Less bicarbonate with the same PaCO2 lowers the ratio, so pH falls below 7.35.

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: The lungs compensate within hours: lower arterial pH drives the carotid bodies, breathing deepens, and PaCO2 falls in the same direction as bicarbonate.

variables.name: Ammonium excreted by her kidneys
variables.why: Acid inside tubule cells speeds H+ secretion and ammonium production. Each ammonium excreted adds a new bicarbonate, though the kidneys cannot keep up with liters of stool.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Stool carries potassium; heavy diarrhea removes a lot of it, so she can be both acidotic and short of potassium.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Stool losses are close to isotonic, so the ECF shrinks and blood pressure tends to fall. The baroreflex raises the heart rate.

scenarios.title: COPD: a bad week, first hours and five days later
scenarios.misconception: compensation returns every number to normal
scenarios.setup: A woman with severe COPD catches a chest infection. Her alveolar ventilation falls, and within a few hours her PaCO2 climbs from 40 to 60 mm Hg, where it stays. First predict her blood in those first hours; then predict five days later, with her PaCO2 still 60 mm Hg.

stages.label: The first hours
stages.prompt: A few hours after her PaCO2 reached 60 mm Hg, compared with before the infection.
stages.start: Alveolar ventilation falls below carbon dioxide production

steps.co2: Carbon dioxide builds up: PaCO2 rises
steps.h: More carbonic acid forms and releases H+
steps.o2: Less fresh air reaches the alveoli, so alveolar PO2 falls
steps.brain: High carbon dioxide dilates the brain’s arterioles

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: At a steady carbon dioxide production, PaCO2 rises as alveolar ventilation falls. The primary change is respiratory.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: The bottom of the ratio has risen by half with bicarbonate barely changed, so the ratio falls to about 14 and pH to about 7.26.

variables.name: PaO2
variables.why: Hypoventilation brings in less fresh air, so oxygen in the alveoli, and then in arterial blood, falls as carbon dioxide rises.

variables.name: Blood flow to her brain
variables.why: Carbon dioxide dilates the brain’s arterioles, adding headache; together with the acidemia it causes drowsiness and confusion.

stages.label: Five days later
stages.prompt: Five days on, with PaCO2 still 60 mm Hg, compared with the first hours.
stages.start: The high PCO2 keeps H+ production high in her tubule cells

steps.secrete: Tubule cells secrete more H+ and make more ammonium
steps.new: Each H+ excreted adds a new bicarbonate to the blood
steps.hco3: Plasma bicarbonate rises, to about 31 mmol/L
steps.cl: Plasma chloride falls as bicarbonate rises

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Carbon dioxide diffuses into tubule cells and makes more H+ there. Over 3 to 5 days, extra H+ secretion and ammonium excretion add new bicarbonate: renal compensation.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: With bicarbonate up and PaCO2 unchanged, the ratio rises from about 14 toward 17, and pH from 7.26 to about 7.34: partially compensated, still just below 7.35.

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: Compensation does not fix the cause. Her lungs still move too little air, so PaCO2 stays at 60 mm Hg until the infection clears.

variables.name: Ammonium in her urine
variables.why: Ammonium production by the proximal tubule rises over days; it is the adjustable part of acid excretion and the main reason renal compensation is slow.

variables.name: Plasma chloride
variables.why: Chloride and bicarbonate are the two main anions. As the kidneys add bicarbonate, they excrete more chloride, so the total negative charge stays matched to sodium.

scenarios.title: Ten minutes of panic breathing
scenarios.misconception: the kidneys correct a short bout of hyperventilation
scenarios.setup: A 22-year-old has a panic attack and breathes fast and deep for ten minutes. Her lips and fingers tingle. Predict her arterial blood now, compared with before the attack.
scenarios.start: Alveolar ventilation far exceeds carbon dioxide production

steps.co2: Carbon dioxide is blown off: PaCO2 falls
steps.buf: Buffers release a little H+, lowering bicarbonate slightly
steps.time: Ten minutes is far too short for the kidneys to act
steps.alb: Albumin gives up H+ and binds more calcium
steps.total: Calcium only moves between its bound and free forms
steps.nerve: Nerves and muscles fire too easily

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: Breathing out carbon dioxide faster than cells make it lowers PaCO2, to about 28 mm Hg in the notes’ example.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: The bottom of the ratio falls while bicarbonate barely moves, so the ratio rises above 20 and pH above 7.45.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Within minutes, buffers such as hemoglobin release a little H+, which uses up a little bicarbonate: from about 24 to 22 mmol/L, still in range.

variables.name: Bicarbonate excreted by her kidneys
variables.why: Renal compensation takes days to build. A panic attack is over in minutes, so the gas stays uncompensated.

variables.name: Ionized calcium
variables.why: In alkalemia, albumin gives up H+ and binds more calcium, so less calcium is free.

variables.name: Total calcium
variables.why: No calcium enters or leaves the plasma; some just moves from the free form to the albumin-bound form, so the total is unchanged.

variables.name: Tingling and muscle spasm
variables.why: Low ionized calcium lets voltage-gated sodium channels open more easily, so nerves fire on their own: tingling around the mouth and fingers and cramping of the hands.

scenarios.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis: the blood panel
scenarios.misconception: a normal or high plasma potassium means the body has plenty of potassium
scenarios.setup: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes misses insulin doses during a chest infection. Two days later her glucose is 540 mg/dL and her beta-hydroxybutyrate 6 mmol/L. Predict her blood and urine now, compared with before she fell ill.
scenarios.start: Insulin is nearly absent and glucagon is high

steps.ket: The liver turns a flood of fatty acids into ketone bodies faster than tissues burn them
steps.h: Ketone acids release H+, which uses up bicarbonate
steps.gap: Ketone anions take bicarbonate’s place: the anion gap rises
steps.kuss: The carotid bodies drive deep, fast (Kussmaul) breathing
steps.glu: Blood glucose rises, raising plasma osmolality
steps.shift: Potassium leaves cells: fewer pumps working, and water drawn out of cells carries potassium with it
steps.urine: Glucose spills into the urine and holds water with it
steps.loss: Water, sodium and potassium are lost in large volumes of urine

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate release hydrogen ions, and bicarbonate is used up buffering them.

variables.name: Anion gap
variables.why: Each ketone acid leaves its anion behind, which the routine panel does not measure. Bicarbonate falls with chloride unchanged, so the gap rises: a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: The falling pH drives the carotid bodies, and deep, sighing breathing lowers PaCO2 to partly restore the ratio. Expected PaCO2 is about 1.5 × HCO3 + 8.

variables.name: Plasma osmolality
variables.why: Glucose at 540 mg/dL is 30 mmol/L of solute, against about 5 normally, and without insulin it stays outside most cells, so it raises osmolality and draws water out of cells.

variables.name: Potassium moving from cells into the plasma
variables.why: Without insulin, the sodium–potassium pumps move less potassium in, and the high osmolality pulls water, and potassium with it, out of cells. Plasma potassium is often normal or high at first.

variables.name: Total potassium in her body
variables.why: The glucose in her urine carries water, sodium and potassium out. The body’s store is being lost even while the plasma value looks normal or high, which is why potassium is given with insulin.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Glucose above the kidneys’ transport maximum stays in the tubule and holds water with it, so she passes large volumes and becomes badly dehydrated.

scenarios.title: Insulin treatment starts in DKA
scenarios.misconception: insulin alone fixes everything in DKA
scenarios.setup: The same patient with diabetic ketoacidosis is given IV fluids and insulin, but no potassium yet. Predict her state six hours later, compared with the untreated state.
scenarios.start: Insulin reaches her tissues

steps.pump: Sodium–potassium pumps speed up and cells take up glucose
steps.ket: Ketone production falls, and tissues burn the ketone bodies already made
steps.back: Burning ketone anions takes up H+, restoring bicarbonate

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Insulin drives potassium into cells within minutes. Because her total store is already low, plasma potassium can fall dangerously, which is why fluids, insulin and potassium are given together.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Insulin lets muscle and fat cells take up glucose and stops the liver releasing it.

variables.name: Ketone body production by her liver
variables.why: Insulin switches off lipolysis, so fewer fatty acids reach the liver to be made into ketone bodies.

variables.name: Anion gap
variables.why: As the ketone anions are burned they leave the unmeasured anion pool, and the bicarbonate restored takes their place, so the gap closes.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Bicarbonate rises back toward normal, the ratio rises, and pH climbs toward 7.4.

scenarios.title: Cardiac arrest: two disorders at once
scenarios.misconception: a blood gas can show only one disorder at a time
scenarios.setup: A man collapses in cardiac arrest. During resuscitation, chest compressions keep some blood moving, but he is breathing very poorly. Predict his arterial blood ten minutes in, compared with before the arrest.
scenarios.start: Ventilation and blood flow both fail

steps.vent: Almost no carbon dioxide is breathed out
steps.flow: Tissues get too little blood and oxygen
steps.anaer: Anaerobic metabolism releases H+ and lactate
steps.hco3: Bicarbonate is used up buffering the H+: metabolic acidosis
steps.gap: Lactate, an unmeasured anion, raises the anion gap
steps.ph: Both disorders push pH down together

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: Carbon dioxide is still made but not breathed out, so it builds up in the blood.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Poorly perfused tissues release H+ and lactate faster than they can be cleared, and bicarbonate is used up buffering the H+.

variables.name: Blood lactate
variables.why: Lactate is made faster than the liver and other tissues can burn it; a high lactate is a sign of poor perfusion.

variables.name: Anion gap
variables.why: Lactate takes the place of the bicarbonate used up, so the gap rises.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: PaCO2 up and bicarbonate down have moved in opposite directions, which compensation never does. Each lowers the ratio, so together they drive pH far lower than either alone, to about 7.11.

scenarios.title: Sperm that cannot capacitate
scenarios.misconception: sperm that swim well are ready to fertilize as soon as they are ejaculated
scenarios.setup: In an IVF lab, washed sperm are kept for several hours in a medium with no albumin, no bicarbonate and no calcium, then placed next to an oocyte. Compare them with sperm kept in a medium that copies the fluids of the female tract.
scenarios.start: The medium lacks albumin, bicarbonate and calcium

steps.chol: Nothing pulls cholesterol out of the sperm’s plasma membrane
steps.ions: Bicarbonate and calcium cannot flow into the sperm
steps.hyper: The tail keeps its gentle, even beat instead of switching to hyperactivated motility
steps.acro: Without capacitation, the sperm cannot undergo the acrosomal reaction
steps.zona: No sperm digests a path through the zona pellucida
steps.swim: The tail’s basic machinery and ATP supply are unchanged

variables.name: Cholesterol left in the sperm’s plasma membrane
variables.why: In the female tract, albumin pulls cholesterol out of the sperm membrane, making it more fluid. With no albumin, the cholesterol stays, so the membrane keeps more of it than a capacitated sperm’s.

variables.name: Share of sperm with hyperactivated, whip-like beating
variables.why: The switch to a strong, asymmetric beat is triggered by calcium entering the sperm. With no calcium or bicarbonate to enter, the tail stays in its gentle beat.

variables.name: Sperm able to release their acrosome’s enzymes
variables.why: Only a capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosomal reaction. Its membrane must first be stripped and destabilized, and that step never happened here.

variables.name: Chance the oocyte is fertilized
variables.why: A sperm that cannot release acrosin cannot cut a tunnel through the zona pellucida, so none reaches the oocyte’s plasma membrane to fuse with it.

variables.name: Ability of the sperm to swim forward
variables.why: Freshly ejaculated sperm already swim well; capacitation changes the kind of beat, not the ability to move. That is why good swimming alone does not mean a sperm can fertilize.

scenarios.title: An oocyte whose cortical granules cannot release
scenarios.misconception: the first sperm to fuse physically plugs the way in for the others
scenarios.setup: In a lab study, an oocyte’s cortical granules cannot fuse with its plasma membrane, although calcium waves still sweep through it after the first sperm fuses. Many capacitated sperm surround it. Compare it with a normal oocyte after sperm entry.
scenarios.start: The calcium waves cannot make the cortical granules release their contents

steps.enzyme: The enzyme that cuts ZP2 is not released under the zona pellucida
steps.bind: ZP2 stays intact, so new sperm can still bind the zona and push through
steps.poly: A second sperm can reach and fuse with the oocyte
steps.three: Two sperm plus the oocyte give three sets of chromosomes
steps.meiosis: The calcium waves still release the pause in metaphase II

variables.name: Intact ZP2 left in the zona pellucida after the first sperm fuses
variables.why: In the cortical reaction, an enzyme released from the granules cuts ZP2. With no release, ZP2 stays intact, so the zona keeps more of it than a normal fertilized oocyte’s.

variables.name: Sperm binding to the zona after the first sperm has entered
variables.why: Sperm bind the zona through ZP2. Because it was never cut, the zona stays sticky for sperm instead of shutting them out.

variables.name: Chance of polyspermy
variables.why: The zona block is missing, so more sperm reach the membrane. Only the slower membrane block, the loss of the sperm-binding protein, is left to stop them.

variables.name: Chromosome number if two sperm enter
variables.why: Each sperm adds 23 chromosomes to the oocyte’s 23, giving 69 instead of 46. An embryo with three sets cannot develop normally.

variables.name: Completion of meiosis II in the oocyte
variables.why: The same calcium waves that normally trigger the cortical reaction also restart meiosis II. The calcium still rises here, so meiosis II still finishes and a second polar body forms.

scenarios.title: The corpus luteum is removed early
scenarios.misconception: once an embryo has implanted, it no longer depends on the ovary
scenarios.setup: About four weeks after fertilization (six weeks on the clinical count), a pregnant woman needs surgery that removes the ovary holding her corpus luteum. She is not given progesterone. Predict the changes over the next days.
scenarios.start: The corpus luteum, her main source of progesterone at this stage, is removed

steps.lining: The endometrium loses the hormone that keeps it intact
steps.shed: The lining breaks down and is shed, carrying the implanted embryo with it
steps.hcg: The syncytiotrophoblast keeps secreting hCG for now, but its target is gone

variables.name: Progesterone in her blood
variables.why: At this stage the corpus luteum, kept alive by hCG, makes most of the progesterone. The trophoblast’s own output is not yet large enough to replace it.

variables.name: Stability of the endometrium
variables.why: Progesterone holds the endometrium in place. When it falls, the lining starts to break down, as it does at the end of a cycle without pregnancy.

variables.name: Chance of losing the pregnancy
variables.why: The embryo is buried in the endometrium, so shedding the lining sheds the embryo. Removing the corpus luteum before about week 7 on the clinical count ends the pregnancy unless progesterone is given; from about week 9, it does no harm.

variables.name: hCG secretion in the first hours after surgery
variables.why: hCG comes from the syncytiotrophoblast, not from the ovary, so removing the ovary does not stop it at once. What is lost is the gland hCG acts on.

scenarios.title: A placenta that does not keep up
scenarios.misconception: a fetus takes what it needs from the mother whatever the state of the placenta
scenarios.setup: Early in a pregnancy, the cytotrophoblast invades the spiral arteries only shallowly. They keep their smooth muscle and stay narrow. Predict the fetus’s state in the last months, compared with a pregnancy with a healthy placenta.
scenarios.start: The spiral arteries stay narrow and muscular

steps.flow: Less maternal blood flows into the intervillous space
steps.o2: Less oxygen and glucose diffuse across the villi to the fetus
steps.redirect: The fetus redirects blood toward its brain and heart and away from its kidneys, gut and limbs
steps.kidney: Less blood reaches the fetal kidneys, so they make less urine
steps.fluid: Less urine enters the amniotic cavity

variables.name: Maternal blood flow through the intervillous space
variables.why: Remodeled spiral arteries are wide tubes that cannot constrict. Narrow, muscular ones keep a high resistance, so less of the mother’s blood reaches the villi.

variables.name: Oxygen crossing to the fetus each minute
variables.why: Oxygen diffuses from maternal blood into the villi. With less maternal blood flowing past, the gradient across the barrier is kept up less well, so less oxygen crosses each minute.

variables.name: Fetal growth rate
variables.why: Everything the fetus builds with comes across the placenta. Less oxygen and glucose means slower growth: a small baby is the classic result.

variables.name: Share of the fetus’s blood flow going to its brain
variables.why: Low blood oxygen makes the fetus narrow the vessels to its kidneys, gut and limbs, so a larger share of its output goes to the brain and heart.

variables.name: Amniotic fluid volume
variables.why: In the second half of pregnancy, fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid. Less kidney blood flow means less urine, so the fluid volume falls.

scenarios.title: A mother who smokes
scenarios.misconception: the placenta filters out harmful chemicals before they reach the fetus
scenarios.setup: A pregnant woman smokes a pack of cigarettes a day. Compare her fetus with the fetus of a woman who does not smoke.
scenarios.start: Carbon monoxide and nicotine enter her blood

steps.co: Carbon monoxide diffuses across the placental barrier and builds up in fetal blood
steps.hb: Carbon monoxide takes up hemoglobin’s oxygen-binding sites
steps.nic: Nicotine constricts the uterine blood vessels
steps.flow: Less maternal blood reaches the intervillous space
steps.grow: Less oxygen reaches the fetal tissues, so the fetus grows more slowly

variables.name: Carbon monoxide in fetal blood
variables.why: Carbon monoxide is a small gas and crosses by simple diffusion. It reaches a higher level in fetal blood than in the mother’s and leaves more slowly.

variables.name: Oxygen the fetal blood can carry
variables.why: Hemoglobin that holds carbon monoxide cannot hold oxygen, so each liter of fetal blood carries less oxygen.

variables.name: Maternal blood flow to the intervillous space
variables.why: Nicotine constricts the uterine blood vessels, raising their resistance, so less blood reaches the villi.

variables.name: Birth weight
variables.why: Less blood flow to the placenta and less oxygen carried per liter both starve the fetus of oxygen, so it grows more slowly and is born smaller.

scenarios.title: The mother’s glucose runs high
scenarios.misconception: the mother’s insulin crosses the placenta and controls the fetus’s glucose
scenarios.setup: For several weeks in the second half of pregnancy, a mother’s blood glucose runs well above normal. Compare her fetus with the fetus of a mother whose glucose is normal.
scenarios.start: Maternal blood glucose is high

steps.cross: More glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion, down a steeper gradient
steps.ins: Maternal insulin is a large protein and does not cross the placenta
steps.fins: The fetal pancreas secretes more insulin
steps.grow: Fetal insulin drives the fetus to store fuel and grow

variables.name: Fetal blood glucose
variables.why: Glucose crosses on carrier proteins down its gradient, from higher maternal glucose to lower fetal glucose. A higher maternal level pushes more across, so fetal glucose follows the mother’s up.

variables.name: Maternal insulin reaching the fetus
variables.why: Insulin is a protein, too large to cross the placental barrier in useful amounts. The fetus has to make its own.

variables.name: Insulin secreted by the fetal pancreas
variables.why: The fetus’s beta cells answer its high glucose the way any pancreas does, by secreting more insulin.

variables.name: Fetal growth
variables.why: Insulin is a growth-promoting hormone in the fetus: with extra glucose and extra insulin, the fetus stores more fat and grows larger.

scenarios.title: Ibuprofen late in pregnancy
scenarios.misconception: drugs taken for the mother’s pain have no effect on the fetal heart and vessels
scenarios.setup: At 32 weeks, a pregnant woman takes high doses of ibuprofen for several days. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin synthesis and crosses the placenta. Predict the changes in the fetus.
scenarios.start: Prostaglandin synthesis is blocked in the fetus and placenta

steps.pg: Less prostaglandin reaches the smooth muscle of the ductus arteriosus
steps.narrow: The ductus arteriosus constricts before birth
steps.less: Less of the right ventricle’s output can pass into the aorta
steps.lungs: More of that output is forced into the high-resistance fetal lungs
steps.pressure: Pressure in the pulmonary trunk and the right ventricle rises

variables.name: Diameter of the ductus arteriosus
variables.why: Before birth, prostaglandins and low oxygen keep the ductus’s smooth muscle relaxed. Blocking prostaglandin synthesis removes one of those signals, so the ductus narrows.

variables.name: Blood flow from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta
variables.why: A narrower channel carries less blood for the same pressure difference, so less of the right ventricle’s output bypasses the lungs.

variables.name: Blood flow into the fetal lungs
variables.why: The right ventricle’s output has to go somewhere. With its bypass narrowed, more of it enters the pulmonary arteries.

variables.name: Pressure in the pulmonary trunk
variables.why: The fetal lungs resist flow strongly. Pushing more blood into them raises pressure in the pulmonary trunk and the work of the right ventricle, which is why such drugs are avoided late in pregnancy.

scenarios.title: XY with androgen insensitivity
scenarios.misconception: a Y chromosome alone decides that every structure develops as male
scenarios.setup: An XY embryo has working testes, but its receptor protein for testosterone and DHT does not work. Compare its development with a typical XY embryo’s.
scenarios.start: No tissue can respond to androgens

steps.sry: SRY still makes the gonads testes
steps.amh: Sertoli cells still secrete anti-Müllerian hormone
steps.wolff: Without a response to testosterone, the mesonephric ducts break down
steps.ext: Without a response to DHT, the external structures develop as female

variables.name: Anti-Müllerian hormone secretion
variables.why: Anti-Müllerian hormone comes from the Sertoli cells, and its action does not use the androgen receptor protein, so it is secreted and works as in any XY embryo.

variables.name: Development of a uterus and uterine tubes
variables.why: Anti-Müllerian hormone still removes the paramesonephric ducts, so, as in a typical XY embryo, no uterus or uterine tubes form.

variables.name: Development of the epididymis and ductus deferens
variables.why: Testosterone keeps the mesonephric ducts. Here the testes make it, but the ducts cannot respond, so they break down as in a female.

variables.name: Growth of the external bump into a penis
variables.why: DHT makes the bump grow into a penis and the swellings fuse into a scrotum. With no working receptor protein, the external genitalia develop as female.

scenarios.title: A glucocorticoid before a preterm birth
scenarios.misconception: the steroid given before a preterm birth is for the mother
scenarios.setup: At 30 weeks, a woman is in early preterm labor. She is given a glucocorticoid, which crosses to the fetus, and the baby is born two days later. Compare the baby with one born at 30 weeks without it.
scenarios.start: The glucocorticoid reaches the fetal lungs

steps.type2: Type II alveolar cells mature faster
steps.tension: Surface tension in the alveoli is lower after birth
steps.open: Fewer alveoli collapse at the end of each breath

variables.name: Surfactant in the lungs at birth
variables.why: Surfactant is usually enough only by about weeks 34 to 36. The glucocorticoid speeds the type II cells toward making it, so more is present at 30 weeks.

variables.name: Alveoli collapsing at the end of each breath
variables.why: Surfactant lowers the surface tension that pulls the wet alveolar walls together, so fewer alveoli collapse when the baby breathes out.

variables.name: Lung compliance after birth
variables.why: Surface tension is a major part of what makes lungs stiff. Lowering it makes the lungs easier to stretch.

variables.name: Work of breathing
variables.why: With alveoli staying partly open and the lungs more compliant, each breath does not have to reopen collapsed alveoli from scratch.

scenarios.title: A large ventricular septal defect after birth
scenarios.misconception: a hole between the ventricles lets oxygen-poor blood reach the body
scenarios.setup: A baby is born with a large hole in the membranous part of the interventricular septum. Predict the changes a few weeks after birth, once pressures on the left are well above those on the right, compared with a baby with an intact septum.
scenarios.start: Left ventricular pressure is higher than right ventricular pressure, and a hole joins them

steps.shunt: In systole, blood flows through the hole from the left ventricle to the right
steps.lungs: That blood is pumped into the pulmonary trunk along with the normal right-sided flow
steps.back: The extra lung blood returns to the left atrium and left ventricle
steps.mix: Oxygen-rich blood enters the right side; no oxygen-poor blood enters the left

variables.name: Blood flow through the lungs
variables.why: Blood flows down the pressure gradient from the left ventricle into the right, which pumps it to the lungs on top of its own share: the extra blood recirculates through the lungs.

variables.name: Volume load on the left atrium and left ventricle
variables.why: The extra blood sent to the lungs comes back through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and left ventricle, so they handle more volume each beat.

variables.name: Oxygen saturation of blood in the aorta
variables.why: Flow is left to right: oxygen-rich blood leaks into the right side, but no oxygen-poor blood crosses to the left. The aorta still receives fully oxygenated blood, so the baby is not blue.

scenarios.title: Lying flat on the back at 34 weeks
scenarios.misconception: lying down always raises venous return
scenarios.setup: At 34 weeks, a pregnant woman lies flat on her back on an examination table. Within minutes she feels dizzy and sweaty. Predict the changes, compared with lying on her left side.
scenarios.start: The heavy uterus presses on the inferior vena cava

steps.vr: Less blood returns from the lower body to the right atrium
steps.sv: Preload falls, so stroke volume falls
steps.baro: Baroreceptors fire less, and the baroreceptor reflex speeds the heart
steps.plac: Less blood flows to the uterus and placenta

variables.name: Venous return from the lower body
variables.why: The inferior vena cava runs just behind the uterus. When she lies on her back, the uterus squeezes it, so less blood gets back to the heart.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less venous return means less filling of the ventricles. By the Frank–Starling mechanism, a less stretched ventricle ejects less.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Cardiac output falls with stroke volume. With resistance already low in pregnancy, blood pressure drops, which is why she feels dizzy.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The fall in pressure unloads the baroreceptors, and the reflex raises sympathetic drive to the heart, which speeds it.

variables.name: Blood flow to the placenta
variables.why: The uterine vessels cannot constrict to protect their flow, so placental flow falls with the mother’s pressure and output. Turning her onto her left side lifts the uterus off the vein.

scenarios.title: Blood at 32 weeks of pregnancy
scenarios.misconception: a lower hemoglobin in pregnancy means fewer red cells
scenarios.setup: Compare a healthy woman’s blood and circulation at 32 weeks of pregnancy with her values before pregnancy.
scenarios.start: Progesterone and other signals relax arterioles, and the placenta adds a low-resistance bed

steps.raas: The circulation is sensed as underfilled, and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system switches on
steps.na: The kidneys keep more sodium, and water follows
steps.plasma: Plasma volume rises by about 40 to 50%
steps.epo: Erythropoietin drives the marrow to make more red cells, a rise of about 20 to 30%
steps.dilute: Plasma rises more than red cells, so the blood is diluted

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: With resistance low, the kidneys sense the circulation as underfilled and release renin, which switches on angiotensin II and aldosterone.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium, and water follows the solute, so plasma volume climbs, peaking around weeks 32 to 34.

variables.name: Total red cell mass
variables.why: Erythropoietin rises in pregnancy, so the marrow makes more red cells. The body ends up with more red cells than before.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: Plasma rises by 40 to 50% but red cells by only 20 to 30%, so each liter of blood holds a smaller share of cells: dilutional anemia of pregnancy.

variables.name: Hemoglobin concentration
variables.why: Hemoglobin is measured per deciliter, so the same dilution lowers it, to about 11 g/dL in a healthy pregnancy, even though total hemoglobin has risen.

scenarios.title: Progesterone and breathing in pregnancy
scenarios.misconception: breathlessness in early pregnancy means the lungs are squeezed by the uterus
scenarios.setup: In early pregnancy, a woman’s progesterone climbs. Her oxygen use rises only a little, yet she often feels short of breath. Follow her blood gases.

stages.label: As progesterone rises
stages.prompt: In the first days of the change, before her kidneys have responded, compared with before pregnancy.
stages.start: Progesterone makes the brainstem’s chemoreceptors more sensitive to carbon dioxide

steps.vent: The same carbon dioxide level drives more breathing, so minute ventilation rises
steps.co2: She breathes off carbon dioxide faster than she makes it, so PaCO2 falls
steps.ph: Less carbon dioxide means less carbonic acid, so pH rises: a respiratory alkalosis
steps.grad: The carbon dioxide gradient from fetal to maternal blood is steeper

variables.name: Minute ventilation
variables.why: More sensitive chemoreceptors respond to her normal carbon dioxide as if it were high, so tidal volume, and with it minute ventilation, rises.

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: Breathing rises more than her carbon dioxide production, so she clears carbon dioxide faster than she makes it and PaCO2 falls; later in pregnancy it settles near 30 mm Hg.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Lower carbon dioxide shifts the carbonic acid equilibrium toward less acid, so H+ falls and pH rises: a respiratory alkalosis.

variables.name: Ease with which the fetus unloads carbon dioxide across the placenta, once it depends on the placenta
variables.why: Carbon dioxide diffuses from fetal to maternal blood down its gradient. A lower maternal PaCO2 makes that gradient steeper.

stages.label: After the kidneys respond
stages.prompt: Weeks later, once her kidneys have compensated, compared with the first stage.
stages.start: Her kidneys respond to the alkalosis

steps.excrete: The kidneys excrete more bicarbonate and secrete less H+
steps.hco3: Plasma bicarbonate falls, to about 18 to 22 mEq/L
steps.ph: pH returns toward normal, near 7.40 to 7.45
steps.drive: Progesterone keeps her breathing drive high

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Renal compensation for a respiratory alkalosis is to excrete bicarbonate, so the plasma bicarbonate falls.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: With both carbon dioxide and bicarbonate lower, their ratio moves back toward normal, so pH falls back toward the normal range, ending near 7.40 to 7.45.

variables.name: PaCO2
variables.why: The cause, progesterone’s effect on the chemoreceptors, is still there, so she keeps breathing more and PaCO2 stays near 30 mm Hg. The kidneys correct the pH, not the carbon dioxide.

scenarios.title: Preeclampsia
scenarios.misconception: preeclampsia is just high blood pressure caused by the extra blood volume
scenarios.setup: Early in a woman’s first pregnancy, the spiral arteries are remodeled only shallowly. At 34 weeks she develops preeclampsia. Predict her state compared with a healthy pregnancy at 34 weeks.
scenarios.start: The spiral arteries stay narrow, so the placenta is short of blood

steps.factors: The stressed placenta releases factors that block blood vessel growth into her blood
steps.endo: Her endothelium is damaged throughout her body
steps.leak: Her capillaries leak, so fluid moves into the tissues
steps.glom: The glomerular endothelium swells and leaks protein
steps.plt: Platelets are used up on the damaged endothelium
steps.fetus: Less blood reaches the villi, so the fetus gets less oxygen and glucose

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Healthy endothelium keeps arterioles relaxed. Damaged endothelium lets them constrict, so resistance climbs, reversing the usual fall of pregnancy.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. With resistance up, pressure rises to 140/90 mm Hg or more.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Leaky capillaries let fluid move out of the plasma into the tissues, which is why she has edema while her plasma volume falls.

variables.name: Protein in her urine
variables.why: The damaged glomerular endothelium lets protein through the filter, and GFR falls.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Platelets stick to damaged endothelium and are used up faster than the marrow replaces them.

variables.name: Fetal growth
variables.why: The same shallow remodeling that starts the disease limits blood flow to the placenta, so the fetus often grows too slowly.

scenarios.title: Gestational diabetes
scenarios.misconception: the mother’s insulin protects the fetus from her high glucose
scenarios.setup: At 28 weeks, a woman’s beta cells cannot secrete enough extra insulin to overcome the insulin resistance of late pregnancy. Compare her and her baby with a pregnancy in which glucose stays normal.
scenarios.start: Placental hormones reduce her cells’ response to insulin, and her beta cells cannot keep up

steps.mglu: Her glucose rises higher and stays up longer after meals
steps.cross: More glucose crosses the placenta, down a steeper gradient
steps.fins: The fetal pancreas secretes more insulin
steps.big: Fetal insulin drives growth, so the baby grows large
steps.cut: After birth, cutting the cord stops the supply of the mother’s glucose
steps.low: The baby’s pancreas is still secreting extra insulin, so its glucose falls

variables.name: Her blood glucose after a meal
variables.why: Human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol and a placental growth hormone make her cells respond less to insulin. When her beta cells cannot make up for it, glucose climbs after meals.

variables.name: Fetal insulin secretion
variables.why: Glucose crosses the placenta but her insulin does not, so fetal glucose rises and the fetal pancreas answers with more insulin of its own.

variables.name: Birth weight
variables.why: Extra glucose plus extra fetal insulin means more fuel stored as fat and more growth, which also makes the shoulders more likely to get stuck at delivery.

variables.name: The baby’s blood glucose in the first hours after birth
variables.why: The mother’s glucose supply ends when the cord is cut, but the baby’s pancreas has been secreting extra insulin and does not stop at once, so its glucose can fall dangerously low. It is checked soon after birth.

scenarios.title: A progesterone blocker in late pregnancy
scenarios.misconception: labor can begin only once progesterone in the blood has fallen
scenarios.setup: Mifepristone, a drug that blocks progesterone receptor proteins, is given to a woman late in pregnancy. Predict the changes over the next day, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: Progesterone can no longer act on the myometrium and cervix

steps.blood: Progesterone keeps circulating; only its effect is blocked
steps.quiet: The brake that keeps the myometrium quiet is lifted

variables.name: Progesterone in her blood
variables.why: The drug blocks the receptor proteins, not the placenta’s production, so the hormone level stays high. This copies the functional progesterone withdrawal of natural labor.

variables.name: Uterine contractions
variables.why: Progesterone acting on its receptor proteins keeps the myometrium quiet. Blocking that action frees the muscle to contract.

variables.name: Softening of the cervix
variables.why: Losing progesterone’s effect lets the cervix’s collagen be broken down and rearranged, so it ripens, at any stage of pregnancy.

scenarios.title: An oxytocin drip for weak contractions
scenarios.misconception: giving oxytocin is what starts the positive feedback loop from nothing
scenarios.setup: A woman in the dilation stage has weak, infrequent contractions and her cervix is opening slowly. Synthetic oxytocin is started through a drip. Predict the immediate effects.
scenarios.start: More oxytocin reaches the myometrium

steps.bind: Oxytocin binds its receptor proteins on myometrial cells, which are very numerous at term
steps.ca: Calcium is released inside the cells, so each contraction is stronger
steps.pg: The uterine lining releases more prostaglandins

variables.name: Strength of each contraction
variables.why: Through a G protein and IP3, oxytocin releases calcium inside the smooth muscle cells, and more calcium means a stronger contraction.

variables.name: Prostaglandin release in the uterus
variables.why: Oxytocin also makes the uterine lining release prostaglandins, which add to the contraction.

scenarios.title: A soft uterus after the placenta is out
scenarios.misconception: clotting is the main brake on bleeding after birth
scenarios.setup: Minutes after delivering the placenta, a woman’s uterus feels soft and relaxed instead of firm. Predict the changes over the next half hour if nothing is done, compared with a firmly contracted uterus.
scenarios.start: The myometrium stays relaxed (uterine atony)

steps.pinch: The crisscrossing muscle fibers do not pinch the placental-bed arteries shut
steps.bleed: Blood pours out of the open vessels
steps.bp: Venous return and cardiac output fall, so blood pressure falls
steps.baro: The baroreceptor reflex speeds her heart

variables.name: Compression of the vessels at the placental site
variables.why: The fibers of the upper uterus wrap around the vessels that fed the placenta. They clamp them shut only when they contract firmly; a relaxed uterus leaves them open.

variables.name: Blood loss
variables.why: About half a liter a minute reached the placental bed. With the vessels left open, bleeding is heavy: atony causes most postpartum hemorrhage.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Losing blood volume lowers venous return, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall, and pressure drops once the reflexes cannot make up for it.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The falling pressure unloads the baroreceptors, and sympathetic drive speeds the heart to prop up cardiac output.

scenarios.title: The first breath and the cord clamp
scenarios.misconception: the shunts close because the baby no longer needs them
scenarios.setup: A term baby is born, takes its first breaths and cries, and the umbilical cord is clamped. Predict the changes over the first minutes to hours, compared with just before birth.
scenarios.start: Air fills the lungs and the cord is clamped

steps.expand: Air stretches the lungs open and oxygen in the alveoli rises
steps.relax: Rising oxygen and nitric oxide relax the pulmonary arterioles
steps.lungflow: Blood flow through the lungs rises about eightfold
steps.la: Much more blood returns to the left atrium, raising its pressure
steps.clamp: Clamping removes the low-resistance placenta from the circuit
steps.svr: Systemic resistance and aortic pressure rise
steps.ra: No blood arrives from the umbilical vein, so right atrial pressure falls
steps.fo: The flap of the foramen ovale is pressed shut
steps.da: Oxygen-rich blood reverses through the ductus arteriosus, and falling prostaglandin lets it constrict

variables.name: Pulmonary vascular resistance
variables.why: Before birth, low oxygen kept the pulmonary arterioles constricted. Air brings oxygen, which, with nitric oxide, relaxes them, and inflating the lungs opens their vessels.

variables.name: Blood flow through the lungs
variables.why: With resistance in the lungs far lower, the right ventricle’s output flows into them instead of past them.

variables.name: Systemic vascular resistance
variables.why: The placenta was a wide, low-resistance bed taking a large share of the output. Clamping the cord removes it, so resistance in the systemic circuit rises.

variables.name: Left atrial pressure
variables.why: All that extra lung blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, so its pressure climbs.

variables.name: Right atrial pressure
variables.why: Blood from the placenta no longer arrives through the umbilical vein and inferior vena cava, so less returns to the right atrium.

variables.name: Flow through the foramen ovale
variables.why: With left atrial pressure now above right, the septum primum is pushed against the rim of the opening like a door shut from the far side, and flow stops within minutes to hours.

variables.name: Oxygen saturation of the baby’s arterial blood
variables.why: The lungs, not the placenta, now load oxygen, and they deliver it at far higher partial pressures than the umbilical vein did.

variables.name: Diameter of the ductus arteriosus
variables.why: With aortic pressure above pulmonary pressure, flow through the ductus reverses, bringing oxygen-rich blood to its wall. Rising oxygen and falling prostaglandin E2 make its smooth muscle contract over one to three days.

scenarios.title: The ductus arteriosus stays open
scenarios.misconception: a patent ductus arteriosus makes a baby blue
scenarios.setup: A baby born at 27 weeks has a ductus arteriosus that is still open a week after birth. Compare the baby with one whose ductus has closed.
scenarios.start: The ductus stays open while aortic pressure is now higher than pulmonary pressure

steps.flow: Blood flows from the aorta back into the pulmonary trunk, in systole and diastole
steps.left: The extra blood returns to the left atrium and left ventricle
steps.run: Blood draining out of the aorta during diastole lowers diastolic pressure
steps.sat: No oxygen-poor blood enters the aorta

variables.name: Blood flow through the lungs
variables.why: After birth the pressure difference runs the other way from before: aorta higher than pulmonary trunk. So blood crosses left to right and adds to the flow the right ventricle sends to the lungs.

variables.name: Volume handled by the left ventricle each beat
variables.why: The blood that leaked into the lungs comes back through the pulmonary veins, so the left heart pumps that extra volume on every beat.

variables.name: Diastolic blood pressure
variables.why: Normally the aorta holds its pressure during diastole. With an open ductus, blood keeps running off into the low-pressure pulmonary circuit, so diastolic pressure sags.

variables.name: Pulse pressure
variables.why: With diastolic pressure lower and systolic held up by the larger stroke volume, the gap between them widens, and the pulses feel bounding.

variables.name: Oxygen saturation of blood reaching the body
variables.why: The shunt runs from the aorta to the lungs. Blood already oxygenated recirculates through the lungs, but no oxygen-poor blood reaches the body, so the baby is not blue.

scenarios.title: A wet newborn in a cool room
scenarios.misconception: newborns warm themselves mainly by shivering
scenarios.setup: A term baby is born into a delivery room about 10 °C cooler than the uterus and is left wet and uncovered for a few minutes. Follow its temperature and its brown fat.

stages.label: The first minutes
stages.prompt: In the first minutes, before its defenses have caught up, compared with just before birth.
stages.start: Wet skin meets cool air

steps.evap: Amniotic fluid evaporates from the skin, carrying heat away
steps.surface: The large surface for its size loses heat fast by radiation and convection
steps.core: Heat loss outruns heat production, so core temperature falls

variables.name: Rate of heat loss
variables.why: Evaporating fluid takes heat with it, and a newborn has about three times as much skin per kilogram as an adult, so it loses heat far faster than in the uterus.

variables.name: Skin temperature
variables.why: The skin is where the heat leaves, so it cools first, which is also what the cold-sensing sensory receptors detect.

variables.name: Core temperature
variables.why: With thin insulation and weak shivering, heat production cannot match the loss at first, so the baby can lose a degree or more within minutes.

stages.label: Once brown fat is running
stages.prompt: Some minutes later, once the brown fat response is under way, compared with the first stage.
stages.start: Cold skin sends signals to the hypothalamus

steps.symp: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto brown fat
steps.burn: Brown fat cells break down their fat and let H+ leak back across their mitochondria’s inner membrane
steps.heat: The energy leaves as heat instead of ATP
steps.cost: Burning fat uses oxygen and glucose fast

variables.name: Heat production
variables.why: Nonshivering thermogenesis in brown fat is the newborn’s main defense: the channel protein lets H+ flow back without making ATP, so the energy becomes heat.

variables.name: Oxygen use
variables.why: Running the mitochondria flat out to make heat consumes oxygen fast, so a cold baby can run short of oxygen.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: The heat-making work draws on glucose as well as fat, so a baby kept cold can become low in blood glucose. Drying it and placing it skin to skin avoids that cost.

scenarios.title: Born at 28 weeks without surfactant
scenarios.misconception: a preterm baby breathes badly mainly because its muscles are weak
scenarios.setup: A baby is born at 28 weeks, before its type II alveolar cells make enough surfactant, and its mother did not receive a glucocorticoid. Compare it with a term baby over the first hours.
scenarios.start: Too little surfactant lines the alveoli

steps.tension: Surface tension in the wet alveoli stays high
steps.collapse: Many alveoli collapse at the end of every breath
steps.stiff: The lungs are stiff, so each breath is like the first
steps.tire: The baby tires and breathes less effectively
steps.gas: Less of the lung exchanges gas

variables.name: Alveoli collapsing at the end of each breath
variables.why: Surfactant is what lowers surface tension once the alveoli have opened. Without it, the tension pulls the walls together each time the baby breathes out.

variables.name: Lung compliance
variables.why: High surface tension and collapsed alveoli make the lungs hard to stretch, so each breath needs a larger pressure.

variables.name: Breathing rate
variables.why: Stiff lungs take in only small breaths, so the baby breathes fast, over 60 a minute, often with grunting to hold some pressure in its airways.

variables.name: Arterial oxygen
variables.why: Collapsed alveoli take no part in gas exchange, so less oxygen is loaded into the blood.

variables.name: Arterial carbon dioxide
variables.why: As the baby tires, its breaths move too little air, and carbon dioxide builds up in the blood.

scenarios.title: Pain and fear during a feed
scenarios.misconception: a mother whose milk will not flow must not be making any
scenarios.setup: A week after birth, a mother tries to feed her baby while in pain from a sore wound and anxious. Her breasts are full, but the baby gets little milk. Compare this feed with a calm, painless one.
scenarios.start: Pain, fear and stress act on the hypothalamus

steps.oxy: Oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary is inhibited
steps.myo: The myoepithelial cells around the alveoli contract less
steps.flow: Less milk is squeezed into the ducts toward the nipple
steps.made: The milk already made by the alveolar cells is still there

variables.name: Oxytocin released during the feed
variables.why: The hypothalamus sits in the milk ejection reflex, so the brain can stop it: pain, fear and stress inhibit the oxytocin neurons.

variables.name: Contraction of the myoepithelial cells
variables.why: Oxytocin is the signal that makes the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus contract. Less oxytocin, weaker squeeze.

variables.name: Milk reaching the baby
variables.why: A baby cannot suck milk out of the alveoli; it must be squeezed toward the nipple. Without let-down, little reaches the baby.

variables.name: Milk the alveolar cells made before this feed began
variables.why: Making milk is prolactin’s job and happened between feeds. The milk is there; it is simply not ejected. That is why the breasts can feel full while the baby gets little.

scenarios.title: A piece of placenta left behind
scenarios.misconception: milk comes in as soon as the baby is born because prolactin rises at birth
scenarios.setup: After a birth, a small piece of placenta stays attached inside the uterus. Compare the mother’s first week with that of a mother whose placenta was delivered whole.
scenarios.start: Placental tissue keeps secreting progesterone

steps.p4: Progesterone stays high instead of falling within days
steps.block: Progesterone keeps blocking prolactin’s action on the alveolar cells
steps.prl: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stays high

variables.name: Progesterone in her blood in the first days
variables.why: Delivering the placenta normally removes the main source of progesterone. Tissue left behind keeps making it.

variables.name: Milk production on day 3
variables.why: High progesterone is the brake that held back full production in pregnancy. While it stays up, the alveolar cells do not switch on, so the milk is late to come in.

variables.name: Prolactin
variables.why: Prolactin is high in late pregnancy and after birth either way. The problem is not a lack of prolactin but progesterone blocking its effect.

scenarios.title: A mother of 40 instead of 25
scenarios.misconception: every kind of Down syndrome is more likely with an older mother
scenarios.setup: Compare a pregnancy in a woman of 40 with a pregnancy in the same woman at 25. Her chromosomes are normal.
scenarios.start: Her oocyte has been paused in meiosis I for 40 years instead of 25

steps.glue: The proteins holding its paired chromosomes together have weakened
steps.nd: Nondisjunction in meiosis I is more likely
steps.t21: More of her oocytes carry two copies of chromosome 21, so a fertilized one is more likely to be trisomic
steps.trans: A translocation form arises from a rearrangement, not from the pause

variables.name: Chance of nondisjunction in her oocyte
variables.why: The protein links laid down before her birth are never replaced, so after four decades homologs are more likely to separate wrongly in meiosis I.

variables.name: Chance of trisomy 21 in the pregnancy
variables.why: About 95% of trisomy 21 comes from nondisjunction, mostly in the mother’s meiosis I. The risk climbs from about 1 in 1,200 births at 25 to about 1 in 100 at 40.

variables.name: Chance of the translocation form of Down syndrome
variables.why: In about 4% of cases, the extra chromosome 21 is attached to another chromosome. That form comes from a rearrangement, in about a quarter of cases carried by a parent, and does not depend on the mother’s age.

scenarios.title: PKU found by newborn screening
scenarios.misconception: a genotype fixes the phenotype whatever the environment
scenarios.setup: Newborn screening shows a baby has phenylketonuria: two nonworking alleles for the enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine. The baby is fed a low-phenylalanine diet. Compare the child with an untreated child who has the same genotype.
scenarios.start: Little phenylalanine is eaten

steps.phe: Phenylalanine does not build up in the blood
steps.brain: The developing brain is not damaged

variables.name: Blood phenylalanine
variables.why: The enzyme still does not work, but the diet supplies little phenylalanine, so there is little to build up.

variables.name: Brain damage by school age
variables.why: It is the buildup of phenylalanine that damages the developing brain. Kept low, the child grows up with normal intelligence: same genotype, different phenotype.

variables.name: Number of nonworking alleles the child carries
variables.why: Diet changes the phenotype, not the genotype. The child still has two nonworking alleles and can pass one to each of its children.

scenarios.title: Human cells dividing in a dish
scenarios.misconception: normal body cells can divide without limit if they are well fed
scenarios.setup: Normal human fibroblasts, which make almost no telomerase, are grown in a dish and allowed to divide 40 times. Compare them with the same cells at the start.
scenarios.start: Each division leaves a little of each chromosome’s end uncopied

steps.short: Telomeres lose about 50 to 100 base pairs per division
steps.cap: Some telomeres become too short for their protective cap
steps.damage: The cell reads the bare end as damaged DNA, and checkpoint proteins such as p53 stop the cycle

variables.name: Average telomere length
variables.why: DNA polymerase cannot copy the very tip of one new strand, the end-replication problem, and without telomerase nothing adds the lost repeats back.

variables.name: Share of cells that have stopped dividing for good
variables.why: When a telomere gets too short, its cap fails, checkpoint proteins read the end as broken DNA, and the cell enters senescence. This is the Hayflick limit.

variables.name: Divisions the culture has left
variables.why: Normal human cells manage only about 40 to 60 divisions. After 40, most of that allowance is used up.

scenarios.title: A stiff aorta at 75
scenarios.misconception: blood pressure rises with age mainly because the heart pumps harder
scenarios.setup: Compare the aorta and heart of a healthy 75-year-old with those of the same person at 30.
scenarios.start: Elastic fibers in the aorta fragment and are replaced by stiff, cross-linked collagen

steps.stretch: The aorta cannot stretch to absorb each stroke volume
steps.recoil: Less energy is stored for recoil in diastole
steps.pp: The gap between systolic and diastolic pressure widens
steps.after: The left ventricle pumps against a higher afterload
steps.lvh: The left ventricle thickens and stiffens
steps.fill: It fills more slowly early in diastole

variables.name: Systolic pressure
variables.why: A compliant aorta balloons out to take each stroke volume, blunting the peak. A stiff one cannot, so the same ejection gives a higher systolic pressure.

variables.name: Pulse pressure
variables.why: Systolic pressure rises while diastolic stays level or falls, because a stiff aorta stores less energy to recoil on. The gap widens: isolated systolic hypertension.

variables.name: Thickness of the left ventricular wall
variables.why: Pumping against a higher pressure every beat is a higher afterload, and the muscle thickens in response.

variables.name: Filling of the left ventricle early in diastole
variables.why: A thicker, stiffer ventricle relaxes and stretches more slowly, so it relies more on the atrium’s contraction to finish filling.

scenarios.title: Standing up quickly at 80
scenarios.misconception: dizziness on standing in older adults is just part of normal resting blood pressure
scenarios.setup: A healthy 80-year-old and a healthy 25-year-old each stand up quickly from lying down. Compare the 80-year-old with the 25-year-old in the first half minute.
scenarios.start: Standing pools blood in the legs, and the stiffer arteries of the older person stretch less

steps.signal: The baroreceptors in stiff arterial walls signal the fall in pressure more weakly
steps.slow: The baroreceptor reflex responds more slowly
steps.hr: The heart responds less to sympathetic stimulation
steps.drop: Blood pressure falls further before it is corrected
steps.brain: Less blood reaches the brain for a few seconds

variables.name: Rise in heart rate on standing
variables.why: A weaker, slower baroreceptor signal and a heart less responsive to sympathetic stimulation give a smaller heart rate response.
