variables.name: Size of the fall in blood pressure
variables.why: The reflex that should restore pressure within seconds acts late and weakly, so pressure falls further: orthostatic hypotension.

variables.name: Risk of a fall
variables.why: Briefly low blood flow to the brain causes dizziness, and together with weaker muscles and poorer balance it makes a fall likely.

scenarios.title: A usual adult dose at 85
scenarios.misconception: a normal plasma creatinine means an older person’s kidneys clear drugs normally
scenarios.setup: An 85-year-old with a normal plasma creatinine is given the usual adult dose of a water-soluble drug that the kidneys clear. Compare her with a 35-year-old given the same dose.
scenarios.start: Her kidneys have lost nephrons over the decades

steps.muscle: She has less muscle, so she makes less creatinine
steps.clear: She clears the drug more slowly
steps.water: Her total body water is lower, so the drug is less diluted
steps.level: The drug’s level in her blood climbs higher and stays up longer

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: GFR falls on average by about 1 mL/min a year after about 40, as nephrons are lost.

variables.name: Plasma creatinine
variables.why: Lower GFR would raise creatinine, but she makes less of it from less muscle, so it can stay in the normal range, which is why eGFR, corrected for age, is used.

variables.name: Drug level in her blood
variables.why: A lower GFR clears the drug more slowly, and less body water leaves it more concentrated, so the same dose gives a higher level: “start low and go slow”.

scenarios.title: Influenza at 82
scenarios.misconception: an older person with normal values at rest will handle an illness like a younger one
scenarios.setup: Mrs. Castillo, 82, had normal heart rate, blood pressure, sodium and oxygen saturation at her checkup. Two months later she catches influenza. Compare her first days with those of a 30-year-old with the same infection.
scenarios.start: The infection loads systems whose reserve has narrowed

steps.rest: At rest, before the infection, her values were in range
steps.immune: An aging immune system and blunted fever response
steps.thirst: Blunted thirst and kidneys that conserve water less well
steps.na: She loses water faster than she replaces it, so her blood sodium climbs
steps.brain: Less brain reserve, plus infection and dehydration

variables.name: Her resting values before the infection
variables.why: Normal aging usually keeps resting values in range. What shrinks is reserve, the extra capacity called on under stress.

variables.name: Height of her fever
variables.why: Fever is often blunted in older adults, so a serious infection can show little or no fever.

variables.name: Blood sodium
variables.why: Her thirst is blunted and her kidneys concentrate urine less well, so water lost to fever and fast breathing is not replaced and sodium rises.

variables.name: Chance of confusion
variables.why: An infection in an older person often shows first as confusion: the brain has less reserve, and dehydration and abnormal sodium add to the strain.

scenarios.title: Resistance training at 70
scenarios.misconception: the loss of muscle with age cannot be reversed
scenarios.setup: A healthy but inactive 70-year-old starts supervised resistance training three times a week. Compare her after three months with before.
scenarios.start: Repeated heavy loads stimulate her skeletal muscle

steps.fibers: Her muscle fibers enlarge and her motor units are recruited more effectively
steps.falls: Stronger legs and better balance make a fall less likely
steps.hr: Maximum heart rate is set by age, not by strength training

variables.name: Leg strength
variables.why: Resistance training reverses much of sarcopenia at any age: nervous system changes come first, then larger fibers. People in their nineties have more than doubled their leg strength in eight weeks.

variables.name: Risk of a fall
variables.why: Weak muscles are a major cause of falls. Stronger legs catch a stumble and steady a turn.

variables.name: Maximum heart rate
variables.why: Maximum heart rate falls by roughly 0.7 to 1 beat per minute each year as the SA node loses pacemaker cells and the heart responds less to sympathetic stimulation. Strength training does not change that.

scenarios.title: The pubic symphysis through pregnancy and after
scenarios.misconception: a joint that loosens in pregnancy has changed into a different kind of joint
scenarios.setup: Ms. Reyes is 32 weeks pregnant. Her pubic symphysis, a pad of fibrocartilage between the two pubic bones, is normally about 4 to 5 mm wide. Follow the joint through late pregnancy and then through the months after delivery.

stages.label: Late pregnancy
stages.prompt: In late pregnancy, compared with before she was pregnant.
stages.start: Pregnancy hormones loosen the collagen in the fibrocartilage pad and the ligaments over it

steps.stretch: The pad and its ligaments stretch more under load
steps.gap: The gap between the pubic bones widens by a few millimeters
steps.shift: The bones shift more each time weight moves from one leg to the other
steps.canal: The front of the pelvic ring gives a little, so the birth canal widens slightly

variables.name: Width of the gap between the pubic bones
variables.why: Looser collagen stretches farther under the same load, so the pad and ligaments let the two pubic bones drift apart by a few millimeters.

variables.name: Movement at the joint with each step
variables.why: The tissue that limits movement is now stretchier, and movement at a joint is set by how much its connecting tissue gives. So each shift of weight moves the bones more.

variables.name: How well the joint resists being pushed out of line
variables.why: Mobility and stability pull against each other: tissue that gives more also holds the bones less firmly, so shearing forces move the joint surfaces more easily.

variables.name: Width of the birth canal
variables.why: The pubic symphysis is the front of the pelvic ring. A wider, looser joint there lets the ring open slightly, which is the extra give that helps at birth.

variables.name: Amount of fibrocartilage joining the two pubic bones
variables.why: The pad is still there and still fibrocartilage, so the joint is still a symphysis. Only how stretchy its collagen is has changed, and the movement followed.

stages.label: Months after delivery
stages.prompt: Some months after delivery, compared with late pregnancy.
stages.start: After delivery, the collagen of the pad and its ligaments tightens again

steps.stiff: The pad and its ligaments stretch less under load
steps.narrow: The gap narrows back toward its usual 4 to 5 mm
steps.less: The bones shift less each time weight moves from one leg to the other
steps.ease: The joint surfaces shear less, so the pain with walking and stairs eases

variables.name: Width of the gap between the pubic bones
variables.why: Tighter collagen pulls the bones back together, and the gap usually returns to near normal within months.

variables.name: Movement at the joint with each step
variables.why: Tissue that stretches less allows the bones to move less, so the joint goes back to being only slightly movable, an amphiarthrosis.

variables.name: How well the joint resists being pushed out of line
variables.why: The same trade-off in reverse: as the tissue tightens and mobility falls, the joint holds its bones more firmly.

variables.name: Pain at the front of the pelvis on stairs
variables.why: The pain came from the joint surfaces shearing as the loose joint shifted. Less shift means less shearing, so the pain fades.

scenarios.title: A growth plate closes
scenarios.misconception: the epiphyseal plate is a movable joint that stiffens when it closes
scenarios.setup: At 13, the epiphyseal plate of a boy’s femur is still open. By 20 he has stopped growing taller. Compare the site of the plate at 20 with the same site at 13.
scenarios.start: Growth in length of the femur stops

steps.replace: Bone replaces the hyaline cartilage of the epiphyseal plate
steps.line: The plate becomes a thin line of dense bone, the epiphyseal line
steps.fuse: The epiphysis and diaphysis are now one piece of bone: the synchondrosis has become a synostosis

variables.name: Hyaline cartilage at the site of the plate
variables.why: When growth in length ends, bone replaces the plate’s hyaline cartilage, so almost none is left at that site.

variables.name: Growth in length at that end of the femur
variables.why: Growth in length happens in the plate’s cartilage. Once it is replaced by the bone of the epiphyseal line, that end can no longer lengthen.

variables.name: Movement between the epiphysis and the diaphysis
variables.why: A synchondrosis is already a synarthrosis: the hyaline cartilage held the two parts almost immobile. Fusing them into one bone does not change that.

variables.name: Number of separate bony pieces making up that end of the femur
variables.why: Before, cartilage joined two pieces, the epiphysis and diaphysis. Once bone fills the gap, the two fuse into one: a synostosis.

scenarios.title: A skull suture fuses too early
scenarios.misconception: a baby’s skull grows by expanding evenly in every direction regardless of its sutures
scenarios.setup: In an infant, bone grows across the sagittal suture months after birth, fusing the two parietal bones, while the brain keeps growing fast. Compare the skull over the following months with a baby whose sutures are all open.
scenarios.start: Bone replaces the fibrous tissue of one suture

steps.fuse: The two bones on either side of that suture fuse into one: a synostosis
steps.stop: The skull can no longer grow at that seam
steps.other: The growing brain pushes the skull out along the sutures that are still open
steps.shape: The head grows long in the direction of the fused seam and narrow across it

variables.name: Skull growth across the fused seam
variables.why: A skull grows at its sutures, where the fibrous tissue lets the bone edges move apart and new bone form. Once bone bridges the seam, that growth stops.

variables.name: Skull growth at the sutures that are still open
variables.why: The brain keeps growing and presses outward. Blocked at one seam, the skull grows more at the open sutures instead.

variables.name: Length of the head from front to back
variables.why: With the sagittal seam fused, the skull cannot widen across it, so extra growth goes front to back and the head becomes long and narrow. This is craniosynostosis.

variables.name: Width of the head from side to side
variables.why: Side-to-side growth of the top of the skull happens at the sagittal suture, which runs front to back. With it fused, the head stays narrow compared with a baby whose sutures are open.

scenarios.title: A knee held still in a brace
scenarios.misconception: articular cartilage is fed by its own blood vessels
scenarios.setup: After an injury, a patient keeps his knee completely still in a brace, bearing no weight on it, for many weeks. Compare the knee’s articular cartilage with its state before the brace.
scenarios.start: The knee is neither loaded nor moved

steps.pump: The cartilage is no longer squeezed and released
steps.fluid: Less synovial fluid is pushed out of the cartilage and drawn back in
steps.feed: Less oxygen and fewer nutrients reach the chondrocytes by diffusion
steps.thin: Poorly fed chondrocytes cannot maintain the cartilage, and it softens and thins

variables.name: Movement of fluid in and out of the cartilage
variables.why: Loading squeezes fluid out of cartilage, and unloading lets it spring back and draw fresh synovial fluid in. With no loading, that pumping stops.

variables.name: Nutrients reaching the chondrocytes
variables.why: Chondrocytes get their oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid by diffusion. Less fresh fluid drawn in means less delivered.

variables.name: Blood flow inside the articular cartilage
variables.why: Articular cartilage has no blood vessels at all, before or after the brace. That is exactly why it depends on movement to be fed.

variables.name: Thickness of the articular cartilage
variables.why: Chondrocytes that are poorly fed make less new matrix, so over weeks the cartilage softens and thins. Gentle movement and loading, when allowed, restart the pumping.

scenarios.title: A torn ACL left unrepaired
scenarios.misconception: the knee is held together mainly by the shape of its bones
scenarios.setup: Jada, 19, tore the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of her right knee planting her foot to cut past a defender. For months before surgery she keeps playing. Compare her right knee with her healthy left knee.
scenarios.start: The anterior cruciate ligament is torn through

steps.loose: Nothing restrains the tibia from sliding forward under the femur
steps.shift: When she twists, the tibia shifts and turns too far under the femur
steps.grind: The femoral condyles grind across the menisci and cartilage with each abnormal shift

variables.name: How far the tibia can be pulled forward under the femur
variables.why: The ACL runs from the front of the tibia up and back to the femur and is the main restraint on forward slide. Torn, it no longer stops the tibia.

variables.name: How far the tibia can be pushed backward under the femur
variables.why: Backward slide is stopped by the posterior cruciate ligament, which runs from the back of the tibia and is intact.

variables.name: Episodes of the knee giving way when she pivots
variables.why: The femoral condyles sit on nearly flat tibial condyles, so the knee depends on its ligaments. Without the ACL, a twist lets the tibia shift out from under the femur.

variables.name: Wear on the menisci over the following months
variables.why: Every abnormal shift drags the femur across the menisci and shears them. This is why meniscus tears, especially of the medial meniscus, become more common in knees that stay unstable.

variables.name: How far the knee can be pushed inward at its inner side
variables.why: That movement is limited by the tibial collateral ligament on the inner side, which was not torn.

scenarios.title: Osteoarthritis develops in a knee
scenarios.misconception: osteoarthritis affects only the articular cartilage
scenarios.setup: A 62-year-old who carries extra body weight and had a knee injury in her twenties develops osteoarthritis of that knee over several years. Compare the knee now with the knee before the disease began.
scenarios.start: Abnormal loading damages the articular cartilage faster than its chondrocytes can repair it

steps.thin: The cartilage softens, frays and thins
steps.space: The cartilage-filled space between the bones becomes narrower
steps.bone: Where cartilage wears through, bone grinds on bone; the bone beneath thickens and spurs grow at the edges
steps.syn: Fragments irritate the synovial membrane, which becomes mildly inflamed and makes extra fluid
steps.stiff: The joint hurts with use, is stiff after rest and moves less

variables.name: Thickness of the articular cartilage
variables.why: Cartilage has no blood supply to bring in repair cells, and its chondrocytes cannot keep up, so the damaged cartilage frays and thins.

variables.name: Space between the bones on an X-ray
variables.why: Cartilage does not show on an X-ray; the dark gap between the bones is where it sits. Thinner cartilage fills a narrower gap.

variables.name: Bony spurs at the edges of the joint
variables.why: Once bone meets bone, the bone reacts to the abnormal load by thickening and growing spurs at the joint margins.

variables.name: Volume of synovial fluid in the joint
variables.why: Fragments of cartilage and damaged tissue irritate the synovial membrane. The mildly inflamed membrane makes extra fluid, so the knee may look puffy.

variables.name: Range of movement at the knee
variables.why: Rough surfaces, bony spurs and pain all limit how far the knee bends and straightens.

scenarios.title: The rotator cuff stops working
scenarios.misconception: the shoulder joint is held together mainly by its bony socket
scenarios.setup: Suppose the four short muscles of the rotator cuff could not act at all, while the bones, capsule and labrum of the shoulder stayed normal. Compare the glenohumeral joint with a healthy shoulder.
scenarios.start: The rotator cuff tendons no longer pull across the joint

steps.press: Nothing presses the humeral head into the glenoid cavity
steps.hold: The head sits loosely against a small, shallow socket inside a loose capsule
steps.slip: A modest force can push the head out of line or out of the socket

variables.name: Force pressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity
variables.why: The cuff tendons blend into the capsule and press the head into the socket whenever their muscles act. With the muscles out, that force is lost.

variables.name: Stability of the glenohumeral joint
variables.why: The glenoid cavity is only about a third the size of the head and the capsule is loose, so the shoulder relies on its muscles for stability. Remove them and little holds it.

variables.name: Risk of the shoulder dislocating or partly slipping out
variables.why: With a shallow socket, a loose capsule and no active cuff, the head can be pushed out of the glenoid cavity much more easily.

variables.name: Depth of the socket formed by the glenoid cavity and labrum
variables.why: The glenoid cavity and its labrum are bone and fibrocartilage; they do not depend on the muscles, so the socket is no deeper or shallower.

scenarios.title: A toddler swung by the arms
scenarios.misconception: a child who will not use an arm after a pull must have a broken bone
scenarios.setup: A 2-year-old is swung by the hands. Afterward he holds one arm still at his side and will not use it. X-rays show no break. Compare that elbow with the other one.
scenarios.start: A sharp pull slides the small radial head partly out of the loose annular ligament

steps.sub: The joint surfaces still touch but are out of line: a subluxation
steps.turn: The radial head cannot turn smoothly inside its ring of ulna and annular ligament

variables.name: Ease of turning the palm up and down
variables.why: Turning the palm depends on the radial head spinning inside the annular ligament at the proximal radioulnar joint, a pivot joint. With the head caught partly out of the ring, that turning hurts and is blocked.

variables.name: Number of breaks in the radius
variables.why: This is a ligament and joint problem, not a fracture: the bone slipped partly out of place without breaking, which is why the X-ray is normal.

variables.name: How well the radial head lines up with its ring
variables.why: In a subluxation the surfaces still touch but are out of line. A clinician can usually turn the forearm to slip the head back in.

scenarios.title: A rolled ankle
scenarios.misconception: a sprained ankle is a small fracture
scenarios.setup: A runner lands on the outer edge of her foot and the sole rolls sharply inward. The outer side of her ankle swells; X-rays show no break. Compare the ligaments with their state before the fall.
scenarios.start: The sole is forced sharply inward

steps.stretch: The outer side of the ankle is pulled open, stretching the three small ligaments there
steps.atfl: The anterior talofibular ligament, the weakest, stretches or tears first
steps.unstable: The outer side of the ankle holds the talus less firmly

variables.name: Damage to the anterior talofibular ligament
variables.why: Forced inward rolling stretches the outer side, and of its three separate, smaller ligaments the anterior talofibular gives way first. A stretch or tear of a ligament is a sprain.

variables.name: Damage to the deltoid ligament
variables.why: The broad, strong deltoid ligament is on the inner side. Rolling the sole inward pulls the outer side open, not the inner side, so it is spared.

variables.name: Stability of the outer side of the ankle
variables.why: A stretched or torn ligament no longer limits movement as well, and because ligaments have a poor blood supply, they heal slowly and the ankle can stay loose.

scenarios.title: The ankle joint is fused
scenarios.misconception: turning the sole inward and outward happens at the ankle joint
scenarios.setup: After years of severe osteoarthritis, a surgeon fuses a patient’s talocrural (ankle) joint so that the talus and tibia become one solid unit. The joints below the talus are left alone. Compare the foot’s movements with a healthy foot.
scenarios.start: The talus can no longer swing on the tibia and fibula

steps.hinge: The hinge that tips the foot up and down is gone
steps.up: The top of the foot cannot be lifted toward the shin
steps.down: The foot cannot be pointed down
steps.sub: The subtalar joint, between the talus and calcaneus, still moves

variables.name: Range of dorsiflexion
variables.why: Dorsiflexion, lifting the top of the foot toward the shin, happens at the talocrural joint, a hinge. Fused, it cannot swing.

variables.name: Range of plantar flexion
variables.why: Plantar flexion is the same hinge swinging the other way, so it is lost too.

variables.name: Range of inversion and eversion
variables.why: Turning the sole inward and outward happens mostly at the subtalar joint and between the other tarsal bones, not at the ankle joint, so fusing the ankle leaves them.

variables.name: Ability to walk on the heels with the toes lifted
variables.why: Walking on the heels needs dorsiflexion to hold the front of the foot up, and the fused hinge cannot provide it.

scenarios.title: A scapula that will not turn
scenarios.misconception: raising the arm overhead happens only at the glenohumeral joint
scenarios.setup: Scar tissue binds a patient’s scapula to the back of the rib cage so that it cannot turn. His glenohumeral joint is healthy. He tries to lift his straight arm out to the side and up over his head.
scenarios.start: The scapula cannot rotate superiorly

steps.tip: The glenoid cavity cannot tip upward as the arm rises
steps.stop: The humerus reaches the limit of the glenohumeral joint a little past shoulder height
steps.gh: The glenohumeral joint itself still moves normally within its own range

variables.name: How high he can abduct the arm
variables.why: Raising the arm overhead needs superior rotation of the scapula to tip the glenoid cavity upward. Without it, abduction stops a little past shoulder height.

variables.name: Movement at the glenohumeral joint when tested alone
variables.why: The ball-and-socket joint is healthy; only the scapula’s contribution is missing, so the shoulder joint moves normally within its own range.

variables.name: How high he can flex the arm forward to point at the ceiling
variables.why: Lifting the arm forward overhead also needs the glenoid cavity to tip upward, so full flexion is limited in the same way.

scenarios.title: A rear-end car crash
scenarios.misconception: hyperextension is just a large flexion
scenarios.setup: A car is hit from behind. The driver’s body is pushed forward with the seat, and his head is thrown backward past its upright position. Compare his neck at the moment of the crash with anatomical position.
scenarios.start: The head is thrown backward beyond anatomical position

steps.hyper: The neck is extended past anatomical position: hyperextension
steps.front: The ligaments at the front of the neck are stretched
steps.back: The back of the neck is folded shorter

variables.name: Stretch on the ligaments at the front of the neck
variables.why: Extension carries the head backward. Going past anatomical position pulls the front of the neck longer, stretching its ligaments beyond what they normally allow.

variables.name: Stretch on the tissues at the back of the neck
variables.why: Tipping the head back folds the back of the neck shorter, so its tissues are slackened, not stretched.

variables.name: Distance from the chin to the chest
variables.why: Flexion brings the chin toward the chest; extension, and more so hyperextension, carries it away. A head-on crash does the opposite, hyperflexion.

scenarios.title: An insertion farther from the elbow
scenarios.misconception: a muscle that attaches farther from the joint gains strength with no cost
scenarios.setup: Two people hold the same 40-newton weight in the hand, elbow bent at a right angle, with the hand 32 cm from the elbow. In one, the large muscle on the front of the upper arm inserts 4 cm from the elbow; in the other, 5 cm. Predict how the second person compares with the first.
scenarios.start: The insertion sits 5 cm from the fulcrum instead of 4 cm

steps.arm: The effort arm is longer, while the load arm stays 32 cm
steps.ma: Mechanical advantage (effort arm ÷ load arm) rises from 0.125 to about 0.16
steps.force: Balancing the same load takes less pull: 40 × 32 ÷ 5 = 256 N instead of 320 N
steps.range: Each centimeter the muscle shortens swings the hand through a smaller arc: 32 ÷ 5 = 6.4 cm instead of 8 cm
steps.load: The weight and where the hand holds it are unchanged

variables.name: Effort arm
variables.why: The effort arm is the distance from the fulcrum (the elbow) to where the muscle pulls. Moving the insertion from 4 cm to 5 cm lengthens it by definition.

variables.name: Pull the muscle needs to hold the weight
variables.why: Effort × effort arm must equal load × load arm. With the load side fixed at 40 N × 32 cm, a longer effort arm lets a smaller effort balance it: 256 N instead of 320 N.

variables.name: Distance the hand moves for each centimeter the muscle shortens
variables.why: The hand and the insertion turn through the same angle, so the hand moves load arm ÷ effort arm times as far. That ratio falls from 8 to 6.4: the lever gains force and gives up range and speed.

variables.name: Load arm
variables.why: The load arm runs from the elbow to the weight in the hand. Moving the insertion does not move the hand, so it stays 32 cm.

scenarios.title: A pennate muscle and a parallel muscle of the same size
scenarios.misconception: the muscle with the longest fibers is always the strongest
scenarios.setup: Compare a pennate muscle with a parallel (strap) muscle of the same volume and weight. Predict how the pennate muscle compares.
scenarios.start: The fascicles attach at an angle to a central tendon instead of running in line with the pull

steps.pack: Many more short fibers fit side by side in the same volume
steps.xb: More fibers side by side means more cross-bridges pulling at the same moment
steps.series: Each fiber has fewer sarcomeres in series
steps.travel: The whole muscle shortens a shorter distance, and more slowly

variables.name: Number of fibers packed into the muscle
variables.why: Short fibers set at an angle to a long tendon pack together like the barbs of a feather, so the same volume holds far more fibers than a strap of long fibers.

variables.name: Maximum force the muscle can produce
variables.why: Force depends on how many cross-bridges pull at once, which depends on how many fibers lie side by side. The pennate muscle has more, so it is stronger for its size.

variables.name: Distance the muscle can shorten
variables.why: Every sarcomere shortens a little at the same time, so a long chain of sarcomeres shortens farther. The pennate muscle’s short fibers have short chains, so it shortens less, and less quickly.

scenarios.title: A pull-up: the insertion stays still
scenarios.misconception: a muscle’s origin can never move
scenarios.setup: You hang from a bar and pull yourself up. The muscle on the front of your upper arm that bends your elbow when you lift a cup does the same job here. Predict the changes as you rise, compared with hanging.
scenarios.start: Your hands grip a fixed bar, so the forearm becomes the stable end

steps.swap: The usual insertion, on the forearm, is held still (a reverse action)
steps.pull: The muscle shortens and pulls the upper arm toward the forearm
steps.trunk: The upper arm, and the trunk with it, move up toward the hands

variables.name: Angle at the elbow
variables.why: Bending the elbow is flexion, which decreases the angle between upper arm and forearm. That is the same whichever bone moves.

variables.name: Height of your trunk
variables.why: With the forearm held by the bar, the muscle pulls its origin’s bone toward its insertion instead of the usual way round, so the upper arm and trunk rise.

variables.name: Height of your hands
variables.why: The hands grip a fixed bar, so the forearm is now the stable end. In a reverse action the attachment that usually moves stays still.

scenarios.title: A torn distal biceps tendon
scenarios.misconception: if the main elbow flexor is torn, the elbow cannot bend at all
scenarios.setup: Jordan, 34, tears the tendon of the biceps brachii away from the radial tuberosity while lifting a heavy box. His brachialis, brachioradialis and pronators are unhurt. Predict the changes, compared with his other arm.
scenarios.start: The biceps brachii no longer pulls on the radius

steps.loss: One of the three elbow flexors is lost
steps.others: The brachialis and brachioradialis still pull on the ulna and radius
steps.sup: The strongest supinator of the forearm is lost; the supinator muscle is left alone
steps.recoil: The belly, attached only at its origins on the scapula, recoils toward the shoulder
steps.pron: The pronator teres and pronator quadratus are untouched

variables.name: Strength of elbow flexion
variables.why: The biceps brachii is one of the three elbow flexors, so flexion weakens. It does not disappear: the brachialis and brachioradialis still bend the elbow.

variables.name: Strength of supination (turning a screwdriver palm-up)
variables.why: The biceps brachii is the strongest supinator. With it gone, only the smaller supinator muscle turns the palm up, so twisting against resistance is weak.

variables.name: Distance of the muscle’s bulge from the elbow
variables.why: A cut or torn muscle shortens toward its remaining attachment. The biceps is still attached at the shoulder, so its belly bunches up high on the arm.

variables.name: Strength of pronation
variables.why: Pronation is done by the pronator teres and pronator quadratus, which were not injured. The biceps brachii does the opposite movement.

scenarios.title: A torn supraspinatus tendon
scenarios.misconception: the deltoid raises the arm alone, so a rotator cuff tear should not weaken it
scenarios.setup: Mr. Brooks, 58, has a tear limited to the supraspinatus tendon, which runs under the acromion. Predict the changes in his shoulder, compared with a healthy shoulder.
scenarios.start: The supraspinatus can no longer pull on the greater tubercle

steps.abd: One of the two muscles that abduct the arm together is lost
steps.seat: Less pull holds the head of the humerus pressed into the glenoid cavity
steps.slide: The deltoid’s upward pull slides the head up toward the acromion instead of only rotating it
steps.pinch: Tissues in the tight space under the acromion are squeezed
steps.others: The infraspinatus and teres minor, which rotate the arm laterally, are intact

variables.name: Strength of raising the arm out to the side
variables.why: The supraspinatus and deltoid work together from the start of abduction. Losing the supraspinatus removes force, and without it the deltoid’s pull partly slides the head upward instead of swinging the arm out.

variables.name: How firmly the head of the humerus is held in its socket
variables.why: The four rotator cuff tendons press the head of the humerus into the shallow glenoid cavity. With one of them gone, the head is held less firmly.

variables.name: Pain when he lifts his arm to the side
variables.why: As the poorly held head rides up, the torn tendon and the tissue around it are pinched between the head of the humerus and the acromion.

variables.name: Strength of lateral rotation
variables.why: Lateral rotation is done by the infraspinatus and teres minor, which insert on the greater tubercle behind the supraspinatus and are not torn here.

scenarios.title: A paralyzed serratus anterior
scenarios.misconception: the scapula is held on the rib cage by a joint
scenarios.setup: The nerve to a woman’s right serratus anterior is injured, and the muscle stops working. Her other shoulder muscles are normal. Predict the changes on the right, compared with the left.
scenarios.start: The serratus anterior no longer pulls the scapula forward around the chest wall

steps.flat: Nothing holds the medial border of the scapula flat against the ribs
steps.wing: Pushing against a wall lifts the medial border away from the ribs: a winged scapula
steps.prot: The scapula can no longer be pulled forward strongly
steps.rot: The scapula cannot rotate fully so the socket faces upward
steps.overhead: The humerus has no upward-facing base to rise from above shoulder height
steps.rhomb: The rhomboids, which pull the scapula toward the spine, are intact

variables.name: How far the scapula’s medial border lifts off the ribs when she pushes on a wall
variables.why: The serratus anterior normally holds the scapula flat against the rib cage. When she pushes, the push drives the scapula backward and, with no serratus to hold it, its medial border lifts away: a winged scapula.

variables.name: Force of a forward punch or push
variables.why: Protraction of the scapula, pulling it forward around the chest, is the serratus anterior’s main job. Without it, a push loses much of its drive.

variables.name: How high she can raise her arm
variables.why: Raising the arm above the head needs the scapula to rotate so the glenoid cavity faces upward. The serratus anterior and trapezius do this together; with the serratus gone, the arm cannot go fully overhead.

variables.name: Strength of squeezing her shoulder blades together
variables.why: Retraction is done by the rhomboids and the middle trapezius, which are normal. They are the serratus anterior’s antagonists, not its helpers.

scenarios.title: Swollen tendon sheaths in the carpal tunnel
scenarios.misconception: carpal tunnel symptoms come from the wrist bones rubbing together
scenarios.setup: After months of long hours of repeated gripping, the sheaths around a worker’s finger flexor tendons swell inside the carpal tunnel. Predict the changes, compared with before.
scenarios.start: The tendon sheaths swell in a tunnel bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum

steps.room: The tunnel cannot widen, so the space left for the other contents shrinks
steps.nerve: The nerve that passes through the tunnel with the tendons is squeezed
steps.numb: Numbness and tingling spread over the thumb and first fingers
steps.thenar: In severe, long-standing cases the thenar muscles that nerve supplies waste away
steps.ext: The wrist extensors run on the back of the forearm and hand, outside the tunnel

variables.name: Pressure inside the carpal tunnel
variables.why: The carpal bones and the tough flexor retinaculum cannot stretch, so swelling inside the tunnel raises the pressure on everything in it.

variables.name: Numbness and tingling in the thumb and first fingers
variables.why: The nerve shares the tunnel with the flexor tendons. As the pressure rises it is squeezed, and the skin it supplies, on the thumb side of the hand, tingles and goes numb.

variables.name: Bulk of the thenar eminence
variables.why: The squeezed nerve also supplies the thenar muscles at the base of the thumb. When compression is severe and lasts, those muscles waste: a late sign.

variables.name: Strength of wrist extension
variables.why: The wrist extensors start on the lateral epicondyle and run down the back of the forearm; their tendons never enter the carpal tunnel on the palm side.

scenarios.title: The facial muscles on one side stop working
scenarios.misconception: drooping of the face means the chewing muscles are weak too
scenarios.setup: Ms. Alvarez, 45, wakes with the nerve that controls the facial muscles on her right side swollen, so those muscles no longer contract. Predict the changes on the right side of her face, compared with the left.
scenarios.start: The muscles of facial expression on the right side no longer contract

steps.front: The right frontalis cannot pull the forehead skin up
steps.oculi: The right orbicularis oculi cannot close the eyelids
steps.zyg: The right zygomaticus major cannot pull the corner of the mouth up and back
steps.oris: The right half of the orbicularis oris cannot seal the lips
steps.bucc: The right buccinator cannot press the cheek against the teeth
steps.chew: The masseter, temporalis and pterygoids are controlled separately and still work

variables.name: How high she can raise her right eyebrow
variables.why: The frontalis raises the eyebrows by pulling the forehead skin toward its origin on the epicranial aponeurosis. With it silent, the right eyebrow stays down.

variables.name: How fully her right eye closes
variables.why: The orbicularis oculi is the circular muscle that closes the eyelids. Without it, the right eye cannot close fully, even in a blink.

variables.name: Height of the right corner of her mouth when she smiles
variables.why: The zygomaticus major pulls the corner of the mouth up and back. The left one still works, so her smile pulls to the left and the right corner droops.

variables.name: Food collecting in her right cheek
variables.why: The buccinator normally presses the cheek against the teeth, pushing food back onto them. A slack right cheek lets food pocket there.

variables.name: Drink leaking from the right corner of her mouth
variables.why: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter around the lips. With its right half slack, the lips do not seal on that side and liquid dribbles out.

variables.name: Biting force on the right
variables.why: Biting is done by the muscles of mastication, which insert on the mandible and are controlled by a different nerve. They are spared, so she chews normally.

scenarios.title: From breathing at rest to hard breathing
scenarios.misconception: breathing out always takes muscle work
scenarios.setup: A student sitting quietly starts running up several flights of stairs, and her breathing becomes deep and fast. Predict how her breathing muscles change, compared with breathing at rest.
scenarios.start: Each breath in must be deeper, and each breath out faster and more complete

steps.dia: The diaphragm contracts harder and flattens further
steps.neck: The scalenes and sternocleidomastoids lift the top of the rib cage harder
steps.active: Breathing out changes from passive recoil to an active squeeze
steps.int: The internal intercostals pull the ribs down and in
steps.abs: The abdominal wall muscles compress the abdomen and push the diaphragm up

variables.name: Work done by the diaphragm
variables.why: The diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing in at rest and in exercise. It contracts harder, pulling the central tendon farther down to make the chest taller.

variables.name: Activity of the scalenes
variables.why: The scalenes lift the first two ribs. Recordings show they are already active in most breaths at rest, and they work hardest in heavy breathing, joined by the sternocleidomastoids.

variables.name: Activity of the internal intercostals
variables.why: At rest, breathing out is passive: the stretched lungs and chest wall recoil. In hard breathing, most of the internal intercostals contract to pull the ribs down and in and squeeze air out faster.

variables.name: Pressure inside the abdomen during each breath out
variables.why: The abdominal wall muscles squeeze the soft, nearly incompressible abdominal contents, so pressure rises and pushes the relaxed diaphragm up into the chest, driving air out.

scenarios.title: A cough with a weak pelvic floor
scenarios.misconception: leaking urine on coughing means the bladder itself is diseased
scenarios.setup: Dana, 32, had her second baby three months ago, and her levator ani was stretched during the birth. She coughs hard. Predict the changes during the cough, compared with a woman whose pelvic floor is strong.
scenarios.start: Her abdominal wall muscles contract hard, but her levator ani tightens late and weakly

steps.squeeze: The rectus abdominis, obliques and transversus abdominis squeeze the abdomen
steps.pressure: Pressure in the abdomen rises sharply
steps.up: The pressure pushes the relaxed diaphragm up, driving air out of the lungs
steps.down: The same pressure pushes down on the bladder and other pelvic organs
steps.weak: Her levator ani does not tighten in time to hold the organs up and squeeze the urethra shut
steps.leak: Pressure on the bladder beats the closing force around the urethra, and a little urine leaks

variables.name: Pressure inside the abdomen during the cough
variables.why: Her abdominal wall muscles are normal, so they squeeze the abdomen just as hard as in the other woman. Her problem lies below, in the pelvic floor.

variables.name: Force driving air out of her lungs
variables.why: The cough’s force comes from the abdominal pressure pushing the diaphragm up. That part of the chain is unchanged, so her cough is as strong.

variables.name: Support holding up her bladder during the cough
variables.why: Normally the levator ani contracts at the same moment as the abdominal wall. Stretched by the birth, hers lags and pulls weakly, so the bladder is less well held.

variables.name: Urine leaking during the cough
variables.why: The rising pressure pushes the bladder down while the weak pelvic floor fails to squeeze the urethra shut in time, so a little urine escapes. Pelvic floor exercises help by strengthening the levator ani.

scenarios.title: The diaphragm contracts
scenarios.misconception: the diaphragm pushes air out when it contracts
scenarios.setup: You take a slow, deep breath in. Predict what the contraction of your diaphragm changes, compared with the moment before.
scenarios.start: The diaphragm’s muscle fibers shorten

steps.tendon: The fibers pull the central tendon down toward their origins on the lower edge of the rib cage and the lumbar vertebrae
steps.belly: The flattening dome presses down on the abdominal organs

variables.name: Height of the top of the diaphragm’s dome
variables.why: The central tendon at the top of the dome is the diaphragm’s insertion. Its fibers pull it down toward their origins, so the dome flattens and drops.

variables.name: Size of the chest cavity
variables.why: As the floor of the thoracic cavity drops, the chest cavity gets taller, and air flows into the lungs.

variables.name: Pressure inside the abdomen
variables.why: The descending diaphragm presses on the abdominal organs, which cannot be compressed, so the pressure in the abdomen rises. That is why a held deep breath stiffens the trunk before a heavy lift.

scenarios.title: Standing on a leg with weak hip abductors
scenarios.misconception: the gluteus medius matters only for moving the leg out to the side
scenarios.setup: A man’s right gluteus medius and minimus are weak after a hip operation. He stands on his right leg and lifts his left foot. Predict the changes, compared with a person with strong hip abductors.
scenarios.start: His body weight hangs to the left of the right hip joint, and the right hip abductors cannot pull hard enough to hold it

steps.torque: His weight tends to tip the pelvis down on the left, unsupported side
steps.weak: The weak right gluteus medius and minimus cannot pull the ilium toward the greater trochanter hard enough
steps.drop: The left side of the pelvis drops (a positive Trendelenburg sign)
steps.sway: He leans his trunk over the right leg, moving his weight nearer the hip joint
steps.knee: The quadriceps femoris is not affected

variables.name: Height of the left side of his pelvis
variables.why: On the standing leg, the gluteus medius and minimus pull from the greater trochanter on the ilium to hold the pelvis level. Too weak to balance his weight, they let the unsupported side drop.

variables.name: Lean of his trunk toward the right
variables.why: Leaning over the standing leg shortens the lever arm of his body weight about the right hip, so the weak abductors have less to hold.

variables.name: Strength of moving his right thigh out to the side
variables.why: The gluteus medius and minimus are the main abductors of the thigh, so the same weakness shows when he lifts the leg sideways.

variables.name: Strength of straightening his right knee
variables.why: Knee extension is done by the quadriceps femoris on the front of the thigh, which is not weak here.

scenarios.title: A ruptured calcaneal tendon
scenarios.misconception: the foot cannot point at all after the Achilles tendon ruptures
scenarios.setup: Lunging for a ball, a tennis player ruptures his right calcaneal (Achilles) tendon. Predict the changes on the right, compared with his left leg.
scenarios.start: The gastrocnemius and soleus are cut off from the calcaneus

steps.cut: The two main plantar flexors can no longer pull the heel up
steps.toes: He cannot rise onto the toes of that foot
steps.squeeze: Squeezing the calf no longer points the foot
steps.deep: Smaller muscles behind the ankle, such as the tibialis posterior and fibularis longus, can still plantar flex weakly
steps.front: The tibialis anterior and other muscles on the front of the leg are untouched

variables.name: Ability to rise onto his right toes
variables.why: Rising onto the toes needs the calf to pull the calcaneus up through the calcaneal tendon. With the tendon ruptured, that pull cannot reach the heel.

variables.name: Foot movement when the calf is squeezed
variables.why: Squeezing the calf normally shortens the muscle–tendon unit enough to point the foot. With the tendon broken, nothing transmits the squeeze to the heel.

variables.name: Strength of pointing the foot
variables.why: The gastrocnemius and soleus supply most of the force of plantar flexion. The deep plantar flexors remain, so pointing is weak rather than impossible.

variables.name: Strength of lifting the toes toward the shin
variables.why: Dorsiflexion is done by the front group of the leg, led by the tibialis anterior, which is not injured.

scenarios.title: A weak tibialis anterior
scenarios.misconception: the calf muscles lift the front of the foot
scenarios.setup: The muscles in the front compartment of a woman’s left leg are weak. Predict what happens as she walks, compared with her right leg.
scenarios.start: The tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus pull weakly

steps.drag: The toes are not lifted clear as the leg swings forward, so they catch on the ground
steps.slap: After the heel strikes, nothing lowers the front of the foot gently, so it slaps down
steps.calf: The gastrocnemius and soleus, in the back compartment, are normal

variables.name: Strength of lifting her left toes toward the shin
variables.why: Dorsiflexion is the main job of the front group of the leg, and the tibialis anterior is its prime mover. With it weak, lifting the foot is weak.

variables.name: Her left toes catching as the leg swings forward
variables.why: Each time the leg swings forward, the tibialis anterior lifts the foot clear of the ground. Without that lift, the toes drag.

variables.name: Slap of the front of her left foot after the heel lands
variables.why: After the heel strikes, the tibialis anterior normally lowers the front of the foot slowly, lengthening while it works. Weak, it cannot brake the foot, which slaps down.

variables.name: Ability to rise onto her left toes
variables.why: Rising onto the toes is plantar flexion, done by the gastrocnemius and soleus in the back compartment, which are normal.

scenarios.title: The end of a sprinter’s forward leg swing
scenarios.misconception: a muscle’s length depends on only one joint
scenarios.setup: At the end of the forward swing, a sprinter’s hip is flexed and her knee is nearly straight. Predict the changes, compared with standing upright with the knee straight.
scenarios.start: The hip flexes while the knee stays straight

steps.hipH: Hip flexion moves the hamstrings’ origin on the ischial tuberosity away from the knee
steps.kneeH: A straight knee keeps their insertions on the fibula and tibia as far away as they can be
steps.stretch: The hamstrings are stretched across both joints at once
steps.risk: If they contract hard while stretched this far, as they brake the swinging leg, they can strain
steps.rf: Hip flexion and knee extension both bring the ends of the rectus femoris closer together

variables.name: Length of the hamstrings
variables.why: The hamstrings cross the back of both the hip and the knee. Flexing the hip stretches them over the hip, and a straight knee adds no slack, so they are at their longest.

variables.name: Risk of a hamstring strain
variables.why: At this moment the hamstrings are both stretched and working hard to slow the swinging leg, which is when hamstring strains usually happen.

variables.name: Length of the rectus femoris
variables.why: The rectus femoris crosses the front of both joints: it flexes the hip and extends the knee. Doing both at once brings its origin and insertion together, so it is short.

scenarios.title: Compartment syndrome after a tibia fracture
scenarios.misconception: if the pulse in the foot is present, compartment syndrome is ruled out
scenarios.setup: Marcus, 22, breaks his tibia. Bleeding and swelling build inside the anterior compartment of his leg. Follow the compartment before and after the surgeon slits its fascia open.

stages.label: Six hours after the fracture
stages.prompt: Six hours after the fracture, compared with just after the injury.
stages.start: Blood and fluid collect inside a compartment wrapped in deep fascia that barely stretches

steps.vol: The volume inside the compartment grows
steps.press: The fascia cannot stretch, so the pressure in the compartment rises
steps.veins: The thin-walled veins are squeezed shut, so blood cannot drain out and more fluid is trapped
steps.caps: The pressure rises high enough to stop blood flowing through the capillaries
steps.o2: The muscles and nerves in the compartment are starved of oxygen
steps.stretch: Stretching the starved muscles, by pointing the toes down, causes severe pain
steps.artery: The pressure inside the main artery is far higher than the compartment pressure, so it stays open

variables.name: Pressure in the anterior compartment
variables.why: The compartment has a nearly fixed volume because the deep fascia and bones do not stretch. Adding fluid raises the pressure, and squeezing the veins shut traps still more fluid, so it keeps climbing.

variables.name: Blood flow through the compartment’s capillaries
variables.why: Blood flows through capillaries only while the pressure inside them exceeds the pressure squeezing them. Once the compartment pressure rises high enough, capillary flow stops.

variables.name: Pain when the nurse points his toes
variables.why: Pointing the toes stretches the muscles of the front compartment. Muscles starved of oxygen hurt badly when stretched, which is the early warning sign.

variables.name: Pulse felt in his foot
variables.why: The main artery carries blood at a far higher pressure than the compartment, so it keeps pulsing while the capillaries around it are shut. A lost pulse is a late sign.

stages.label: Just after the fascia is slit open
stages.prompt: Minutes after surgery, compared with just before it.
stages.start: The surgeon slits the deep fascia along the whole compartment

steps.room: The swollen contents can bulge out through the opening
steps.fall: The pressure in the compartment falls
steps.veins: The veins open and blood drains out again
steps.caps: Blood flows through the capillaries again
steps.o2: Oxygen reaches the muscles and nerves before they die
steps.artery: The main artery was never blocked

variables.name: Pressure in the anterior compartment
variables.why: The fascia was what fixed the compartment’s volume. Once it is open, the contents have room to swell outward, so the pressure drops.

variables.name: Blood flow through the compartment’s capillaries
variables.why: With the squeezing pressure gone, the veins drain and blood can again flow from the arteries through the capillaries.

variables.name: Oxygen reaching the muscles in the compartment
variables.why: Capillaries are where oxygen leaves the blood for the tissue. Restored capillary flow feeds the muscle, which is why surgery must come within hours.

variables.name: Pulse felt in his foot
variables.why: The pulse was present before surgery because the high-pressure artery was never closed, so opening the fascia does not change it.

scenarios.title: The suprahyoid muscles contract in a swallow
scenarios.misconception: the hyoid bone is held in place by a joint
scenarios.setup: With your lips sealed and your teeth together, you swallow. Predict the changes as the suprahyoid muscles contract, compared with the moment before.
scenarios.start: The suprahyoid muscles contract while the jaw-closing muscles hold the mandible still

steps.fixed: The mandible and skull are held still, so they act as the origins
steps.lift: The suprahyoids pull the hyoid bone up toward the mandible
steps.box: The voice box, hanging from the hyoid, rises with it
steps.stretch: The infrahyoid strap muscles below the hyoid are stretched

variables.name: Height of the hyoid bone
variables.why: The hyoid forms no joint with any other bone and hangs in muscles. With the mandible held still, the suprahyoids pull their insertion on the hyoid up toward it.

variables.name: Height of the voice box
variables.why: The voice box hangs from the hyoid, so it rises with it; that is the jump you feel under your finger when you swallow.

variables.name: Length of the infrahyoid muscles
variables.why: The infrahyoids run from the hyoid down to the sternum, voice box and scapula. As the hyoid rises, they are stretched, ready to pull it back down after the swallow.

variables.name: Opening of the mouth
variables.why: The jaw-closing muscles hold the mandible still. The suprahyoids open the mouth only when the hyoid is held still instead, by the infrahyoids.

scenarios.title: A curare-type drug at the end plate
scenarios.theme: a drug blocks acetylcholine receptors at the end plate
scenarios.misconception: the nerve impulse passes directly into the muscle
scenarios.setup: During surgery, a patient receives rocuronium, a curare-type drug that occupies most of the acetylcholine binding sites on the nicotinic receptor proteins of her motor end plates without opening them. Her motor neurons keep firing normally. Predict the changes, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: Most ACh binding sites on the end plate are occupied by the drug

steps.nerve: The motor neuron and its axon terminal are untouched by the drug
steps.fewer: Released ACh finds few free binding sites, so few ACh-gated channels open
steps.epp: Less sodium enters, so the end plate potential is smaller
steps.below: The end plate potential no longer brings the neighboring sarcolemma to threshold
steps.limp: Without action potentials, the fibers release no calcium and do not contract

variables.name: ACh released by the axon terminal per nerve impulse
variables.why: Release depends on the action potential opening calcium channels in the terminal, and the drug acts only on the muscle side of the cleft. The same packets of ACh are released as before.

variables.name: Size of the end plate potential
variables.why: Each receptor protein needs two ACh molecules to open. With most binding sites taken by the drug, few channels open, so less positive charge flows in and the end plate potential shrinks.

variables.name: Action potentials in the muscle fibers
variables.why: The safety margin is used up: once the end plate potential falls below threshold, the voltage-gated sodium channels beside the end plate never open, so no action potential starts.

variables.name: Strength of her skeletal muscle contractions
variables.why: A fiber that fires no action potential releases no calcium from its SR, so its myosin heads never bind actin. Every skeletal muscle goes limp, including the breathing muscles, which is why a ventilator breathes for her.

scenarios.title: Neostigmine slows acetylcholinesterase
scenarios.misconception: blocking acetylcholinesterase makes the terminal release more acetylcholine
scenarios.setup: A drug partly inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. Predict the changes after a single nerve impulse, compared with the same impulse before the drug.
scenarios.start: Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft splits ACh more slowly

steps.terminal: The action potential and calcium entry in the axon terminal are unchanged
steps.linger: ACh stays in the cleft longer before it is split
steps.rebind: ACh keeps binding and rebinding receptor proteins, reopening their channels
steps.long: The end plate stays depolarized longer
steps.choline: Choline, a product of splitting ACh, is formed more slowly

variables.name: ACh released by the terminal
variables.why: Release is set by the action potential opening voltage-gated calcium channels in the terminal. The drug acts on the enzyme in the cleft, after release.

variables.name: Time ACh stays in the synaptic cleft
variables.why: Acetylcholinesterase normally clears the cleft within a millisecond or two. With the enzyme slowed, ACh lingers.

variables.name: Duration of the end plate potential
variables.why: Each receptor protein lets ACh go after binding it briefly. Lingering ACh binds again and reopens the channels, so positive charge keeps flowing in for longer.

variables.name: Action potentials in the muscle fiber per nerve impulse
variables.why: A long end plate potential can bring the neighboring membrane to threshold again after its refractory period, so one nerve impulse can trigger several action potentials instead of one. That is why the muscles quiver.

variables.name: Rate at which choline is returned to the axon terminal
variables.why: Choline comes only from splitting ACh. Slower splitting makes choline more slowly, so less is taken back up per second.

scenarios.title: Botulinum toxin at the junction
scenarios.misconception: botulinum toxin paralyzes muscle by stopping the nerve impulse
scenarios.setup: A man eats home-canned vegetables contaminated with botulinum toxin, which destroys the proteins his synaptic vesicles need to fuse with the axon terminal membrane. Predict the changes at his neuromuscular junctions a day later, compared with before.
scenarios.start: Vesicles in the axon terminal can no longer fuse with its membrane

steps.ap: Action potentials still travel along the axon to the terminal
steps.ca: Calcium still enters the terminal through its voltage-gated channels
steps.fuse: Calcium binds the vesicles, but they cannot fuse and empty
steps.noach: Little or no ACh reaches the cleft
steps.noepp: No end plate potential reaches threshold, so the fiber does not fire

variables.name: Action potentials reaching the axon terminal
variables.why: The toxin acts inside the terminal on the fusion proteins. The axon still conducts, so each impulse still arrives.

variables.name: Calcium entering the terminal per impulse
variables.why: The arriving action potential still depolarizes the terminal and opens its calcium channels; the block is on the step after calcium entry.

variables.name: ACh released into the synaptic cleft
variables.why: Calcium triggers release by making vesicles fuse. With the fusion proteins destroyed, the vesicles stay full, so almost no ACh is released.

variables.name: Strength of his muscle contractions
variables.why: Without ACh the end plate is not depolarized, the fibers fire no action potentials, and weakness spreads. It can stop his breathing muscles, although his nerves still work.

scenarios.title: A nerve–muscle preparation without calcium
scenarios.misconception: skeletal muscle needs calcium from outside the cell to contract
scenarios.setup: In a lab, a frog nerve–muscle preparation is moved into a bath with no calcium. For the next few minutes, the experimenter stimulates it in two ways: through its nerve, and directly with an electrode on the muscle. Predict the changes, compared with the normal bath.
scenarios.start: Calcium is removed from the extracellular fluid around the junction and the fibers

steps.nerveap: Nerve action potentials still reach the axon terminals
steps.noca: No calcium enters the terminals, so the vesicles do not fuse
steps.noach: No ACh is released, so the fibers do not fire
steps.direct: The electrode depolarizes the sarcolemma to threshold directly
steps.sr: The fiber action potential opens the SR release channels, and calcium comes from the SR inside the fiber

variables.name: Action potentials reaching the axon terminals
variables.why: Action potentials run on sodium and potassium, not calcium, so the nerve keeps conducting.

variables.name: Contraction when the nerve is stimulated
variables.why: Transmitter release needs calcium to enter the terminal from outside. With none there, no ACh is released and the fibers stay still.

variables.name: Contraction when the muscle is stimulated directly
variables.why: A skeletal fiber’s trigger is voltage, and its calcium comes from the SR. Stimulated directly, it keeps contracting normally for a while in a calcium-free bath.

scenarios.title: Dantrolene blocks the release channels
scenarios.misconception: a drug that weakens muscle must act at the neuromuscular junction
scenarios.setup: A muscle fiber is treated with dantrolene, a drug that blocks the ryanodine receptor proteins, the calcium release channels of the SR. Its motor neuron is then stimulated. Predict the changes, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: The SR’s calcium release channels are blocked

steps.junction: ACh release and the end plate are unaffected
steps.ap: The fiber still fires action potentials that run down the T tubules
steps.sensor: The voltage sensors in the T tubules still change shape, but cannot pull the blocked channels open
steps.tropo: Less calcium binds troponin, so fewer binding sites on actin are uncovered

variables.name: End plate potential
variables.why: The drug acts deep inside the fiber, on the SR. ACh release and its receptor proteins at the end plate work as before.

variables.name: Action potentials in the sarcolemma and T tubules
variables.why: The voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels of the sarcolemma are untouched, so the fiber is excited normally.

variables.name: Calcium in the sarcoplasm after each action potential
variables.why: The voltage sensor opens the SR by pulling on the release channel. With the channel blocked, little calcium flows out of the terminal cisternae.

variables.name: Force of contraction
variables.why: Calcium is the switch: less of it on troponin leaves more binding sites covered by tropomyosin, so fewer myosin heads can bind and pull.

scenarios.title: The SR calcium pumps are blocked
scenarios.misconception: relaxation happens on its own once the nerve stops firing
scenarios.setup: An experimental drug blocks the calcium pumps of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Immediately afterward, a single action potential is triggered in the fiber. Predict the changes, compared with a normal fiber.
scenarios.start: The SR calcium pumps stop moving calcium back into the SR

steps.release: The action potential opens the release channels as usual
steps.stay: Released calcium is not pumped back, so it stays high in the sarcoplasm
steps.bound: Calcium stays on troponin, and tropomyosin stays off the binding sites
steps.pull: Myosin heads keep binding actin and pulling while ATP lasts

variables.name: Calcium released from the SR by this action potential
variables.why: Release flows through the release channels, pulled open by the voltage sensors. The pumps play no part in it, so this first pulse is normal.

variables.name: Time calcium stays high in the sarcoplasm
variables.why: The pumps are what lower calcium after each release. Without them, calcium stays in the sarcoplasm.

variables.name: Time until the fiber relaxes
variables.why: Relaxation needs calcium to leave troponin so tropomyosin can cover actin again. With calcium kept high, the filaments keep pulling.

variables.name: Calcium stored in the SR afterward
variables.why: The calcium that left is not pumped back, so the store is lower for the next action potential.

scenarios.title: T tubules pinched off the surface
scenarios.misconception: the action potential on the fiber surface is enough to reach every myofibril
scenarios.setup: In an experiment, a chemical treatment pinches the T tubules off from the sarcolemma, leaving the rest of a thick fiber intact. The fiber is then stimulated. Predict the changes, compared with an untreated fiber.
scenarios.start: The T tubules are no longer connected to the surface membrane

steps.surface: The action potential still sweeps along the sarcolemma on the surface
steps.notube: The action potential cannot travel into the fiber
steps.nosensor: Voltage sensors at the triads deep in the fiber are not depolarized
steps.nocal: The SR beside the inner myofibrils releases little calcium
steps.weak: Only myofibrils near the surface are switched on

variables.name: Action potential on the surface sarcolemma
variables.why: The surface membrane and its voltage-gated channels are intact, so the fiber still fires along its length.

variables.name: Calcium released around the central myofibrils
variables.why: Calcium release needs the voltage change to reach each triad. Without T tubules, the deep triads never see it, and calcium drifting inward from the surface would be far too slow.

variables.name: Force of the whole fiber
variables.why: Most myofibrils lie deep in the fiber. With only the outer ones contracting, the fiber pulls weakly.

scenarios.title: Blood calcium falls after neck surgery
scenarios.misconception: low blood calcium weakens skeletal muscle because calcium triggers contraction
scenarios.setup: After neck surgery, a patient’s blood calcium falls well below normal. Predict the changes in her nerves and skeletal muscles, compared with before surgery.
scenarios.start: Calcium in the extracellular fluid falls

steps.easy: Voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle membranes open more easily, closer to the resting potential
steps.fire: Nerve and muscle fibers reach threshold on their own and fire
steps.spasm: Muscles contract without a command: cramps and spasms
steps.sr: Each skeletal fiber still takes its contraction calcium from its own SR

variables.name: Excitability of her nerve and muscle membranes
variables.why: Low outside calcium lets the sodium channels open at voltages nearer rest, so less of a push is needed to reach threshold.

variables.name: Action potentials fired with no command from the brain
variables.why: Membranes that sit so close to threshold fire on their own, and every nerve action potential still reaches the muscle.

variables.name: Involuntary muscle spasms
variables.why: Each unplanned action potential releases calcium from the SR and causes a contraction, so the hands and feet can lock in painful spasms.

variables.name: Calcium released from the SR by each action potential
variables.why: A skeletal fiber stores its own calcium in the SR and releases it by voltage alone. Low blood calcium does not starve the filaments, which is why the result is spasm, not weakness.

scenarios.title: A leaky release channel meets an anesthetic
scenarios.misconception: the fever of this reaction comes from an infection
scenarios.setup: Daniel has an inherited fault in his SR release channels. During surgery he breathes an anesthetic gas that makes the faulty channels leak calcium continuously. Follow his muscles and his temperature before and after the team gives dantrolene, which blocks the release channels.

stages.label: The gas is breathed
stages.prompt: In the minutes after the gas reaches his muscles, compared with before it.
stages.start: The faulty release channels leak calcium out of the SR

steps.leak: Calcium pours into the sarcoplasm and stays high
steps.bind: Calcium stays on troponin, so myosin heads keep binding actin and pulling in every fiber
steps.burn: Calcium pumps and myosin heads split ATP nonstop
steps.heat: The energy released by splitting ATP warms the muscle

variables.name: Calcium in his muscle fibers’ sarcoplasm
variables.why: The leaking channels let calcium out faster than the pumps can return it, so the level stays high.

variables.name: Stiffness of his muscles
variables.why: With calcium bound to troponin, tropomyosin stays off actin and the myosin heads keep pulling. The muscles lock without any nerve command.

variables.name: Rate at which his muscles use ATP
variables.why: The pumps spend ATP trying to return the calcium, and every pull of a myosin head splits another ATP.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: Much of the energy of split ATP is released as heat. With so much muscle working nonstop, temperature can climb above 40 °C quickly.

stages.label: After dantrolene
stages.prompt: Some minutes after dantrolene reaches his muscles, compared with the first stage.
stages.start: Dantrolene blocks the release channels

steps.pump: The pumps, now winning, return calcium to the SR
steps.off: Calcium leaves troponin and tropomyosin covers actin again
steps.relax: Myosin heads stop binding actin and the muscles relax
steps.cool: ATP use and heat production fall

variables.name: Calcium in his muscle fibers’ sarcoplasm
variables.why: With the leak plugged, the pumps return calcium to the SR faster than it escapes, so the sarcoplasm’s calcium falls.

variables.name: Stiffness of his muscles
variables.why: Once calcium leaves troponin, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again. Heads with ATP let go, and none rebind.

variables.name: Heat produced by his muscles
variables.why: With the myosin heads idle and the pumps no longer fighting a leak, far less ATP is split, so less heat is released and his temperature can come down.

scenarios.title: ATP runs out after death
scenarios.misconception: rigor mortis is a strong contraction
scenarios.setup: A few hours after death, ATP in the muscle fibers has run out. Predict the changes, compared with a living, relaxed muscle.
scenarios.start: Circulation stops, and the fibers can no longer make ATP

steps.pumps: The SR calcium pumps stop, and membranes grow leaky
steps.leak: Calcium leaks into the sarcoplasm, binds troponin and uncovers actin
steps.bind: Myosin heads bind actin and complete their power stroke
steps.lock: With no ATP to bind, no head can let go
steps.stiff: Locked cross-bridges bolt the thick and thin filaments together

variables.name: Calcium pumped into the SR
variables.why: Each SR calcium pump is an ATPase that splits ATP to move calcium. With no ATP, the pumps stop.

variables.name: Number of cross-bridges attached
variables.why: Calcium seeping out of the SR and in from outside uncovers the binding sites, so the heads bind actin, as they would in a contraction.

variables.name: Myosin heads letting go of actin
variables.why: A head lets go only when a new ATP binds it. With none left, every attached head stays attached.

variables.name: Resistance of the muscles to being stretched
variables.why: Filaments bolted together cannot slide past each other, so joints are fixed in place. The muscle is stiff, not pulling hard: rigor develops little force of its own.

scenarios.title: Calcium stays high, ATP plentiful
scenarios.misconception: any muscle that cannot relax is in rigor
scenarios.setup: In a living fiber with plenty of ATP, calcium in the sarcoplasm stays high because the SR calcium pumps have been blocked. Predict the changes, compared with a fiber whose pumps work.
scenarios.start: Calcium stays bound to troponin

steps.open: Tropomyosin stays off the binding sites on actin
steps.atp: ATP binds each head after its stroke, and the head lets go
steps.cycle: Heads recock, rebind farther along and pull again

variables.name: Binding sites on actin left uncovered
variables.why: Calcium on troponin keeps tropomyosin rolled into the groove, so the sites stay open to myosin.

variables.name: Cross-bridge cycling
variables.why: Both conditions for cycling hold: the sites are uncovered and ATP is available to release and recock each head.

variables.name: Time the fiber stays contracted
variables.why: Relaxation needs calcium to leave troponin, and the pumps that would lower calcium are blocked.

variables.name: Heads locked on actin as in rigor
variables.why: Rigor needs a lack of ATP. Here every head can still bind ATP and let go, so the heads keep cycling instead of locking. This is a sustained contraction, not rigor.

scenarios.title: From 2 to 80 stimuli per second
scenarios.misconception: a stronger contraction needs a bigger calcium release per action potential
scenarios.setup: A researcher raises the rate at which she stimulates a single muscle fiber from 2 per second to 80 per second. Predict the changes.
scenarios.start: Action potentials arrive every 12.5 ms instead of every 500 ms

steps.gap: A new action potential arrives before the last pulse of calcium has been pumped back
steps.same: Each action potential is all-or-none and releases about the same pulse of calcium
steps.high: Calcium in the cytosol stays high
steps.norelax: The fiber has no time to relax between stimuli
steps.taut: Cross-bridges keep cycling long enough to pull the elastic parts fully taut

variables.name: Calcium released by each action potential
variables.why: The fiber’s action potential is all-or-none, and each one opens the release channels the same way. What changes is how often the pulses come.

variables.name: Average calcium level in the cytosol
variables.why: At 80 per second the pumps cannot clear one pulse before the next arrives, so calcium stays high.

variables.name: Relaxation between contractions
variables.why: With calcium never falling back to rest, troponin stays switched on and the fiber cannot relax between stimuli.

variables.name: Peak tension
variables.why: Sustained calcium keeps cross-bridges pulling until the elastic parts are fully taut. The twitches fuse into complete tetanus, several times the tension of one twitch.

scenarios.title: From a mug to a full kettle
scenarios.misconception: a muscle pulls harder by making each fiber contract harder
scenarios.setup: You lift a mug, then lift a full kettle with the same arm. Predict how the muscle that bends your elbow changes for the kettle, compared with the mug.
scenarios.start: The load on your forearm is much larger

steps.drive: The brain and spinal cord drive the motor neurons harder
steps.large: By the size principle, larger motor units join once the small ones are active
steps.rate: Each active motor unit fires faster, moving toward tetanus

variables.name: Number of active motor units
variables.why: Recruitment is the main way to raise force: more motor neurons reach threshold and each brings its whole set of fibers.

variables.name: Average size of the motor units that are firing
variables.why: Small motor neurons reach threshold first. Only a stronger drive brings in the large units, each adding a big step of force.

variables.name: Firing rate of each active motor unit
variables.why: Faster firing lets calcium stay high between action potentials, so each unit’s twitches sum toward tetanus.

variables.name: Calcium released per action potential in one fiber
variables.why: A fiber’s action potential is all-or-none, so each one releases the same pulse of calcium. Force rises through more units and faster firing, not a bigger response per action potential.

scenarios.title: Stimulated while overstretched
scenarios.misconception: a stretched muscle always pulls harder
scenarios.setup: A muscle fiber is stretched to 160 percent of its resting sarcomere length and then stimulated into tetanus. Predict the changes, compared with stimulating it at its resting length.
scenarios.start: The thin filaments are pulled out almost to the ends of the thick filaments

steps.overlap: Thick and thin filaments overlap much less
steps.heads: Few myosin heads can reach actin

variables.name: Overlap of thick and thin filaments
variables.why: Stretching slides the thin filaments out along the thick ones, leaving only a short zone where they overlap.

variables.name: Cross-bridges that can form at once
variables.why: A myosin head can bind only where a thin filament lies beside it, so less overlap means fewer cross-bridges.

variables.name: Active tension the fiber produces
variables.why: Tension is the sum of attached cross-bridges pulling. At 160 percent it falls to a small fraction of maximum, and at about 170 percent it reaches zero.

scenarios.title: The end of an all-out 400 m run
scenarios.misconception: ATP runs out in hard exercise
scenarios.setup: A student runs 400 meters as fast as she can, which takes about a minute. Predict the changes in her leg muscles at the finish, compared with rest.
scenarios.start: Her leg fibers spend ATP many times faster than at rest

steps.cp: Creatine kinase remakes ATP from creatine phosphate in the first seconds
steps.gly: Glycolysis speeds up and supplies much of the ATP
steps.lac: Pyruvate is made faster than the mitochondria take it in, so it becomes lactate
steps.glycogen: Glycolysis runs on glycogen stored in the fibers
steps.remake: The three systems remake ATP almost as fast as it is spent

variables.name: Creatine phosphate in the fibers
variables.why: Creatine phosphate is spent in the first seconds to remake ATP, and it is not rebuilt until she rests.

variables.name: Lactate in the fibers
variables.why: Converting pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+, which glycolysis needs to keep running at this pace.

variables.name: Muscle glycogen
variables.why: Glycolysis draws mainly on glycogen in the working fibers, and it is wasteful, so the store drops quickly.

variables.name: ATP in the fibers
variables.why: It falls only modestly, to roughly three quarters of its resting level, far less than creatine phosphate, because ATP is remade almost as fast as it is spent.

scenarios.title: A 30-second sprint, then rest
scenarios.misconception: the extra breathing after exercise only pays back lactic acid
scenarios.setup: A cyclist sprints all-out for 30 seconds, then sits still for 10 minutes. Predict the changes in her leg muscles during the sprint, and then during recovery.

stages.label: At the end of the sprint
stages.prompt: At the end of the 30-second sprint, compared with rest.
stages.start: Her leg fibers spend ATP at a very high rate

steps.cp: Creatine phosphate hands its phosphate to ADP
steps.gly: Glycolysis outpaces the mitochondria, making lactate
steps.mb: Myoglobin gives up its oxygen as oxygen inside the fibers falls
steps.o2: Aerobic respiration climbs and oxygen use rises

variables.name: Creatine phosphate
variables.why: Creatine phosphate is the fastest source of new ATP, and it is used up within seconds of all-out work.

variables.name: Lactate in the fibers
variables.why: Thirty seconds in, glycolysis supplies a large share of the ATP and makes pyruvate faster than the mitochondria can use it.

variables.name: Oxygen held by myoglobin
variables.why: Myoglobin binds oxygen tightly and releases it only when oxygen in the fiber falls very low, as it does during hard contractions.

variables.name: Oxygen use by the leg muscles
variables.why: All three systems run from the first second, and the aerobic share grows as the sprint goes on.

stages.label: During 10 minutes of rest
