stages.prompt: Over the first 10 minutes of rest, compared with the end of the sprint.
stages.start: ATP demand falls back toward rest, but the stores are depleted

steps.epoc: Extra oxygen keeps aerobic respiration running above resting levels
steps.rebuild: Creatine kinase uses ATP from the mitochondria to rebuild creatine phosphate
steps.reload: Oxygen from the blood reloads myoglobin
steps.clear: Lactate leaves the fibers and is burned or made into glucose

variables.name: Creatine phosphate
variables.why: The creatine kinase reaction runs backward at rest, so about half the store returns in 30 seconds and nearly all within a few minutes.

variables.name: Oxygen held by myoglobin
variables.why: With oxygen use falling and blood still flowing fast, oxygen in the fibers rises and myoglobin refills.

variables.name: Lactate in the fibers
variables.why: Lactate is a fuel, not a waste: resting fibers and heart muscle burn it, and the liver turns it into glucose.

variables.name: Oxygen use
variables.why: It falls from its peak but stays above resting for minutes. That excess post-exercise oxygen consumption pays for rebuilding the stores and the other costs of recovery.

scenarios.title: Mile 20 of a marathon on no food
scenarios.misconception: hitting the wall means the muscles have run out of ATP
scenarios.setup: A runner who has eaten nothing during a marathon suddenly slows sharply at about mile 20. Predict the changes in her leg muscles, compared with mile 10.
scenarios.start: Her muscle glycogen is nearly used up

steps.glycogen: Little glycogen is left to feed glycolysis and aerobic respiration
steps.fat: Fatty acids become the main fuel
steps.slow: Burning fat alone cannot remake ATP fast enough for her pace
steps.atp: Force falls before ATP can fall far

variables.name: Share of ATP made from fatty acids
variables.why: With glycogen gone, the fibers lean on fatty acids from fat stored in and around them.

variables.name: Pace she can hold
variables.why: Fatty acids supply ATP more slowly than glucose does, so the fibers cannot keep up with her race pace. Runners call this hitting the wall.

variables.name: Glycogen in her leg muscles
variables.why: Hours of running have drawn on the glycogen stored in her fibers, and she has eaten nothing to spare it.

variables.name: ATP in her fibers
variables.why: Fatigue slows the fibers before ATP can fall far. If ATP did run out, the heads could not let go of actin and the muscle would lock rigid.

scenarios.title: Marathon pace, then a sprint to the line
scenarios.misconception: the same fibers do all the work at every intensity
scenarios.setup: A runner has held marathon pace for hours, then breaks into an all-out sprint for the finish line. Predict the changes in her leg muscles during the sprint, compared with marathon pace.
scenarios.start: Her leg muscles must produce near-maximal force

steps.drive: Her motor neurons are driven much harder
steps.fg: By the size principle, the large motor units, made of fast glycolytic fibers, join in
steps.gly: Fast glycolytic fibers make their ATP mainly by glycolysis
steps.lac: Glycolysis outruns the mitochondria, so lactate is made
steps.tire: Glycogen falls and phosphate builds up quickly in these fibers

variables.name: Fast glycolytic fibers working
variables.why: At marathon pace, small motor units of slow oxidative fibers do most of the work. Only near-maximal force brings in the largest units.

variables.name: Rate of anaerobic glycolysis
variables.why: The newly recruited fibers have few mitochondria and plenty of glycolytic enzymes, and every working fiber’s ATP demand rises steeply.

variables.name: Lactate production
variables.why: Pyruvate from fast glycolysis outpaces the mitochondria and is turned into lactate, regenerating NAD+.

variables.name: Share of ATP from aerobic respiration
variables.why: Aerobic respiration keeps running, but glycolysis now supplies a much bigger share of a far larger total.

variables.name: How long she can hold this pace
variables.why: Fast glycolytic fibers fatigue within a minute or two, so the sprint cannot last the way the steady pace did.

scenarios.title: Eight weeks of endurance running
scenarios.misconception: training changes how many muscle fibers you have
scenarios.setup: A previously inactive adult runs 30 minutes a day, five days a week, for eight weeks. Predict the changes in his leg muscles, compared with before training.
scenarios.start: His leg fibers repeatedly work hard aerobically

steps.mito: Fibers build more mitochondria and aerobic enzymes
steps.lowo2: Low oxygen and fast blood flow during each session release VEGF
steps.shift: Fast glycolytic fibers take on the properties of fast oxidative fibers
steps.count: Adult skeletal muscle adds few if any fibers

variables.name: Mitochondria per fiber
variables.why: Repeated aerobic work stimulates each fiber to build more mitochondria, so it can make more ATP with oxygen.

variables.name: Capillaries around each fiber
variables.why: VEGF makes the endothelial cells of nearby capillaries divide and sprout, shortening the diffusion distance for oxygen.

variables.name: Myoglobin content
variables.why: More myoglobin stores and shuttles more oxygen from the fiber surface to its mitochondria.

variables.name: Proportion of fibers with fast glycolytic properties
variables.why: Training shifts fast glycolytic fibers toward fast oxidative ones; conversion between slow and fast types is small in adults.

variables.name: Total number of fibers in the muscle
variables.why: Training changes what each fiber is like, not how many there are.

scenarios.title: Six weeks in a cast
scenarios.misconception: a muscle shrinks because it loses fibers
scenarios.setup: A soccer player’s lower leg is in a cast for six weeks. Predict the changes in his calf muscle, compared with the other leg.
scenarios.start: His calf muscle is used far less than usual

steps.break: Protein is broken down faster than it is made
steps.myo: Each fiber loses myofibrils and gets thinner

variables.name: Myofibrils per fiber
variables.why: Disuse tips the balance toward breaking down actin, myosin and other proteins, so fibers lose myofibrils.

variables.name: Diameter of each fiber
variables.why: Myofibrils fill most of a fiber, so losing them shrinks its diameter. That is disuse atrophy.

variables.name: Number of fibers in the muscle
variables.why: The fibers shrink but survive, and they rebuild their myofibrils once the leg is used again.

scenarios.title: The nerve to a muscle is cut
scenarios.misconception: a muscle with no nerve supply atrophies no more than one kept still in a cast
scenarios.setup: A deep cut severs the nerve to a man’s forearm muscles, and the axons do not regrow. Predict the changes in those muscles over the following months, compared with a forearm kept in a cast for the same time.
scenarios.start: The fibers receive no action potentials at all

steps.silent: No ACh is released at any end plate
steps.none: The fibers never contract, not even with low-level activity
steps.replace: Over months to years, fibers are replaced by fat and connective tissue

variables.name: Voluntary contraction of the muscles
variables.why: A skeletal fiber contracts only when its motor neuron tells it to. With the axons cut, no command arrives.

variables.name: Severity of atrophy
variables.why: A muscle in a cast still gets some action potentials; a muscle that has lost its motor neurons gets none, so it wastes far more.

variables.name: Muscle fibers remaining after many months
variables.why: Unless the axons regrow, the fibers are gradually replaced by fat and connective tissue. Disuse atrophy, by contrast, reverses when the limb is used again.

scenarios.title: A drug blocks myosin light-chain kinase
scenarios.misconception: smooth muscle is switched on by troponin, as skeletal muscle is
scenarios.setup: An experimental drug blocks myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) in a strip of intestine wall, which is then stimulated. Predict the changes, compared with a strip without the drug.
scenarios.start: MLCK cannot be switched on

steps.entry: Depolarization still opens calcium channels, and calcium enters
steps.nophos: Calcium–calmodulin cannot activate the blocked kinase, so no phosphate is put on the myosin heads
steps.nocycle: Unphosphorylated heads do not bind actin and cycle

variables.name: Calcium entering the fibers
variables.why: The drug acts on a step after calcium entry, so the calcium channels still open when the fibers depolarize.

variables.name: Calcium bound to calmodulin
variables.why: Calmodulin is smooth muscle’s calcium sensor and still binds the calcium that arrives. The block is on the enzyme it would switch on.

variables.name: Phosphorylated myosin heads
variables.why: MLCK is the enzyme that moves a phosphate from ATP onto each myosin head. Blocked, it phosphorylates none.

variables.name: Force of contraction
variables.why: In smooth muscle the on switch is on myosin. Without phosphate, the heads cannot cycle, so the strip barely contracts despite the calcium.

scenarios.title: A calcium channel blocker in artery walls
scenarios.misconception: blocking calcium entry would weaken skeletal muscle as much as smooth muscle
scenarios.setup: Mrs. Dube takes a drug that blocks voltage-gated calcium channels in the sarcolemma of the smooth muscle in her artery walls. Predict the changes in that smooth muscle, and in her skeletal muscles, compared with before the drug.
scenarios.start: Less calcium enters her arterial smooth muscle fibers from the extracellular fluid

steps.lessca: Calcium in the smooth muscle cytosol rises less
steps.cam: Less calcium–calmodulin forms, so less MLCK is active
steps.relax: Fewer myosin heads are phosphorylated, and the muscle relaxes
steps.sr: Skeletal fibers take their contraction calcium from the SR, released by voltage alone

variables.name: Calcium in her arterial smooth muscle cytosol
variables.why: Smooth muscle takes much of its calcium from outside the cell through these channels, so blocking them lowers it.

variables.name: Tension in her artery walls
variables.why: With less calcium–calmodulin, MLCK phosphorylates fewer heads and myosin phosphatase wins, so fewer cross-bridges cycle.

variables.name: Diameter of her arteries
variables.why: Relaxed smooth muscle in the wall lets the vessel widen: vasodilation.

variables.name: Strength of her skeletal muscle contractions
variables.why: A skeletal fiber’s voltage sensor pulls its SR release channel open directly, and its calcium comes from inside the fiber, so the drug leaves it unaffected.

scenarios.title: An artery wall enters the latch state
scenarios.misconception: holding tension always costs as much ATP as building it
scenarios.setup: After a period of contraction, calcium in an artery’s smooth muscle falls partway, and myosin phosphatase removes phosphate from heads that are still attached to actin. Predict the changes as the fiber enters the latch state.
scenarios.start: Calcium falls partway, and heads lose their phosphate while still attached

steps.kinase: Less calcium–calmodulin forms, so less MLCK is active
steps.latch: Dephosphorylated heads stay attached, detaching and reattaching very slowly
steps.cheap: Each slow cycle still splits one ATP, but cycles are rare
steps.hold: Attached latch-bridges keep holding the thin filaments

variables.name: MLCK activity
variables.why: MLCK needs calcium–calmodulin to work, and the lower calcium makes less of it.

variables.name: Rate of cross-bridge cycling
variables.why: A head that loses its phosphate while bound does not let go at the normal rate; it becomes a latch-bridge.

variables.name: ATP used per second
variables.why: Slow cycling means few ATP split per second, often under a tenth of what skeletal muscle would need for the same force.

variables.name: Tension in the vessel wall
variables.why: The latch-bridges stay attached and keep holding the filaments, so tension stays close to its level before calcium fell, for hours.

scenarios.title: The bladder fills over three hours
scenarios.misconception: pressure in a hollow organ always rises as it fills
scenarios.setup: Mr. Yusuf’s urinary bladder slowly fills from 50 mL to 400 mL over three hours. Predict the changes in its wall, compared with when it held 50 mL.
scenarios.start: Urine slowly stretches the smooth muscle of the bladder wall

steps.stretch: The wall is stretched to several times its resting size
steps.jump: Each bit of stretch raises tension in the wall at first
steps.settle: Filaments and cross-bridges rearrange, and tension falls back at the new length
steps.ready: The fibers can still produce force at the longer length

variables.name: Length of the smooth muscle fibers in the wall
variables.why: The wall stretches to hold the extra volume, so its fibers are much longer.

variables.name: Pressure inside the bladder
variables.why: Stress-relaxation lets the wall’s tension fall back after each stretch, so pressure barely rises as the bladder fills slowly.

variables.name: Force the wall can produce when he empties it
variables.why: Thin filaments can slide along the whole length of each thick filament, so smooth muscle produces force over a wide range of lengths and the full bladder still contracts strongly.

scenarios.title: Blood flow stops to part of the heart wall
scenarios.misconception: heart muscle can switch to anaerobic glycolysis and keep beating
scenarios.setup: During a heart attack, a clot stops blood flow to part of the heart wall. Follow the cardiac muscle in that region over the first minute and then after half an hour.

stages.label: The first minute
stages.prompt: About a minute after flow stops, compared with before.
stages.start: No oxygen reaches the cardiac muscle fibers in the region

steps.aerobic: Aerobic respiration, the fibers’ main source of ATP, stops
steps.little: The fibers have little capacity for anaerobic glycolysis
steps.stop: ATP supply falls, and the fibers stop contracting

variables.name: ATP made by aerobic respiration in the region
variables.why: Cardiac fibers are packed with mitochondria and depend on oxygen from the blood, which has stopped arriving.

variables.name: Contraction of the fibers in the region
variables.why: With little glycolytic capacity to fall back on, the fibers cannot keep up their ATP supply, and they stop contracting within about a minute.

variables.name: Contraction of heart muscle whose blood flow is intact
variables.why: Other regions still receive oxygen and keep making ATP aerobically, so they keep beating.

stages.label: After half an hour
stages.prompt: About 30 minutes after flow stops, if it has not been restored, compared with the first minute.
stages.start: The fibers in the region have gone without oxygen for 20 to 30 minutes

steps.leak: Dying fibers leak their contents, including cardiac troponin, into the blood
steps.norepair: Dead cardiac fibers are not replaced by new muscle

variables.name: Dead cardiac muscle fibers in the region
variables.why: Cardiac muscle stops contracting within a minute but begins to die only after 20 to 30 minutes without flow, which is why restoring flow quickly saves muscle.

variables.name: Cardiac troponin in the blood
variables.why: Cardiac troponin differs slightly from the skeletal form, so a blood test that finds it shows heart muscle has been damaged.

variables.name: Force this part of the wall can produce later
variables.why: Heart muscle does not rebuild itself the way skeletal muscle does with its stem cells, so fibers that die leave that part of the wall weaker.

scenarios.title: A loop of intestine cut off from its nerves
scenarios.misconception: smooth muscle contracts only when nerves tell it to
scenarios.setup: A surgeon removes a short loop of intestine and places it in warm, oxygenated fluid, cut off from all nerves from the brain and spinal cord. Predict the changes in its wall over the next hour, compared with in the body.
scenarios.start: No signals arrive from the brain and spinal cord

steps.pace: Pacesetter cells keep producing slow, spontaneous waves
steps.gap: Action potentials spread from fiber to fiber through gap junctions

variables.name: Rhythmic contractions of the wall
variables.why: Single-unit smooth muscle is driven by its own pacesetter cells, not by commands from the brain, so the rhythm continues.

variables.name: Coordination of neighboring fibers
variables.why: Gap junctions link the fibers into a sheet, so each wave still spreads and the sheet contracts together.
